Giza Governorate is one of Egypt's governorates. It is located in the center of the country, on the west bank of the Nile River, opposite Cairo. The capital of the governorate is the city of Giza. It includes land on the left bank of the Nile Valley near Giza and also covers a large area of Egypt's western desert, including Bahariya Oasis. On April 14, 2011, the 6th of October Governorate joined Giza Governorate. The Giza Governorate is known for the Great Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza.

José Vítor Roque Jr., also known as Roque Júnior, was born on August 31, 1976, in Santa Rita do Sapucaí. He was a defender who played association football. Roque Júnior last played for Ituano Futebol Clube. He represented Brazil 48 times and was part of the team that won the 2002 World Cup.

In computer architecture, 64-bit integers, memory addresses, or data units are 64 bits wide. A 64-bit CPU and ALU are based on registers, address buses, or data buses that are 64 bits wide. 64-bit microcomputers use 64-bit microprocessors. From a software perspective, 64-bit computing involves using code with 64-bit virtual memory addresses. However, some 64-bit instruction sets only support up to 48 bits of virtual address, like x86-64 and armv8. 64-bit processors have been used in supercomputers since the 1970s and in workstations and servers since the early 1990s. In 2003, x86-64 and PowerPC G5 processors were introduced in mainstream personal computers, and 64-bit ARM processors were introduced in smartphones and tablets in 2012, starting with the iPhone 5s in 2013. A 64-bit register can hold any of over 18 quintillion different values. The range of integer values stored in 64 bits depends on the representation used. With unsigned binary numbers, the range is 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. With two's complement, the range is -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. Thus, a 64-bit memory address allows direct access to 2 bytes (16 exabytes) of memory. A "64-bit computer architecture" usually has 64-bit wide integer and address processor registers, supporting 64-bit data types and addresses. However, a CPU might have different-sized external data or address buses, even larger than the registers, like the 32-bit Pentium with a 64-bit data bus. The term can also refer to the size of low-level data types, such as 64-bit floating-point numbers.
La Chapelle is a town in the Allier department, which is in central France.
Gorno is a town in the Moesa region of the Italian-speaking part of the Swiss canton of Graubünden. On January 1, 2017, the towns of Leggia and Verdabbio joined to form the town of Gorno.

La Riviera is a census-designated place in Sacramento County, California. It is part of the Sacramento–Arden-Arcade–Roseville metropolitan area. The population grew from 10,273 in 2000 to 10,802 in 2010. La Riviera is mainly a residential neighborhood. It is situated between the American River to the north and Highway 50 to the south.

Glenn Howerton, born on April 13, 1976, is an American actor, producer, screenwriter, and director. He was born in Japan. He is famous for playing Dennis Reynolds in the TV show "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia," where he also writes and is an executive producer. He also acted as Jack Griffin in "A.P. Bio." Additionally, he had the lead role in a short-lived TV show called "That '80s Show."

Birdbrook is a village and civil parish in Essex, England. It is about southeast of Haverhill, Suffolk. The village is 34 km (21 miles) north of Chelmsford, the county town. Birdbrook is part of the Braintree district and the Saffron Walden parliamentary constituency. It is in a group of parishes called Bumpsteads and Upper Colne. The village is 93 meters above sea level. In 2011, the population was 397. There is a pub called "The Plough" and a church named "St Augustine of Canterbury." Near Birdbrook, Moyns Park, a special Elizabethan house, is said to be where Ian Fleming finished writing his book "From Russia, with Love."

The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) was a plan to protect the United States from nuclear attacks. President Ronald Reagan announced it on March 23, 1983, as he didn't like the idea of mutually assured destruction ( MAD ). He wanted scientists and engineers to develop a system that would make nuclear weapons useless. The SDI Organization was created in 1984 to oversee the development. Many advanced weapon ideas were studied, like lasers and space-based missiles. They needed sensors, command and control systems, and high-performance computers to work together. Several of these ideas were tested in the late 1980s, and some work continues today. Under the SDI's science and technology office, run by physicist Dr. James Ianson, most funding went to basic research at labs, universities, and companies. This helped fund important research in fields like high-energy physics, supercomputing, and advanced materials. This funding indirectly supported other scientists' work and would have been hard to get outside the defense budget. In 1987, the American Physical Society said the technologies were far away from use, needing at least a decade more research. SDI's budget was cut. By the late 1980s, the plan focused on "Brilliant Pebbles," small orbiting missiles, to reduce costs. SDI was controversial, seen as threatening MAD and possibly starting a new arms race. As the Cold War ended and nuclear weapons were reduced, support for SDI fell. It officially ended in 1993, when the Bill Clinton administration redirected efforts to theatre ballistic missiles and changed the agency to the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization (BMDO).

Michael Joseph Mansfield, born on March 16, 1903, and passed away on October 5, 2001, was an American politician and diplomat. A member of the Democratic Party, he worked as a US Representative from 1943 to 1953 and as a US Senator from 1953 to 1977, representing Montana. He was the longest-serving Senate Majority Leader, serving from 1961 to 1977. During his time, he helped pass Great Society programs in the Senate and criticized the Vietnam War as a mistake near its end, after supporting it for many years. Born in Brooklyn, Mansfield grew up in Great Falls, Montana. During World War I, he joined the US Navy by lying about his age. After the war, he taught history and political science at the University of Montana. In 1942, he was elected to the House of Representatives and worked on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs during World War II. In 1952, Mansfield beat the current senator Zales Ecton to win a seat in the Senate. He was the Senate Majority Whip from 1957 to 1961. When Lyndon B. Johnson left the Senate to become Vice President, Mansfield became the Senate Majority Leader. In the later part of his career, he opposed increasing the Vietnam War and supported President Nixon's plan to replace American soldiers with Vietnamese forces. After retiring from the Senate in 1977, Mansfield served as the US Ambassador to Japan from 1977 to 1988. For his service, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian honor. Mansfield is the longest-serving American ambassador to Japan. After his ambassadorship, he worked as a senior adviser on East Asian affairs for Goldman Sachs, a Wall Street investment firm.

Jacques Marquette, a Jesuit missionary, lived from June 1, 1637, to May 18, 1675. He was sometimes called Père Marquette or James Marquette. Marquette was from France and came to America. He helped found Michigan's first European settlement, called Sault Ste. Marie. Later, he founded St. Ignace, Michigan. In 1673, Marquette, along with Louis Jolliet, who was born near Quebec City, was the first European to explore and map the northern part of the Mississippi River valley.

Ruy Alexandre Guerra Coelho Pereira, born on August 22, 1931, is a film director and screenwriter from Portugal and Brazil. He was born in Lourenço Marques, which is now called Maputo, in Mozambique. At that time, Mozambique was still a Portuguese colony.

Tim Francis, born on May 1, 1928, and passed away on January 2, 2016, was a New Zealand diplomat. He worked as the country's permanent representative to the United Nations from 1978 to 1982. From 1988 to 1991, he was the ambassador to the United States. Between 1984 and 1988, he served as the administrator of Tokelau.

Arthur Garfunkel, born on November 5, 1941, is an American singer, poet, and actor. He is famous for working with Paul Simon as part of the folk rock duo Simon & Garfunkel. As a solo artist, Garfunkel had many hits. His songs reached the top 10, 20, and 40 charts. He also had 14 adult contemporary top 30 songs and five number one hits on the adult contemporary charts. He had two UK number one songs and won a People's Choice Award. Garfunkel has won eight Grammy Awards, including a lifetime achievement award. In 1990, he and Simon were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2008, Garfunkel was ranked 86th in Rolling Stone magazine's list of the "100 greatest singers of all time."

La Bañeza is a town in the province of León, Castile and León, Spain. In 2010, it had 11,050 people. It is the capital of Tierra de La Bañeza. During Roman times, this area was part of Conventus Asturum. La Bañeza was founded in the 9th century by Count Gatón. He built it from two villages, San Pedro de Périz and Bani Eiza. In the late 19th century, La Bañeza became a city when Queen Regent Maria Cristina of Austria gave it the title. The town is known for its churches, like San Salvador and Santa María. It also has big celebrations, like the carnival, Holy Week, and August festivities with a motorcycle race. The motorcycle race is called the La Bañeza Grand Prix. The town has many things to see and do, making it a good place to visit.

The Germanic languages are part of the Indo-European family and are spoken by about 515 million people in Europe, North America, Oceania, and southern Africa. The most widely spoken Germanic language, English, has around 2 billion speakers. All Germanic languages come from a common ancestor called Proto-Germanic, which was spoken in Scandinavia during the Iron Age. West Germanic languages include English, German, and Dutch. English is spoken by 360-400 million people, German by over 100 million, and Dutch by 24 million. Other West Germanic languages are Afrikaans, Low German, Yiddish, Scots, Limburgish, and Frisian languages. The main North Germanic languages are Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish, spoken by about 20 million people in the Nordic countries, with 5 million as second language speakers. They are influenced by Middle Low German. Faroese and Icelandic are more conservative and have limited mutual understanding with other North Germanic languages. East Germanic languages, like Gothic, Burgundian, and Vandalic, are now extinct. The last, Crimean Gothic, disappeared in the late 18th century. Today, there are 48 living Germanic languages, with 41 in the West and 6 in the North. Riograndenser Hunsrückisch German is considered a dialect by linguists. During and after the Migration Period, many Germanic languages disappeared, especially the East Germanic ones. Some West Germanic languages, like Lombardic, also vanished. The German language lost some dialects after World War II, and standard German is increasingly used. Proto-Germanic, the common ancestor of all Germanic languages, was spoken around 500 BC in Scandinavia. It had unique linguistic features, notably Grimm's Law. Early Germanic languages became part of history when Germanic tribes moved south from Scandinavia around 200 BC, settling in northern Germany and southern Denmark.

Millry is a town in Washington County, Alabama, United States. It became a town in 1947. In 1950, it had 546 people. In 2000, there were 615 people. By 2010, the number of people had gone down to 546.

György Sándor Ligeti, born on May 28, 1923, and died on June 12, 2006, was a Hungarian-Austrian composer of contemporary classical music. He was called "one of the most important avant-garde composers" and "one of the most innovative and influential figures of his time." Ligeti was born in Transylvania, Romania, and lived in the Hungarian People's Republic before moving to Austria in 1956. He became an Austrian citizen in 1968. In 1973, he became a professor at the Hamburg Hochschule für Musik und Theater, where he taught until 1989. He faced restrictions in his musical style in communist Hungary but could fully explore avant-garde music in the West. After working with electronic music in Cologne, he made a big breakthrough with works like "Atmosphères," which used a technique called micropolyphony. His later works focused more on polyrhythm. Ligeti is famous for his music used in film soundtracks, although he didn't write directly for films. His work was used in Stanley Kubrick's films, including "2001: A Space Odyssey."

Durrës is the second largest city in Albania and the capital of the Durrës county. It is located on a flat plain by the southeastern Adriatic Sea. Its climate is like the Mediterranean with warm summers and mild winters. Durrës was founded by Greek colonists from Corinth and Corfu around 700 BC and named Epidamnos. Later, it was called Dyrrachium. It grew important when it became part of the Roman and Byzantine empires. The Via Egnatia, an ancient road, began in Durrës and went to Constantinople. In the Middle Ages, Durrës was ruled by Bulgaria, Venice, and the Ottoman Empire. After Albania became independent, Durrës was the capital for a short time. Then, it was taken by Italy and Nazi Germany. During communism, the city grew in population and economy. Durrës has a big port that connects to Italy and nearby countries. One of its main attractions is the amphitheater, which can hold up to 20,000 people and is the largest in the Balkans.

Raise Your Glass" is a song by American singer Pink. It is from her first greatest hits album, "Greatest Hits... So Far!!" (2010). Pink wrote the song with Max Martin and Karl "Shellback" Schuster, who also produced it. This song celebrates Pink's first decade in the music industry since 2000 and is dedicated to her fans. It was released as the first single from the album on October 5, 2010, by Jive Records. The song did very well, getting good reviews from music critics and becoming Pink's third number-one single in the United States. In 2011, it was ranked 13th on the "Top 40 Year End Chart." The song was also used in ads for the 2011 film "Bridesmaids" and in trailers for the films "What's Your Number?" and "New Year's Eve.

During 1833-1836 and from 1845 until 2010, when the Kallikratis reform was implemented, the prefectures were Greece's main administrative units. They no longer exist and have been mostly replaced by regional units. The United Nations calls them departments. Prefectures were second-level local government units, grouped into 13 regions or, before 1987, 10 geographical departments. They were divided into provinces and included many communities and municipalities. In 1994, prefectures became self-governing, and elections were held for the first time. There were 51 prefectures, with Attica, home to over a third of Greece's population, further divided into four prefecture-level administrations. Also, there were three super-prefectures controlling two or more prefectures. With the Kallikratis reform in 2011, prefectures were abolished, replaced by regional units, especially in the mainland, which took over their administrative role.
cotton is a commune in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.

A listed building is one that is on a special list maintained by historic England in England, Historic Environment Scotland in Scotland, the Welsh Government in Wales, and the Northern Ireland Environment Agency in Northern Ireland. In Ireland, buildings are also listed, but the term "protected structure" is used. Without permission from local planning authorities, you can't change, add to, or demolish a listed building. The government must be informed about work involving demolition. For religious buildings, permission can be easier to get if the religious group has its own approval process. If owners don't repair or maintain their listed buildings, they might face problems. When work is allowed, specific materials and methods are often required. Besides buildings, other structures like bridges, monuments, and even special crossings can be listed. Some ancient and uninhabited sites might be protected differently, and parks and gardens are listed but not legally.

Ah, Wilderness! It's a comedy written by Eugene O'Neill, an American playwright. It premiered on Broadway at the Guild Theatre on October 2, 1933. Unlike most of O'Neill's plays, this one has a happy ending for the main character and shows a happy family in America from the late 19th century. It's the only well-known comedy by O'Neill. The play did well in its first Broadway production and after that, on tour. It is now a common part of community theater productions.

Mark Dayton, born on January 26, 1947, is an American politician. He was Minnesota's governor from 2011 to 2019. He was also a U.S. senator for Minnesota from 2001 to 2007 and Minnesota's state auditor from 1991 to 1995. Dayton belongs to the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party, which works with the national Democratic Party. He is from Minnesota and is the great-grandson of businessman George Dayton, who started a department store called Dayton's, later part of Target. After graduating from Yale University in 1969, Dayton taught and worked in social services in New York City and Boston. He worked as an aide to U.S. Senator Walter Mondale and Minnesota Governor Rudy Perpich in the 1970s. In 1978, he became the Minnesota Economic Development Commissioner and married Alida Rockefeller Messinger, from the Rockefeller family. Dayton tried to become a U.S. senator in 1982 but lost to David Durenberger. He returned to work for the Perpich administration until 1990 when he was elected state auditor. In 1998, Dayton tried to become governor but lost the Democratic nomination to Hubert Humphrey III. In 2000, he won a U.S. Senate seat, defeating Republican Rod Grams. As a senator, he opposed the Iraq War and introduced a bill to create a Department of Peace. In 2006, he decided not to run for re-election. In 2010, he won the governorship of Minnesota, defeating Republican Tom Emmer. He was re-elected in 2014 but did not seek a third term in 2018, leaving office in January 2019. As governor, Dayton supported same-sex marriage and helped build U.S. Bank Stadium for the Minnesota Vikings.

In music theory, a theoretical key or impossible key is a key with at least one double-flat or double-sharp in its key signature. Double-flats and double-sharps are usually used as accidentals. However, if they are placed in the key signature, the music becomes difficult to read, especially in equal temperament music.

Samurai Champloo is a Japanese anime series. It was created by a team led by director Shinichirō Watanabe, character designer Kazuto Nakazawa, and mechanical designer Mahiro Maeda. Samurai Champloo was Watanabe’s first directorial effort for an anime television series after the popular Cowboy Bebop. The show aired on Fuji TV from May 20, 2004, to March 19, 2005, for a total of 26 episodes. The story takes place in an alternative version of Japan during the Edo period, with a mix of old and modern styles, including hip hop elements. The main characters are Mugen, a free-spirited swordsman, Jin, a calm and serious rōnin, and Fuu, a brave girl searching for a samurai who smells like sunflowers. Samurai Champloo is similar to Watanabe’s other work, Cowboy Bebop. Both are highly praised, mix different types of stories, follow a series of episodes, and use modern music. The series was dubbed in English and released in North America by Geneon Entertainment. Funimation took over after Geneon stopped making new releases. It was also released in the UK by MVM Films and in Australia and New Zealand by Madman Entertainment.

The Panhard VBL, also known as Panhard VBL or VBL, is a French wheeled 4x4 all-terrain vehicle made by Panhard. It comes in different versions. The VBL was created to be as nimble as the Peugeot P4 while also protecting against small arms, artillery fragments, mines, and NBC weapons. It was produced from 1985 to 2010 and has been used by the French army and other armies in Europe, Africa, and Central America during various conflicts since the 1980s.

Carlito's Way is a 1993 American crime movie directed by Brian De Palma. It is based on novels by Judge Edwin Torres, specifically "After Hours." David Koepp wrote the screenplay. Al Pacino, Sean Penn, and Penelope Ann Miller are among the main actors. The movie tells the story of Carlito Brigante, a Puerto Rican criminal played by Al Pacino. Carlito promises to stop his criminal activities and enjoy retirement in a peaceful place. However, his past catches up with him, and he accidentally becomes involved in criminal activities again. The film uses the title "Carlito's Way" to avoid confusion with Martin Scorsese's 1985 film of the same name. It mainly follows "After Hours." Both Sean Penn and Penelope Ann Miller received Golden Globe nominations for their roles. A prequel based on the first novel was released directly to video in 2005.

neurosis is a type of mental disorder causing ongoing distress. It does not involve delusions or hallucinations. In the United States, this term is no longer used by mental health professionals. It was removed from the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders" (DSM) in 1980 when DSM-III was published. Neurosis should not be confused with psychosis, which involves losing touch with reality. Nor should it be confused with neuroticism, a personality trait in the big five personality theory.

Samantha Bee, born on October 25, 1969, is an American-Canadian comedian, writer, producer, political commentator, actress, and TV host. She became famous as a correspondent on "The Daily Show with Jon Stewart" and was the longest-serving regular correspondent there. In 2015, she left the show after 12 years to start her own show, "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." Bee became a U.S. citizen in 2014, keeping her Canadian citizenship. In 2017, she was named one of the 100 most influential people in the world by Time magazine.

Coriolanus is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, likely written between 1605 and 1608. The play is about the life of the Roman leader Caius Marcius Coriolanus. It is one of the last tragedies Shakespeare wrote, along with Antony and Cleopatra. Coriolanus became a famous Roman general after defeating uprisings against Rome. He later tried to become a political leader. However, his personality didn't fit being popular, and he was removed from power. He then worked with others to seek what he wanted. His friendships led to his downfall.

Anil Adhikari, born on May 30, 1987, and passed away on January 14, 2017, was a Nepalese rapper known by his stage name Yama Buddha. He was one of the most famous rappers in Nepal. Some of his popular songs include "Sathi," "Aama," "Aaudai Chhu Ma," "Yo Prasanga," and "Antya Ko Suruwat." Yama Buddha also created and hosted a popular rap battle show called "Raw Barz."

In telecommunications, dirty paper coding (DPC) or Costa precoding is a method to send digital data through a channel with some interference known to the sender. The process involves coding the data to remove the interference. DPC can achieve the maximum channel capacity without needing extra power and without the receiver knowing the interfering signal. The term "dirty paper coding" comes from a comparison by Max Costa. He said it's like writing a message on a paper with random dirt. By covering the dirt and writing clearly, you can still convey the message just as well, even though the reader doesn't know where the dirt is. Here, the paper is the channel, the dirt is interference, the writer is the transmitter, and the reader is the receiver. Note that DPC at the encoder is similar to Wyner-Ziv coding at the decoder in terms of information theory.

An atlas is a group of maps. Traditionally, atlases are books with maps of the world or a region. Today, they can also be in digital or other multimedia forms. Atlases show places and borders. They often include information about politics, society, religion, and the economy. They also provide details about the maps and places.

Humayun Ahmed (born November 13, 1948, died July 19, 2012) was a writer from Bangladesh. He wrote novels, plays, screenplays, and songs. He also taught and was a scholar. His first novel, "Nondito Noroke," came out in 1972 and was his big break. He wrote more than 200 books, and many of them were bestsellers in Bangladesh. His books were very popular at the Ekushey Book Fair in the 1990s and 2000s. He won important awards, including the Bangla Academy Literary Award in 1981 and the Ekushey Padak in 1994 for his work in literature. In the early 1990s, he started making films based on his novels. He made eight films and won six Bangladesh National Film Awards. He had his own movie production company called Nuhash Chalachitra.

Defunctland is a YouTube show that tells the history of closed amusement parks and rides. Created and hosted by Kevin Perjurer, it covers theme parks and attractions from around the world, especially from Disney, Universal, and Six Flags. The show started on February 15, 2017. People like it because it does thorough research and looks good. It now has more than 700,000 people subscribed. The popularity of Defunctland led to two new shows: Debunkedland and DefunctTV. They began in 2018.

Mexican Americans are people with full or partial Mexican background in the United States. As of July 2018, about 11.3% of the U.S. population, or 37 million people, identified as Mexican American. Mexican Americans make up about 62% of all Latinos in the U.S. Many live in the American Southwest, especially in California and Texas. In 2016, Mexicans were 53% of all foreign-born Latinos, and the U.S. has the second-largest Mexican community globally. Mexican American families have lived in the country for at least 15,000 years. Many historically Hispanic populations in the Southwest eventually adopted English. About 10% of current Mexican Americans are descendants of early colonial settlers who became U.S. citizens after 1848. These settlers were initially seen as white but faced discrimination. Large-scale Mexican immigration continued after the 1910 Mexican Revolution. During the Great Depression, many Mexican Americans were deported, affecting about 500,000 to two million people. These deportations violated U.S. immigration laws. The 1960s and 1970s saw the Chicano Movement, with leaders like Dolores Huerta and César Chávez. The Chicano Movement fought for civil rights and inspired the 1965 Delano Grape Strike. Immigration from Mexico increased in the 1980s and 1990s, peaking in the mid-2000s. In 2008, Barack Obama used "yes we can" in his campaign, reflecting the growing Mexican American vote's importance. The Great Recession caused a significant loss of wealth among Mexican Americans. Immigration from Mexico decreased. In 2015, 157,227 Mexicans immigrated to the U.S., and by November 2016, over 1.3 million Mexicans were waiting to immigrate legally.

Louis-Philippe I (born October 6, 1773, died August 26, 1850) was the king of France from 1830 to 1848 and the last king. As Duke of Chartres, he led troops in the revolutionary wars but disagreed with the Republic's decision to execute King Louis XVI. In 1793, he left France for Switzerland after being linked to a plot to bring back the monarchy. His father, Louis-Philippe II, Duke of Orléans (Philippe Égalité), was also in trouble and was killed. Louis-Philippe lived in exile for 21 years until the Bourbon Restoration. In 1830, he became king after his cousin Charles X had to give up power during the July Revolution. His rule, known as the July Monarchy, was run by rich business owners. He followed traditional policies, especially under François Guizot's influence from 1840 to 1848. He also tried to be friends with Britain and expanded France's influence in colonies, like Algeria. As France's economy worsened in 1847, Louis-Philippe lost support and had to step down when the French Revolution of 1848 started. He lived in England for the rest of his life. His followers were called Orléanists, while those who supported the Bourbon family were called Legitimists.

The Orient Express was a long-distance train service created in 1883 by Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits. The train's route and vehicles changed many times. In the past, other routes also used the Orient Express name. Though the original service was just a normal international train, the name became famous for exciting and luxurious journeys. The main cities for the Orient Express were Paris and Constantinople, the original start and end points. This train offered comfort and luxury when traveling was often difficult. In 1977, the Orient Express stopped going to Istanbul. The train that continued to operate was shortened to run from Paris to Bucharest, then to Budapest, and finally to Vienna. It last ran from Paris on June 8, 2007. After that, the service was changed to start from Strasbourg, using a faster train connection. This train was joined by another overnight service from Amsterdam. In December 2009, the Orient Express completely stopped operating. However, a private train called the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, using old carriages, still runs from London to Venice and other places in Europe, including the original Paris to Istanbul route.

The University of Houston (UH) is a big public school in Houston, Texas. It has over 46,000 students and is part of the University of Houston system. UH was first opened in 1927 and covers 667 acres in southeast Houston. It was known as University of Houston–University Park from 1983 to 1991. It's a top research university that does very important work. UH offers many degree programs through 14 academic colleges. It includes special programs in architecture, law, optometry, and pharmacy. Every year, it does $150 million in research and runs over 40 research centers and institutes. Research topics include superconductivity, space, medicine, energy, and AI. Each year, UH gives out over 9,000 degrees. Its graduates number over 260,000. UH's work adds $3 billion to Texas's economy and creates 24,000 jobs. The school has many events, like plays, concerts, lectures, and traditions like Cat's Back, Homecoming, and Frontier Fiesta. Its sports teams, called the Houston Cougars, are in the American Athletic Conference and play in NCAA Division I. The football team often goes to bowl games, and the men's basketball team has been in the NCAA tournament 21 times, including five times in the Final Four. The men's golf team has won 16 national championships, the most in NCAA history.

Ikaalinen is a town in Finland, part of the Pirkanmaa region. It has about 15,000 people and covers 78 square kilometers, with 20% of that water. Neighboring municipalities are Hämeenkyrö, Jämijärvi, Kankaanpää, Parkano, Sastamala, and Ylöjärvi. Ikaalinen is a Finnish-speaking town. Part of the Seitseminen National Park is in Ikaalinen. Ikaalinen is a popular tourist spot. Its spa history goes back to the last century. Traditional music, especially accordion music, is also a part of the town. The beautiful landscape attracts visitors. In recent years, Ikaalinen has grown into a diverse service center with good business, education, and recreation facilities. Today, about 55% of the population works in services, and 15% in agriculture, an important income source. S. Albert Kivinen, a philosophy professor from the University of Helsinki, is a famous local. He's known for his funny horror stories in a special style. His most famous story, "The Midnight Worm in Ikaalinen," is set in his childhood home. Ikaalinen became a municipality in 1641. The market town was founded in 1858. In 1972, the market town and municipality merged, and Ikaalinen became a town in 1977. The town center is near Lake Kyrösjärvi and Highway 3. Major industries include Upofloor, Georgia Pacific Paper, E Avenue, and Katsa.

In 1972, the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) started using the term "after-school special." These were TV films often about important topics, usually shown late afternoon, for school kids, especially teenagers. ABC broadcast these specials 4 to 6 times a year, instead of local shows that were normally on at that time. CBS made its own specials called "CBS Afternoon Playhouse," later "CBS Schoolbreak Special." They also had "Famous Classic Tales," which aired Australian cartoons based on books. NBC had shows called "Special Treat" for after-school viewing. ABC had "ABC After School Special," along with "ABC Saturday Superstar Movie" and "ABC Weekend Special."
Coyolles is a commune in the Aisne department, which is in Hauts-de-France in northern France. Before the French Revolution, Coyolles was the seat of the deanery of the Diocese of Soissons.

Bisma Karisma, born on November 27, 1990, in Bandung, is known as a member of the boy band SM*SH. Before joining SM*SH, she was a national bboy and played the drums, percussion, and sang. In SM*SH, she released two albums and had over forty achievements. Their first album sold more than one million copies in six months and was awarded platinum. In mid-2014, Bisma started his solo career with the single "Lakukanlah," which he wrote himself. In 2016, he was in a TV soap opera called Cinta Cenat Cenut with his SM*SH bandmates. He also became a co-producer, wrote the original soundtrack, and was a main cast member in the show Juara.

"Troublemaker" is a song by English singer Olly Murs. It was released as the first single from his third album, "Right Place Right Time," in 2012. The song features American rapper Flo Rida. Murs, Flo Rida, and others wrote the song, and Steve Robson produced it. It first played on Capital FM radio on October 8, 2012, and was available to download on October 12 in some countries. "Troublemaker" was very successful. It topped the UK singles chart when it came out, and Murs's first single to stay at number one for more than a week. The song was also played at Murs's 2013 concert. As of November 2016, it was Murs's most successful single.
Montord is a town in the Allier region of central France.

Mohammed Aamir Hussain Khan, born on March 14, 1965, is an Indian actor, director, and filmmaker. He has been active in Hindi films for over thirty years and is one of the most popular and influential actors in Indian cinema. Khan is well-known worldwide, especially in India and China, and "Newsweek" has called him the biggest movie star in the world. He has won many awards, including nine Filmfare Awards, four National Film Awards, and an AACTA Award. In 2003, the Government of India honored him with the Padma Shri, and in 2010, he received the Padma Bhushan. In 2017, the Chinese government gave him an honorary title. Khan first appeared as a child actor in his uncle Nasir Hussain's film "Yaadon Ki Baaraat" in 1973. As an adult, he starred in the 1988 film "Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak," which earned him a National Film Award in the special mention category. His performance in "Raakh" (1989) also earned him a National Film Award. In the 1990s, Khan became a leading actor in Hindi cinema. His films "Dil" (1990) and "Raja Hindustani" (1996) were commercially successful, and he won his first Filmfare Award for best actor for "Raja Hindustani." He also starred in the thriller "Sarfarosh" (1999). In 1999, he founded Aamir Khan Productions. His first film, "Lagaan" (2001), was nominated for the Academy Award for best foreign language film and won him a National Film Award for best popular film. It also earned him two more Filmfare Awards: best actor and best film. Khan returned to acting in 2006 with the films "Fanaa" and "Rang De Basanti." He directed "Taare Zameen Par" (2007), a big success that won him Filmfare Awards for best film and best director. His films "Ghajini" (2008), "3 Idiots" (2009), "Dhoom 3" (2013), "PK" (2014), and "Dangal" (2016) were very successful and broke box office records. "Secret Superstar" (2017) was the highest-grossing film with a female lead. Khan won his third best actor award for "Dangal." Khan's films often address social issues in India and combine entertainment with important messages. He is also an activist and has worked on various social causes, sometimes leading to political controversy. He hosted the TV talk show "Satyamev Jayate" to discuss sensitive social issues in India, and his work earned him a place on the "Time" 100 list of influential people. Khan was married to Reena Dutta for fifteen years and later to Kiran Rao. He has three children: two with Dutta and one with Rao through surrogacy.

The corn snake (Pantherophis guttatus) is a non-venomous rat snake found in the southeastern and central United States. It catches small prey by squeezing them. People often kill it because it looks like the venomous copperhead. But corn snakes are harmless and actually help control harmful rodents that can damage crops and spread diseases. They are easy to care for and make good pets due to their calm nature and attractive patterns. Corn snakes get their name from being commonly found near stores with grain, where they eat mice and rats that feed on harvested corn. Some say their belly scales look like corn kernels, but the name helps people identify them.

A Brief History of Time is a popular science book about the universe. It was written by Stephen Hawking, an English physicist, and first published in 1988. Hawking wrote the book for readers who know little about the universe and want to learn new things. In the book, Hawking explains basic ideas like space, time, and the forces that shape the universe, using simple language. He talks about important events in the universe, such as the Big Bang and black holes. Hawking also discusses two main theories used by scientists—general relativity and quantum mechanics—to understand the universe. Finally, he talks about the search for a single theory that can explain everything in the universe. The book became very popular and sold over 25 million copies.

Enzymes are proteins that help speed up chemical reactions. The substances they act on are called substrates, and the products formed are different molecules. Almost all cell processes need enzymes to happen quickly enough for life to continue. Enzymes help with individual steps in metabolic pathways. The study of enzymes is called enzymology. A new area called pseudoenzyme analysis looks at enzymes that lost their ability to catalyze reactions during evolution. Enzymes can speed up over 5,000 types of biochemical reactions. RNA molecules called ribozymes can also act as catalysts. Enzymes are specific because of their unique shapes. Like other catalysts, enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy but do not change the reaction's equilibrium or be used up. Other molecules can affect enzyme activity; inhibitors decrease it, while activators increase it. Some drugs and poisons work by inhibiting enzymes. Enzyme activity drops outside their optimal temperature and pH, and high heat can damage them. Enzymes have various commercial uses, such as in antibiotic production. Household products like some biological washing powders and meat tenderizers use enzymes to break down stains and proteins, respectively.

The Presidio Ahú was a prison in Curitiba, a city in Paraná, Brazil. It was the first prison in Curitiba, opening in 1905. The prison closed in 2006. Now, the site is used for filming movies and TV shows.
Rachel Mary Berkeley Portman, OBE, was born on December 11, 1960. She is an English composer famous for scoring films.
Hetepheres was a queen in Egypt during the fourth dynasty, around 2600 BC.

Dr. Lo Wing-lok was a doctor and politician from Hong Kong. He served as a Legislative Councillor for the medical functional constituency from 2000 to 2004. He was also the vice-chairman of the League of Social Democrats, a pro-democracy group, but left the party in late 2007. Dr. Lo tried to become a Legislative Councillor three times in 2004, 2008, and 2012, but did not win. He passed away in 2015 due to lung cancer.

The following list includes the 194 communes in the Essonne department of France. These communes work together in the following intercommunalities as of 2020.
Cumberland is a city in Cass County, Iowa, United States. It was founded in 1884. In 2010, the population was 262. Cumberland has a sister city called Massena, also in Iowa.

Michael P. Botticelli, born on January 2, 1958, is an American public health official. He served as the director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) from March 2014 until the end of President Obama's term. He took over as acting director after Gil Kerlikowske left. Botticelli was confirmed by the United States Senate in February 2015. Before working at ONDCP, he was in the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. After his ONDCP role ended, he became the executive director of the Grayken Center for Addiction Medicine at Boston Medical Center.

Paul the octopus lived from January 26, 2008, to October 26, 2010. He was used to guess the winners of football matches. His predictions became famous during the 2010 World Cup. During divinations, his keepers would give him two boxes of food. Each box had a flag from one of the teams playing. Paul would eat from the box with the flag he liked. The box he chose was seen as his prediction. He mainly predicted matches involving the German national football team at the Sea Life Centre in Oberhausen, Germany. Paul correctly predicted Germany's wins in four out of six Euro 2008 matches and all seven of their matches in the 2010 World Cup, including Germany's win over Uruguay on July 10. He also correctly predicted Spain as the winner of the 2010 World Cup final. In total, he made 12 correct predictions out of 14, which is about 85.7% correct.

Abies nordmanniana, also known as the Nordmann fir or Caucasian fir, is a type of fir tree native to the mountains south and east of the Black Sea. It is found in Turkey, Georgia, and the Russian Caucasus. The tree grows at altitudes between 900 and 2,200 meters in areas that receive more than 1,000 mm of precipitation. During the ice age, the current distribution of the Nordmann fir is linked to forest refugia near the eastern and southern Black Sea coast. Despite the current climate being suitable, the tree is not present in parts of the eastern Greater Caucasus that are more than 400 to 500 kilometers away from the Black Sea coast.
Randall Paul Stout was an architect. He was born on May 6, 1958, and died on July 11, 2014. He worked in Los Angeles, California.

Lisbon is a small village in Claiborne Parish, Louisiana, United States. In 2010, it had 185 people. Lisbon is east of the town of Homer, the parish seat. In the late 1800s, Lisbon was the place where the Lisbon Academy was located. A man named T. H. Harris, who was the state superintendent of education from 1908 to 1940, briefly attended this school. Another important person from Lisbon was John Sparks Patton, an educator who was part of the Louisiana Public Service Commission from 1939 to 1944. He lost two races to become the state superintendent of education against T. H. Harris. Patton is known as the first person to suggest that schools should get money to buy textbooks for students.

Bad Moms is a 2016 American comedy movie. Jon Lucas and Scott Moore directed and wrote it. Mila Kunis, Kristen Bell, Kathryn Hahn, Jay Hernandez, Annie Mumolo, Jada Pinkett Smith, and Christina Applegate star in the film. Principal photography started on January 11, 2016, in New Orleans. The movie premiered on July 19, 2016, in New York City. It was released in theaters on July 29, 2016, by STX Entertainment. Critics had mixed opinions. The film earned over $183 million worldwide. It became the first STX film to make over $100 million domestically. A sequel called "A Bad Moms Christmas" came out on November 1, 2017.
Serres-Sainte-Marie is a village in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques region, in southwestern France.

Respiratory diseases, or lung diseases, affect the organs and tissues that help air-breathing animals breathe. They involve parts like the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, pleurae, pleural cavity, and the breathing muscles and nerves. These diseases can be mild, like a common cold, or very serious, such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, or lung cancer. Doctors who treat these conditions are called pulmonologists. Respiratory diseases can be grouped in different ways, such as by the body part involved, symptoms shown, or what causes them.

Charles Quinton Murphy, born on July 12, 1959, and died on April 12, 2017, was an American actor, comedian, and writer. He was famous for writing and being on the show "Chappelle's Show" on Comedy Central. He also starred in the sitcom "Black Jesus." His older brother is comedian Eddie Murphy.

Hispar Pass (also known as Hispar La) is a high mountain pass in Pakistan's Karakoram range. It is at an elevation of 5,128 meters (16,824 feet). At this pass, two large glaciers meet: the Biafo Glacier, which is 63 kilometers long, and the Hispar Glacier, which is 49 kilometers long. Together, they form a long glacial path, 100 kilometers in length, which is the world's longest non-polar glacier traverse.
Gurdon is a city in Clark County, Arkansas, United States. In 2010, it had 2,212 people.

Brighton is a village in Macoupin County and partly in Jersey County, Illinois. In 2010, it had 2,254 people living there. The current mayor is Michael Roberts. Brighton is in the Metro-East area and also part of the St. Louis region.

Migiko Kaku, born on January 24, 1947, is an American physicist, futurist, and science communicator. He teaches theoretical physics at the City College of New York and the CUNY Graduate Center. Migiko has written many books about physics and related topics. He often appears on TV, radio, and in films, and writes online blogs and articles. He has written several best-selling books, including "Physics of the Impossible" in 2008, "Physics of the Future" in 2011, and "The Future of the Mind" in 2014. Migiko has also hosted TV specials for the BBC, the Discovery Channel, the History Channel, and the Science Channel.

Manuel Luis Quezon y Molina, also known as MLQ, was born on August 19, 1878, and died on August 1, 1944. He was a Filipino leader who served as the first president of the Philippines from 1935 to 1944. During his presidency, he helped poor farmers and worked on strengthening the country's defense and economy. He also wanted to develop Mindanao and reduce corruption. Quezon set up a government in the United States during World War II. He died of tuberculosis in New York and was first buried in Arlington National Cemetery. After the war, his remains were moved to Manila. His final resting place is the Quezon Memorial Circle. Quezon was honored posthumously in 2015. He and the Filipino people were given the Raoul Wallenberg Medal for helping victims of the Holocaust between 1937 and 1941. This was recognized by the International Raoul Wallenberg Foundation.

The chloralkali process is used to make chlorine and sodium hydroxide from sodium chloride solutions. This process began on a large scale in 1892 and produces about 35 million tons of chlorine each year. During the process, the solutions turn into sodium hydroxide, hydrogen, and chlorine. Using other salts like calcium chloride or potassium chloride can result in different products. Related methods can produce chlorine and sodium metal or hydrogen and chlorine from other sources. This process uses a lot of electricity, about 2500 kilowatt-hours for each ton of sodium hydroxide. Chlorine and sodium hydroxide are produced in equal amounts, so they need to be used together. For every mole of chlorine produced, one mole of hydrogen is also produced. Much of this hydrogen is used to make hydrochloric acid, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, or for power and steam production.

James P. Molinaro was born on March 11, 1931. He is an American politician who used to be the borough president of Staten Island. In 2001, he won an election against Jerome X. O’Donovan, a Democratic councilman, with 50% of the votes. Molinaro started his term on January 1, 2002. He was re-elected in 2009 with 62.7% of the votes, defeating his challenger, John Luisi, who got 37.3% of the votes. Luisi also challenged Molinaro in 2005.

Guangdong is a coastal province in southern China near the South China Sea. Its capital is Guangzhou. As of 2018, it had 113.46 million people and covers about 157,000 square kilometers. It is the most populous province in China and has the 15th-largest area. Guangdong's economy is larger than any other province and ranks fourth globally, with a GDP of 1.47 trillion US dollars in 2018. The Pearl River Delta is an important area for technology, manufacturing, and trade, and includes the cities of Guangzhou and Shenzhen, which are among China's most populous and significant cities. Guangdong became the most populous province in China in January 2005, with 79.1 million permanent residents and 31 million migrants. The province's population grew to 108.5 million by 2015. Most of historical Guangdong is now part of the People's Republic of China, but some islands are controlled by the Republic of China. Guangdong's economy is very diverse, and it has been the top provincial-level region in total GDP since 1989. Its GDP in 2018 was over 1.47 trillion US dollars, making it larger than Spain's. Guangdong has a rich cultural influence, spreading languages, music, food, and traditions throughout China, Southeast Asia, and other countries. This cultural influence extends to Hong Kong and Macau, which are special administrative regions, and to Chinese communities in Singapore and Malaysia.

The Tagalog Wikipedia is the Tagalog language version of Wikipedia. It started on December 1, 2003. As of now, it has many articles. However, it has fewer articles than the Cebuano and Waray editions, which have more than 2,000 articles each. Most of the articles in the Cebuano and Waray editions were made by a computer program called Lsjbot. The Tagalog Wikipedia has around 500 articles, which is less than the 2,000 articles in the Waray edition and the 2,000 articles in the Cebuano edition. However, the Tagalog Wikipedia has more active users, with about 150, compared to 50 for the Waray edition and 100 for the Cebuano edition.

In math, the intermediate value theorem says that if ``f'' is a continuous function with the domain including the interval [``a'', ``b''], then ``f'' will take on any value between ``f''(``a'') and ``f''(``b'') at some point within the interval. This has two important results.
Günther Maleuda was an East German politician. He lived from January 20, 1931, to July 18, 2012. From 1989 to 1990, he was the president of the People's Chamber, which was the East German parliament.
Saint-Samson is a commune in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.

The British Rail Class 22, also known as "baby warship," was a type of diesel-hydraulic train made for the western part of British Railways. They looked very much like the Class 21 diesel-electric trains. This name came from their similarity in appearance and internal equipment to the Class D20/2 or Class 41, known as "warship class." The trains in this class were numbered from D6300 to D6357.

Stara Zagora is a province in south-central Bulgaria. It was formerly called the Stara Zagora okrug. The province includes the city of Stara Zagora, which is the sixth-largest town in Bulgaria. Stara Zagora is also the center for administration and industry. As of December 2009, the province had a total population of 350,925 people. It is divided into 11 municipalities. There is a coal production facility in the southeastern part of the province, near the Radnevo municipality. Between 1934 and 1949, Stara Zagora province also included parts of what is now the Kardzhali province.
The COVID-19 pandemic was found in Rwanda in March 2020.

The Kinsey Reports are two important books about human sexual behavior. They were written by Alfred Kinsey, Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin, and Paul Gebhard. The first book, "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male," came out in 1948. The second, "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female," was published in 1953. These books caused a lot of controversy, both among scientists and the general public. They talked about things that people didn't usually discuss openly and used new ways to collect data. Kinsey worked as a zoologist at Indiana University and started the Kinsey Institute for researching sex, gender, and reproduction. The data for the male book came from interviewing about 5,300 men over 15 years. The female book was based on interviews with about 6,000 women. Kinsey looked at how often women engaged in different kinds of sexual activities and how things like age, social status, and religion affected their behavior. He also compared the activities of men and women. Kinsey's methods were criticized. Some thought that getting the data might have involved working with people who had done bad things. The Kinsey Institute said this wasn't true, but they did note that men who had sexual experiences with children were interviewed. Kinsey tried to protect the privacy of these men to get honest answers, but worried that their crimes might continue. Later, the Kinsey Institute said that the data from these interviews didn't significantly change the original findings. Some more recent researchers believe that Kinsey might have overestimated how many people were attracted to the same sex because of problems with how he collected his data. However, his work is still seen as groundbreaking and very important in the history of sex research.

Ellen Louise Axson Wilson (born Axson, May 15, 1860, died August 6, 1914) was Woodrow Wilson's first wife and the mother of their three daughters. Like her husband, she was from the South and the daughter of a minister. She was born in Savannah, Georgia, but grew up in Rome, Georgia. She had an artistic side and studied at the Art Students League in New York before marrying Woodrow Wilson. She continued to make art later in life. She was the First Lady of the United States from when Woodrow Wilson became president in 1913 until her death. During that time, she organized wedding receptions for two of their daughters in the White House.

Hudson Hawk is a 1991 American action comedy film directed by Michael Lehmann. Bruce Willis stars as the main character and also helped write the story and theme song. Danny Aiello, Andie MacDowell, James Coburn, David Caruso, Lorraine Toussaint, Frank Stallone, Sandra Bernhard, and Richard E. Grant appear in the movie. The film uses cartoon-style jokes and funny sounds to make a silly kind of humor. The story mixes ideas about secret groups, mysteries, and futuristic technology. In the film, Hudson and his partner Tommy sing songs at the same time but separately to time their actions. Bing Crosby's "Swinging on a Star" and Paul Anka's "Side by Side" are featured in the movie's songs. The film didn't do well in the United States, earning only $17 million and receiving three Razzie awards. However, it was better received overseas and earned $80 million, bringing the total worldwide earnings to $97 million.
Sargodha division is an administrative area in Pakistan's Punjab province. The capital city is Sargodha. In 2017, the division's population was about 8.18 million people.
Peter Fox, born on September 3, 1971, is a German singer, songwriter, musician, and music video director. He is part of a German reggae and dancehall band called Seeed.

The "Island of the Blue Dolphins" is a 1960 children's book written by Scott O'Dell. It's about a 12-year-old girl named Karana who lives alone on an island off California for many years. The story is based on the real story of Juana Maria, a Native American girl who was left alone on San Nicolas Island for 18 years during the 1800s. O'Dell won the Newbery Medal for his book in 1961. A movie was made in 1964. O'Dell later wrote a sequel called "Zia" in 1976. A special 50th anniversary edition includes a new introduction by Lois Lowry, who also added some writings from Father Gonzales Rubio from the Santa Barbara Mission's book of burials. In 2016, a complete reader's edition was published. This includes two chapters that were removed before the book was printed.
Ahmed Salah Mohamed Hosni Hassan was born on July 11, 1979. He was an Egyptian football player who played as a striker. He is now retired.

Tori Kedar Hunter (born July 18, 1975) is a former American professional baseball player. He played as a center fielder and right fielder. Hunter was in Major League Baseball (MLB) from 1997 to 2015 for the Minnesota Twins, Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim, and Detroit Tigers. He was an all-star five times and won nine consecutive Gold Glove awards for his performances as a center fielder. He also won the Silver Slugger award twice.

Coventry Cathedral, also known as the Cathedral Church of St Michael, is the main church for the Bishop of Coventry and the Coventry Diocese in the Church of England. It is in Coventry, West Midlands, England. The current bishop is Christopher Cocksworth, and the dean is John Witcombe. Coventry has had three cathedrals. The first one was St Mary's, a monastic building. Only some ruins remain of it. The second was St Michael's, a 14th-century Gothic church that was later named a cathedral. This one was destroyed during World War II, leaving only a ruined shell. The third is the new St Michael's Cathedral, built after the old one was destroyed.

The National Assembly of Thailand (abbreviated as NAT) is the legislative branch of the government. It has two parts. It meets in Sappaya-Sapasathan in Bangkok's Dusit District. The National Assembly was created in 1932 when Thailand changed from a monarchy without a constitution to one with a constitution. During a crisis in 2013, the Prime Minister, Yingluck Shinawatra, dissolved the House of Representatives. New elections were called for February 2, 2014, but they were cancelled by the Constitutional Court. After a military coup in 2014, the National Assembly was replaced by the National Legislative Assembly, which had only one part. In 2017, a new constitution was made. The National Assembly was recreated, but the National Legislative Assembly stayed in place until after the 2019 general election.

Vijaya Mulay was born on May 16, 1921, and passed away on May 19, 2019. She was a documentary filmmaker, film historian, writer, educator, and researcher. She had close friendships with famous filmmakers like Satyajit Ray, Louis Malle, and Mrinal Sen, which gave her a special view of Indian cinema and influenced her work. Her work has helped others see India in a new way. Her daughter, Suhasini Mulay, is a well-known actor, and her son-in-law, Atul Gurtu, is a high-energy physicist. Vijaya Mulay is remembered for her animated film "Ek Anek Aur Ekta," which won the National Film Award for the best educational film.
