Wesley Allison Clark was born on April 10, 1927, and died on February 22, 2016. He was an American physicist known for designing the first modern personal computer. Clark was also a computer designer and a key figure, working with Charles Molnar, in creating the LINC computer, which was the first minicomputer and inspired personal computers like the PDP-1. He grew up in Kinderhook, New York, and northern California. His parents moved to California, and Clark attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned a physics degree in 1947. Clark started his career as a physicist at the Hanford site. In 1981, he received the Eckert–Mauchly Award for his work on computer architecture. In 1984, he was given an honorary degree by Washington University. He was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1999. Clark was also awarded the IEEE Computer Society Computer Pioneer Award for his work on the first personal computer.

In physics, the center of mass is a special point in space where the weight of an object seems to be concentrated. It's like a balance point. When a force is applied to this point, the object moves straight without spinning. Calculations become simpler when we use this point. In a solid object, this point is where the object would balance perfectly. For very simple shapes, this point is at the centroid, the geometric center. Even for objects like a horseshoe, which have an open shape, the center of mass can be outside the object. For many objects, like planets, the center of mass is the average position of all the mass. The center of mass frame is a place where the center of all the masses is still, and this makes calculations easier. In space, the movement of planets is calculated as if all their mass is at this point.

Eight Cousins, or The Aunt-Hill, was written by American author Louisa May Alcott in 1875. The story is about Rose Campbell. She is a lonely and sick girl who recently lost her parents. Now, she lives with her great aunts, who are important women in her wealthy family. Rose's uncle, Alec, comes back from traveling. He takes care of Rose. Uncle Alec has new ideas about raising children, and under his care, Rose feels happier and healthier. She also has seven boy cousins and many aunts and uncles. Rose befriends Phebe, a young maid who works for her aunts. Phebe's cheerful attitude helps Rose appreciate her own good fortune.

Cristina Deutekom, born on August 28, 1931, and passed away on August 7, 2014, was a Dutch operatic coloratura soprano. She performed with many famous male singers, including Carlo Bergonzi, José Carreras, Franco Corelli, Plácido Domingo, Nicolai Gedda, Alfredo Kraus, Luciano Pavarotti, and Richard Tucker.

The Wiener Sport-Club, often abbreviated as WSC, was founded in 1883 in Vienna, Austria. It is one of the country's oldest sports clubs. Their main stadium is located in the Dornbach area, which is part of the 17th district of the city.

The Battle of Leipzig, also known as the Battle of the Nations, was fought from October 16 to 19, 1813, in Leipzig, Saxony. The armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden, and Russia, led by Emperor Alexander I and Karl von Schwarzenberg, beat Napoleon's French army. Napoleon's army included Polish, Italian, and German troops. This battle ended the German campaign of 1813, involved 500,000 soldiers, 2,200 guns, used 200,000 rounds of artillery, and resulted in 127,000 casualties. It was the biggest battle in Europe before World War I. Napoleon had to go back to France. The Sixth Coalition continued its effort, breaking the Confederation of the Rhine and invading France early the next year. Napoleon had to give up and was sent to Elba in May 1814.

Helene & Gänget was a dansband in Kristianstad, Sweden. It was formed in 1990 by members of Färmarna dansband. The band became successful in 1995 with the album "Segla Din Båt I Hamn." They stopped performing in 2002. Their singer, Helene Persson, started acting as the host for Kristianstad's program. Some of their famous songs include "Segla Din Båt I Hamn," "En Korg Med Blommor," and "Nånstans Så Finns Du."

Sheringham, with a population of 7,367, is an English seaside town in Norfolk, United Kingdom. The town's motto, given in 1953 to the Sheringham urban district council, is "the sea enriches and the pine adorns," which means the sea makes the town rich and pine trees make it beautiful.

A château is a big house where the important person of a land lived. It can be in the countryside and was often built by nobles or wealthy families. Sometimes, it had defenses. Usually, there are many of these houses in French-speaking places.

Phoenix is a small constellation in the southern sky. It was first shown by Johann Bayer in his 1603 book "Uranometria." Nicolas Louis de Lacaille, a French explorer and astronomer, mapped brighter stars in 1756. Phoenix spans from about -39° to -57° and from 23.5 hours to 2.5 hours in right ascension. Along with Grus, Pavo, and Tucana, these constellations are known as the southern birds. Alpha Phoenicis, the brightest star, is called Ankaa, meaning 'the phoenix' in Arabic. It's an orange giant with a magnitude of 2.4. Beta Phoenicis is actually two yellow giants that together have a magnitude of 3.3. Nu Phoenicis has a dust disk, and there are ten star systems with known planets in this constellation. It also includes the El Gordo and Phoenix galaxy clusters, which are very far away. Phoenix is the source of two annual meteor showers: the Phoenicids in December, and the July Phoenicids.

Calfreisen was a former municipality in the district of Plessur, in the canton of Graubünden, Switzerland. On January 1, 2013, Calfreisen merged with Castiel, Langwies, Lüen, Molinis, Peist, and St. Peter-Pagig to become part of the municipality of Arosa.

County Armagh, named after its town Armagh, is one of Ireland's traditional counties. It is part of Northern Ireland, along with five other counties. Situated near Lough Neagh's southern shore, County Armagh covers 1,326 square kilometers and has about 174,792 people. It's known as the "orchard county" because of its many apple orchards. County Armagh is part of Ulster, a historic province.

Chini Modi, also known by his pen name Irshad ( Gujarati: ઈર્શાદ ), was a poet, novelist, short story writer, and critic who wrote in Gujarati. He was born on September 30, 1939, and died on March 19, 2017. Educated in languages, he taught at different schools and became well-known for his writing. He won several awards, including the Sahitya Akademi Award, Vali Gujarati Award, and Narsinh Mehta Award.

Bell Canada, often called Bell, is a big company that helps people talk and use the internet in Canada. Its main office is in Montreal, Quebec. Bell is an important company in Ontario and Quebec. It became part of a group called Stentor. In the western part of Canada, Bell also competes with other companies. In the Atlantic provinces, its subsidiary, Bell Aliant, provides services. Bell Mobility, part of Bell, offers mobile phone service. Bell TV provides both satellite and IPTV services. Bell's main competitors are Rogers, Telus, Shaw, Videotron, and Telus in different parts of Canada. Bell serves over 13 million phone lines and has its main office at the Bell campus in Montreal. Bell Canada is part of BCE Inc., which used to be called Bell Canada Enterprises. BCE also owns Bell Media, which runs TV networks like CTV, and has investments in sports teams, including the Montreal Canadiens and Toronto Maple Leafs. BCE ranked 262 on the Forbes Global 2000 list in 2011.

Lager Norderney was a Nazi concentration camp on Alderney, one of the Channel Islands. It was named after the East Friesian island of Norderney. The German Organisation Todt (OT) built four labor camps on Alderney for workers on planned fortifications. "Lager Norderney" was located in Saye. "Lager Borkum" was at Platte Saline, "Lager Sylt" near the old telegraph tower at La Foulère, and "Lager Helgoland" was in the northwest corner of the island. From March 1943 to June 1944, "Lager Norderney" was run by the SS-Baubrigade. During this time, it became a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, which was in Hamburg, Germany.

Portage la Prairie is a small city in the central part of Manitoba, Canada. In 2016, it had 13,304 people living there. The city is west of Winnipeg, along the Trans-Canada Highway, near the border between Saskatchewan and Ontario. It sits next to the Assiniboine River, which used to flood frequently until a channel was built to redirect the water to Lake Manitoba. The city is surrounded by the Rural Municipality of Portage la Prairie. According to Environment Canada, Portage la Prairie has the most sunny days in warm months in Canada. It is also the administrative center for the Dakota Tipi First Nations reserve.

Khunjerab Pass is a high mountain pass in the Karakoram Mountains. It is located on the northern border of Pakistan (in Gilgit-Baltistan's Hunza and Nagar districts) and on the southwest border of China (Xinjiang).

A photoreceptor cell is a special type of cell in the retina that changes light into signals for the body. These cells are very important because they help turn light, a type of energy we see, into signals that our body can use. Photoreceptors have proteins that absorb light, changing the cell's energy state. There are three main types of photoreceptor cells in mammals: rods, cones, and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). Rods and cones are the classic photoreceptors. Rods and cones help form images in our vision. Rods are thin and spread across the retina differently from cones, but both use similar chemical processes to change light into signals. ipRGCs were found in the 1990s. Unlike rods and cones, ipRGCs do not help us see. Instead, they help control our sleep cycles and pupil size. Rods and cones work differently. Rods can be activated by just one light particle (photon), making them very sensitive. At low light, only rod signals are active. Cones need more light to send signals. Humans have three types of cones that respond to different light colors. These colors help us see different shades. At low light, only rod cells are active, so we cannot see colors. Cones respond to short, medium, and long wavelengths of light, called s-cones, m-cones, and l-cones. The number of rod and cone cells in the human eye is about 120 million rods and 6 million cones. The ratio of these cells varies in different animals depending on whether they are mainly active during the day or at night. Owls, which are active at night, have many more rod cells. In humans, there are about 2.4 to 3 million ganglion cells, with 1 to 2% being photosensitive. The ganglion cells' axons form the optic nerves. Photoreceptor cells are arranged in a roughly hexagonal pattern called the retinal mosaic. In mammals, the pineal and parapineal glands sense light. Birds have special neurons in their brain that respond to light without eye input. Insects and molluscs have photoreceptors that look and work differently. This article focuses on human photoreceptors.

Ahmed Jibril is the founder and leader of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command (PFLP-GC). During the Syrian civil war, he supported the Assad government. PFLP-GC members helped government forces fight against the Syrian opposition. However, clashes with rebels in Yarmouk camp caused some PFLP-GC members to leave. As a result, the group had to leave the camp, and Jibril fled Damascus.

Homa Rousta, born on September 26, 1946, and passed away on September 26, 2015, was an Iranian actress who performed in films and on stage. She was married to a stage director named Hamid Samandarian. She studied theater and got a degree from the School of Dramatic Arts in Bucharest. Her acting career began in 1971. Her most famous role was in the 1992 film "From Karkheh to Rhine," for which she was nominated for best actress at the Fajr Film Festival. She died of cancer in a hospital in Los Angeles, California, United States, on her birthday. Her body was brought back to Iran and buried in Behesht Zahra next to her husband's grave.

Saint-Étienne is a city in eastern central France, in the Massif Central region. It is southwest of Lyon and on the road between Toulouse and Lyon. Saint-Étienne is the capital of the Loire department. In 2017, the city had 172,565 people, and over 520,000 in the urban area. Recently, Saint-Étienne has undergone big changes, turning from an old industrial city into a modern "European Capital of Design." These changes include important improvements in the city's main areas.

Elliott County is in the state of Kentucky. In 2010, it had 7,852 people. By 2018, the population was 7,508. Sandy Hook is the county seat. Elliott County was created in 1869 from parts of Morgan, Lawrence, and Carter counties. It was named after John Lyle Elliott, who was a U.S. congressman and a Confederate justice. Elliott County does not allow the sale of alcohol anywhere in the county.
Saint-Jouin is a village in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.

In cellular biology, active transport moves molecules from a less concentrated area to a more concentrated area across the cell membrane. This happens against the concentration gradient and needs energy. There are two main types: one uses ATP directly, and the other uses an electrochemical gradient. An example is how glucose is taken up in the intestines.
The Akriaos is a tragedy written by Sophocles, an Athenian playwright from the 5th century BCE. Only fragments of this play survive.

Bob Beckwith, born on September 21, 1933, used to work for the New York City Fire Department. He became famous after standing next to President George W. Bush during a speech at the World Trade Center ruins after the September 11, 2001 attacks. Pictures of Beckwith and the president appeared on the front page of the "New York Daily News" and the cover of "Time" magazine. This brought him into the national spotlight and led to more media attention and interviews. Since then, Beckwith has met President Bush several times, spoken publicly often, and helped raise money for charities.

The ECW World Heavyweight Championship was a professional wrestling title used in Extreme Championship Wrestling (ECW) and later in World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE). It started as ECW's main title in 1994, but was first introduced in 1992 by a precursor promotion called Eastern Championship Wrestling. Jimmy Snuka was the first champion. The title stopped being used in 2001 when ECW closed. In 2003, WWE bought ECW. In 2006, WWE brought back the ECW title as part of their ECW brand, alongside other titles. For a short time in 2008, the ECW title was the main title on WWE's Raw brand. When WWE ended the ECW brand in 2010, the title was retired, with Ezekiel Jackson as the last champion.
Carlos Oscar Reichenbach Filho was a Brazilian filmmaker. He was born on June 14, 1945, and passed away on June 14, 2012.
Örkelljunga is an area and the main town of Örkelljunga municipality, in Skåne county, Sweden. It had about 10,300 people living there in 2020.

Cory Scott Gardner, born on August 22, 1974, is an American lawyer and politician. He has been a U.S. senator for Colorado since 2015. A Republican, Gardner was a U.S. representative for Colorado's 4th district from 2011 to 2015 and a member of the Colorado House of Representatives from 2005 to 2011. In 2014, he won a Senate race against the Democratic incumbent Mark Udall. From 2017 to 2019, Gardner was the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee. After the 2018 midterm elections, Gardner and Heidi Ganahl, a University of Colorado regent, were the only Republicans holding statewide elected offices in Colorado. Gardner is seen as one of the most vulnerable senators running for reelection in 2020.

The Fulbright Program, including the Fulbright-Hays Program, is a cultural exchange program in the United States. It aims to improve relationships and understanding between people in the U.S. and other countries by sending and receiving students, scholars, teachers, professionals, scientists, and artists. Through this program, Americans can get scholarships or grants to study, do research, teach, or perform arts abroad. Citizens from other countries can do the same in the U.S. The Fulbright Program was started in 1946 by Senator J. William Fulbright and is one of the best-known and respected scholarships globally. Each year, about 8,000 grants are given – around 1,600 to U.S. students, 1,200 to U.S. scholars, 4,000 to foreign students, 900 to foreign scholars, and several hundred to teachers and professionals. This program is managed by organizations like the Institute of International Education and operates in more than 160 countries. The U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs sponsors it, and it gets funding from the U.S. Congress. Additional support comes from partner governments, foundations, corporations, and host institutions both inside and outside the U.S. In 49 countries, a bi-national Fulbright commission oversees the program. In other countries, the U.S. embassy's public affairs section handles it. Over 370,000 people have taken part in the program since it began. Many Fulbright alumni have won important awards, including 60 who received Nobel Prizes and 86 who got Pulitzer Prizes.

The 1st United States Congress, which included the Senate and the House of Representatives, met from March 4, 1789, to March 4, 1791. This was during the first two years of George Washington's presidency. They first met at Federal Hall in New York City and later moved to Congress Hall in Philadelphia. When the 1st Congress first met, the U.S. government began operating under the new government system set up by the 1787 Constitution. The number of seats in the House of Representatives was decided based on the Constitution. Both parts of the Congress had more people who supported the president. This Congress passed twelve changes to the Constitution and sent them to the states for approval. The ten that were approved and added to the Constitution on December 15, 1791, are known as the Bill of Rights.

Colonel Reginald Edward Harry Dyer, CB (born October 9, 1864, died July 23, 1927), was an army officer in the Bengal army and later the Indian army. He began his military career in the British army before moving to serve in the Indian army. As a temporary brigadier-general, Dyer was in charge during the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in Amritsar, Punjab. He has been called "the butcher of Amritsar" because he ordered troops to fire on peaceful people. The official report said that at least 379 people were killed and over a thousand were injured. Some people who testified suggested even more deaths occurred. Dyer was later removed from his position and widely criticized in Britain and India. However, he became a hero to some people connected to the British Raj. Some historians say this event was a key step toward ending British rule in India.

The Millennium Dome, also called the Dome, was a large round building used for a big exhibition celebrating the start of the new millennium. It's one of the biggest buildings in the world by space inside. Located on the Greenwich Peninsula in southeast London, it opened in 2000 and closed at the end of 2000. It didn't attract as many visitors as expected, and the project was considered a failure by the media. The Dome and its exhibitions were sold or removed. In 2005, selling the Dome and land increased to 170 acres cost £28.7 million. The 48 acres occupied by the Dome were worth about £48 million, but it was decided to keep the Dome instead of demolishing it. Now, the Dome is a key part of the O2. The Prime Meridian passes near its western edge, and the nearest underground station is North Greenwich on the Jubilee Line.
Gene Autry is a town in Carter County, Oklahoma, United States. In 2010, the town had 158 people, which was more than the 99 people in 2000. It is part of the Ardmore, Oklahoma area.

Sabayon Linux is an Italian Linux distribution based on Gentoo. It was formerly known as rr4 Linux and rr64 Linux. Created by Fabio Erculiani and the Sabayon development team, Sabayon follows the "out of the box" philosophy. This means it comes with many ready-to-use applications and is automatically set up for the user. Sabayon uses a rolling release cycle. It has its own software repository and package management system called Entropy. It is available for both x86 and amd64 architectures. Armv7 support for the Beaglebone is in development. Sabayon is named after the Italian dessert zabaione, made from eggs. Its logo shows a chicken's foot.
Patrick Burke Mayhew, Baron Mayhew of Twysden, was born on September 11, 1929, and died on June 25, 2016. He was a British lawyer and politician.

Alumpeedika is a small village in Oachira, located in the Kollam district of Kerala, India. It is part of Clappana Panchayath and is in the South Kerala division. Alumpeedika is about 31 kilometers north of Kollam, the district headquarters, and 1 kilometer from Oachira. It is also 101 kilometers from the state capital, Thiruvananthapuram. Nearby towns include Kayamkulam, Oachira, and Karunagappalli. Alumpeedika is close to the border of the Kollam and Alappuzha districts and is near the Arabian Sea.

He is better known by his ring name. He was a Japanese professional wrestler who mostly worked for All Japan Pro Wrestling (AJPW). He is famous for being the first triple crown heavyweight champion. He won the PWF Heavyweight Championship, the NWA United National Championship, and the NWA International Heavyweight Championship. He unified all three titles. He is also known for being part of the first-ever world tag team champions with Yoshiaki Yatsu. Together, they won the NWA International Tag Team Championship and the PWF Tag Team Championship, unifying the two titles.

Clean and Sober is a 1988 American drama film. Glenn Gordon Caron directed it. Michael Keaton stars as a real estate agent who has a problem with substances. This was Keaton's second dramatic movie after "Touch and Go." Other actors in the film are Kathy Baker, M. Emmet Walsh, Morgan Freeman, Luca Bercovici, and Tate Donovan. Ron Howard, who previously directed Keaton in comedies like "Night Shift" (1982) and "Gung Ho" (1986), helped produce the movie.

Conficker is a computer worm that targets Microsoft Windows. It was first detected in November 2008. Conficker uses weaknesses in Windows software and tries guessing passwords to spread. It forms a botnet. The worm has been hard to stop due to its use of advanced techniques. It infected millions of computers, including those used by governments, businesses, and homes, in over 190 countries. This is considered the largest computer worm infection since the 2003 Welchia. Despite spreading widely, the worm didn't cause much damage, likely because the suspected Ukrainian criminals who created it were cautious due to the attention. Four people were arrested, and one pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 48 months in prison.

Seattle Sounders FC is an American soccer team in Seattle, Washington. They play in the Western Conference of Major League Soccer (MLS). The team started in 2007 and played their first game in 2009. They were an MLS expansion team. Seattle Sounders is named after a team that played from 1974 to 1983. Adrian Hanauer owns the club, and other owners include Paul Allen's estate, Drew Carey, and 11 Seattle families. Brian Schmetzer became the coach in 2016 after Siggi Schmid left. Their home games are at CenturyLink Field, which holds about 37, 722 people. A marching band called Sound Wave supports the team at home games. Seattle Sounders have rivals Portland Timbers and Vancouver Whitecaps FC. They won their first game on March 19, 2009, against the New York Red Bulls. They have won the U.S. Open Cup four times, the Supporters' Shield in 2014, and the MLS Cup in 2016 and 2019. They have been in the playoffs every year and reached the finals three times. They also played in the Concacaf Champions League five times, reaching the semifinals once. The team had the highest average attendance in MLS for five years. Clint Dempsey and Fredy Montero were top scorers, Osvaldo Alonso was a long-time captain, and Nicolás Lodeiro is the current captain. The team has a players' academy and lower division teams that produced homegrown players like Jordan Morris and DeAndre Yedlin, who now plays for Newcastle United.

Darrell Clayton Hammond was born on October 8, 1955. He is an American actor, comedian, and impersonator. He was a regular cast member on "Saturday Night Live" from 1995 to 2009. Since 2014, Hammond has been the announcer for the show. When he left "Saturday Night Live" at age 53, he was the oldest cast member in the show's history. Hammond appeared on "Saturday Night Live" more times than any other cast member. He impersonated more than 107 celebrities, with Bill Clinton being his most frequent impersonation. On September 19, 2014, Hammond became the new announcer for "Saturday Night Live," replacing Don Pardo, who had passed away in August.

Toffen is a town in the Bern-Mittelland district of the canton of Bern in Switzerland. It is about 10 km south of Bern. There is a castle called Toffen Castle there, which is an important historical site.

Chadwell Heath is a suburb in northeast London, England. It lies between Barking and Dagenham and Redbridge. It is west of Romford and east of Ilford, and north-east of London's central area. The name was first used in the 17th century for a settlement in Dagenham, Essex. Later, it included a nearby hamlet in Barking, which became Ilford. Chadwell Heath railway station, which connects the area to London, opened in 1864. After World War I, the area grew as a residential suburb and became part of the Becontree estate, leading to more people living there. In 1965, the area became part of Greater London. Today, the suburb includes Chadwell Heath Academy. There is also a local pub named after Eva Hart, a survivor of a famous event.

McClure is a small community in Dickinson County, Virginia, United States. It is near the McClure River and Virginia State Route 63, southeast of Clintwood. McClure used to have a post office from 1919 until it closed on July 6, 2011, but it still has its own zip code, 24269. Some people think McClure was named after a pioneer who was killed by Indians.

ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI (born July 12, 1959) is the king of Tonga. He is the younger brother of the late King George Tupou V. His brother was not married and had no children, so ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI was officially named as the heir in 2006. He worked as Tonga's high commissioner in Australia. He lived in Canberra. When King George Tupou V died on March 18, 2012, ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI became the new king, with the same name, ʻAhoʻeitu Tupou VI.

Harold and Kumar go to White Castle, also called Harold and Kumar Get the Munchies in the UK, is a 2004 American stoner comedy film. It's the first movie in the Harold and Kumar series. Jon Hurwitz and Hayden Schlossberg wrote the film, and Danny Leiner directed it. The story is about Harold Lee (John Cho) and Kumar Patel (Kal Penn). After smoking marijuana, they decide to visit the fast-food place White Castle. But their trip leads to funny problems and adventures. Many actors appear in the film. Fred Willard, Paula García, Anthony Anderson, Dan Bochart, Ethan Embry, Jamie Kennedy, Bobby Lee, Christopher Meloni, Ryan Reynolds, Shaun Majumder, David Krumholtz, Eddie Kaye Thomas, Malin Akerman, and Neil Patrick Harris, who plays himself, are some of the stars.

Vitis is a group of 79 plant species in the grape family. Most of these plants are found in the northern part of the world. Grapes and wine come from Vitis plants, making them important economically. The study and growing of grapevines is called viticulture. Vitis plants have small, wind-pollinated flowers with both male and female parts. These flowers grow in bunches called inflorescences. In many Vitis species, such as Vitis vinifera, each flower that is successfully pollinated turns into a grape. The bunches of flowers become clusters of grapes. Even though the flowers are small, the grapes are usually large and colorful, attracting birds and animals that help spread the seeds inside the grapes. For fruit production, grapevines typically need shoots from buds developed the previous year. In viticulture, this is why vines are pruned. For example, they might be pruned into a cane with 8 to 15 buds or into a smaller spur with 2 to 3 buds.

Eric Walter Elst, born in 1936, is a Belgian astronomer working at the Royal Observatory of Belgium in Uccle. He has discovered many asteroids. He is one of the top 10 asteroid discoverers, with thousands of discoveries made at ESO's La Silla Observatory in northern Chile and at the Rozhen Observatory in Bulgaria between 1986 and 2009. An asteroid named 3936 Elst, a stony Vestian asteroid from the inner part of the asteroid belt and about 6 kilometers in diameter, was named after him.

Negligence means failing to be careful in a situation where care is needed. In tort law, negligence involves causing harm by not being careful, possibly with special reasons. The main idea is that people should be careful in their actions to avoid harming others or property. If someone gets hurt or loses something because of another's carelessness, they can ask for money to make up for the harm. This money can cover injuries, damaged property, mental health problems, or money lost. The law looks at negligence using five main parts: duty, breach, actual cause, proximate cause, and damages.

Voeren is a Flemish municipality in Belgium where people speak Flemish Dutch. It has services to help French speakers. Voeren is in the province of Limburg, north of the Netherlands and south of the Walloon province of Liège. Geographically, Voeren is separate from the rest of Flanders, making it an exclave. The town's name comes from a small river called Voer, which runs through it. Voeren became an independent municipality in 1977 due to a reform. On January 1, 2008, it had 4,207 people living there. The area is about 12.8 square kilometers. The population density is around 328 people per square kilometer. About 25% of the people living there are foreigners, mostly with Dutch nationality.

Kelowna is a city by Okanagan Lake in the Okanagan Valley, in the southern part of British Columbia, Canada. It is the main city in the Central Okanagan regional district. The name Kelowna comes from an Okanagan word meaning "grizzly bear." Kelowna is the third-largest metropolitan area in British Columbia (after Vancouver and Victoria), its biggest inland city, and its seventh-largest city overall. It is the 22nd-largest city in Canada. The city itself has about 142,146 people. Including the surrounding areas, the metropolitan area has about 217,229 people. Nearby places include West Kelowna (also called Westbank and Westside) to the west, Lake Country and Vernon to the north, Peachland to the southwest, and Summerland and Penticton to the south.

The Mi-38 is a transport helicopter made by the Moscow Helicopter Plant. It was also developed by Kazan Helicopters. It was created to replace the Mi-8 and Mi-17. It is sold for both military and civil use. The Mi-38 first flew on December 22, 2003. It was certified on December 30, 2015.

Reginald Howard White (December 19, 1961 – December 26, 2004) was an American football player who played as a defensive end. He played for the NFL for 15 seasons in the 1980s and 1990s. White went to the University of Tennessee for college football and was named an all-American. He played for the Memphis Showboats in the USFL for two seasons. Then, he was chosen in the first round of the 1984 supplemental draft. White played for the Philadelphia Eagles, Green Bay Packers, and Carolina Panthers. He became one of the most awarded players in NFL history. He was the NFL Defensive Player of the Year two times, played in 13 Pro Bowls, and was selected as an All-Pro 13 times. He also holds the second spot in career sack leaders with 198, behind Bruce Smith's 200. White was part of the NFL 75th anniversary all-time team, the NFL 1990s all-decade team, and the NFL 1980s all-decade team. During his career, he was known as "the minister of defense" because of his Christian ministry and was ordained as an evangelical minister. White is in both the College Football Hall of Fame and the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Six Flags Discovery Kingdom is an animal theme park in Vallejo, California. It used to be called Six Flags Marine World, Marine World, The New Marine World Theme Park, and Marine World Africa USA. The park covers 135 acres. It has roller coasters and other fun rides. Six Flags Discovery Kingdom has been part of the Six Flags amusement parks since 1999.

The movie "The Usual Suspects" is a 1995 film. It is a neo-noir mystery and was directed by Bryan Singer and written by Christopher McQuarrie. The main actors are Stephen Baldwin, Gabriel Byrne, Benicio del Toro, Kevin Pollak, Chazz Palminteri, Pete Postlethwaite, and Kevin Spacey. The story is about Roger "Verbal" Kint, a small-time crook. He is the only survivor of a ship fire and massacre in Los Angeles. During interrogation, he tells his story with flashbacks. Kint explains how he and his criminal friends met a mysterious boss called Keyser Söze. The movie was made for $6 million. Singer got the idea for the title from a "Spy" magazine column, inspired by a line from "Casablanca." It was first shown at the Cannes Film Festival and then released in some theaters. People liked it and it was shown more widely. McQuarrie won an Oscar for the best original screenplay. Spacey won for best supporting actor. The Writers Guild of America listed the movie as having the 35th best screenplay of all time.

Hälleforsnäs is a small village in Flen municipality, Södermanland county, Sweden. It had about 2,000 people living there in 2020. The village is 15 km (9 miles) from Flen, 32 km (20 miles) from Eskilstuna, and 40 km (25 miles) from Katrineholm. It is also about 150 km (93 miles) southwest of Stockholm. Hälleforsnäs used to be a busy place because of a foundry, which is a place where metal is melted and shaped. The foundry was there for 350 years, starting in 1659, until the early 1990s. It made cannons and sent them to the Swedish army in Europe. Later, it started making things like radiators and stoves for people's homes. From 1920 to 1980, the main products were pipes and other parts for water systems. At its biggest, the foundry had more than 1,000 workers, and many more people were employed around it. In the 1980s, Electrolux bought the foundry and changed its focus to making parts for cookers. They closed the foundry in 1990. Some of the workers took over the foundry, which is now a place for artists. Hälleforsnäs has become a cultural center for the region. There's a restaurant there, and during the summer, a herbal shop opens. There's also a cheese-making company, Jürss Dairy, which makes and sells award-winning cheese.

Văn Cao, born Nguyễn Văn Cao on November 15, 1923, and died on July 10, 1995, was a Vietnamese composer. He created "Tiến quân ca," which is Vietnam's national anthem. Along with Phạm Duy and Trịnh Công Sơn, he is often considered one of the most important figures in modern Vietnamese music. He was also a poet and painter.
The vice-president of Egypt is an important official in the government.

ISONOE, also known as '', is a retrograde irregular satellite of Jupiter. It was discovered in 2000 by a team of astronomers from the University of Hawaii, led by Scott S. Sheppard. ISONOE is about 3.8 kilometers in diameter. It orbits Jupiter at an average distance of 23,833,000 kilometers, taking 751.647 days to complete one orbit. The orbit is inclined at 166° to the ecliptic (169° to Jupiter's equator) and is in a retrograde direction with an eccentricity of 0.166. It was named in October 2002 after Isonoe, one of the Danaïdes in Greek mythology, who was a lover of Zeus (Jupiter). ISONOE belongs to the Carme group, a group of irregular retrograde moons orbiting Jupiter. These moons orbit between 23 and 24 GM and have an inclination of about 165°.

Ostabat-asme, also known as Hostavalem in the Middle Ages, is a small town in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department of France. It used to be part of Lower Navarre, a region in southwestern France. This town was an important meeting point for four different routes to Santiago de Compostela. Three of these routes joined together in Ostabat-asme. The first route came from the center of Europe through Paris, Tours, Poitiers, and Dax. The second route went from Genoa and Lyon via Moissac. The third route, known as the "Toulouse way," connected central Italy with the Languedoc region and Béarn, passing through Lescar-Oloron and Somport in Spain. From Ostabat-asme, the three connected routes continued to Saint-Jean-le-Vieux (43°09'57" N, 1°11'32" W), which is also known as Donazaharre. From there, they led to Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, and finally to the Spanish border at Roncesvalles (42°59'23" N, 1°20'4" W). Ostabat-asme was located in the former province of Lower Navarre. It is also the name of the region called Ostabarret.

"Too Good at Goodbyes" is a song by English singer Sam Smith. It was written by James Napier, Tor Hermansen, Mikkel Eriksen, and Smith. The song was produced by Napes, Steve Fitzmaurice, and Stargate. It was released on September 8, 2017, through Capitol Records. This song was the first single from Smith's second album, "The Thrill of It All," also released in 2017. The song reached number one in the UK. It also topped the charts in Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand. It was a top 10 hit in several countries, including Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, and Switzerland. It also reached the top 20 in Austria, Finland, Germany, and Spain.

Hanna Grönvall, born on December 10, 1879, in Västra Sallerup, Malmöhus County, and passed away on May 22, 1953, was a Swedish Social Democratic politician and trade union worker. She worked as a maid from 1900 to 1934. In 1933, she joined a committee to look at the conditions of maids. In 1934, she became the deputy leader of a maid's trade union in Stockholm. She started the central committee for maids in 1936. Grönvall was also a member of Stockholm Municipality's city council for the Social Democrats.

Peter Brian Hegseth, born on June 6, 1980, is an American contributor for Fox News. He used to be in the Army National Guard and worked as the executive director for two political groups: Vets for Freedom and Concerned Veterans for America. The latter group, funded by the Koch brothers, pushes for more privatization of the Department of Veterans Affairs. In the Trump administration, he was considered for the top job at the Department of Veteran Affairs, but veteran groups didn't agree. In January 2017, David Shulkin was chosen instead.

Troup County is in the central part of Georgia, United States. According to the 2010 census, it had 67,044 people. The main town is Lagrange. Troup County is part of the Lagrange, Georgia, micropolitan area. It is also part of the Atlanta-Athens-Clarke County-Sandy Springs, Georgia, combined statistical area.

A creed, also called a "confession," "symbol," or "statement of faith," is a formula that summarizes important beliefs of a community, often religious. One of the oldest Christian creeds is "Jesus is Lord," which Saint Paul wrote about. A widely used Christian creed is the Nicene Creed, first created in 325 AD at the First Council of Nicaea. It is based on understanding from the Gospels, the New Testament letters, and somewhat the Old Testament. Most Christian groups consider accepting this creed, which talks about the Trinity, a key test of belief. Another commonly accepted creed is the Apostles' Creed. Some Christian groups don't follow these creeds. Muslims say the "Shahada," or testimony: "I believe there is only one God, and Muhammad is His messenger." Some say Judaism isn't creedal, but others believe it has the "Shema Yisrael": "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."

The University of Greenland is the only university in Greenland. It is located in Nuuk, the capital city. Most classes are taught in Danish, with a few in Greenlandic. Lectures by exchange lecturers are often in English. In 2018, the university had about 205 students, mostly Greenlandic. It has around fourteen academic staff and five technical-administrative employees. The small number of students partly results from many Greenlandic students attending universities in Denmark.

Dr. Siti Musdah Mulia is an Indonesian women's rights activist. She is the first woman to become a research professor at the Indonesian Institute of Sciences and also teaches about Islamic political ideas at a university in Indonesia. Since 2007, she has been the chairperson of an NGO called Indonesian Conference on Religion for Peace. Siti was the first woman to get a PhD in Islamic thought from the Syarif Hidayatullah State Islamic University in 1997. From 1999 to 2007, she advised the minister of religious affairs and was part of a team that created a new Islamic legal code in 2004, suggesting changes like banning child marriage and allowing interfaith marriage. In 2000 to 2005, she led the research division of the Council of Indonesian Ulema. She wrote books like "Islam Criticizes Polygamy" (2003), "Reformist Muslimah" (2004), and "Islam and the Inspiration of Gender Equity" (2005). Siti received important awards, including the 2007 International Women of Courage Award, the 2009 Yap Thiam Hien Award, and the 2009 Woman of the Year award from the Italian government.

Palaeognathae, or paleognaths (from ancient Greek "palaió-" meaning "old" and "gnáthos" meaning "jaw"), is one of two living groups of birds—neognathae being the other. Together, these two groups form neornithes. Palaeognathae includes five flightless groups, called ratites, and one flying group, the neotropic tinamous. There are 47 species of tinamous, 5 species of kiwis (Apteryx), 3 species of cassowaries (Casuarius), 1 species of emus (Dromaius), 2 species of rheas (Rhea), and 2 species of ostriches (Struthio). Recent studies suggest that paleognaths form a single group, but the traditional split between flightless and flying forms is not correct; tinamous are part of the ratite family, meaning flightlessness developed separately multiple times. There are three extinct groups that are definitely part of palaeognathae: lithornithiformes, dinornithiformes (moas), and aepyornithiformes (elephant birds). Some other extinct birds have been linked to the palaeognathae by at least one researcher, but their exact relationships are still debated. The term "paleognath" comes from the ancient Greek for "old jaws," referring to their jaw structure, which is more like that of ancient reptiles than other birds. Despite some primitive features, paleognathous birds are not living fossils. Their genetic material continued to evolve at similar rates to neognathae, under selective pressure, even though their basic structures have remained unchanged. There are also debates about their evolutionary history.

Vermilion is a city in Ohio, near Lake Erie. It is about 35 miles west of Cleveland and 17 miles east of Sandusky. In 2010, the population was 10,594. Part of Vermilion in Lorain County is in the Cleveland-Elyria-Mentor metropolitan area. The part in Erie County is in the Sandusky micropolitan area. Both parts are also in the larger Cleveland-Akron-Canton combined statistical area.

In computing, a parallel port is a way to connect devices to a computer. It sends data in groups, unlike serial ports which send one bit at a time. This requires more cables and connectors. Parallel ports were commonly used for printers, especially from the 1970s to the 2000s. They were a standard until the late 1990s when they were officially called IEEE 1284, which included Enhanced Parallel Port (EPP) and Extended Capability Port (ECP). Today, these ports are not used much because USB devices and network printers are more common. Initially called the Parallel Printer Adapter on IBM PCs, it was mainly for printers using IBM's eight-bit character set. It could also connect other devices.

Dexter in the Dark is a 2007 book by Jeff Lindsay. It is the third book in the Dexter series. The first book, Darkly Dreaming Dexter, came out in 2004. It helped make the TV show Dexter. The second book in the series, Dearly Devoted Dexter, came out in 2005. Dexter in the Dark was released on September 18, 2007, in the U.S. and October 3, 2007, in the U.K. The first book was supposed to come out earlier. The first two chapters of Dexter in the Dark can be seen on a computer when you watch the first season DVD of the TV show.

Jorge Zavala Baquerizo was an Ecuadorian politician born on May 13, 1921, and he died on May 9, 2014. He was 92 years old when he died in Guayaquil, Ecuador. He served as the vice president of Ecuador from 1968 to 1970 during José María Velasco Ibarra's presidency. He also served as president of the national congress from 1987 to 1988. He belonged to the Democratic Left party.

New Year is when a new year starts in calendars and the year number goes up by one. Many cultures celebrate this. In most countries, January 1 is a special day and often a holiday. In the widely used Gregorian calendar, New Year's Day is on January 1. Before, in the Julian calendar, New Year's Day was also on January 1, after 153 BC. In the Middle Ages in Europe, the date for New Year's Day varied depending on the place. It was sometimes March 1, March 25, Easter, September 1, or December 25. After 1582, when the Gregorian calendar was adopted, most places in the world began to celebrate New Year's Day on January 1. Other cultures have their own traditional or religious New Year's Day. Chinese New Year, Islamic New Year, Japanese New Year, and Jewish New Year are some examples. In India and some other countries, they celebrate different New Year's Days.
Francisco Fernández can be about: Francisco Fernandez 1 Francisco Fernandez 2 Another Francisco Fernandez

Romain Rolland was born on January 29, 1866, and passed away on December 30, 1944. He was a French writer, known for plays, novels, and essays. He was also an art historian and had spiritual beliefs. In 1915, he received the Nobel Prize for Literature. He was praised for his idealism and truthful descriptions in his works. Rolland supported Stalin in France. He also had important communications with and influenced Sigmund Freud.
Caucasian can mean: People with light skin from Europe or some parts of Asia.

A railway brake is used on train cars to slow down the train, control its speed going downhill, or keep it still when parked. It works similarly to brakes on regular cars, but is more complex because it controls many connected cars. It also needs to work when the engine is not running. Clasp brakes are an older type of railway brake.

M*A*S*H is an American media franchise including novels, films, TV series, and plays. It's owned by 20th Century Studios and based on Richard Hooker's semi-autobiographical works. The story focuses on a fictional group of doctors and nurses at the fictional 4077th Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War, inspired by a real unit. The main character, Hawkeye Pierce, was played by Donald Sutherland in the 1970 film and Alan Alda in the TV series. Spin-off series featured characters from the original show but were set after the war ended. Most versions mix humor and drama, centering on medical practice. To ease stress, the staff did funny things and had light-hearted disagreements when not working. The franchise ended with "Trapper John, M.D." in 1986. Fans still love it, and the studio sells the film and TV seasons on DVD.

extinction means a type of living thing or a group of living things stops existing, usually a species. The exact moment of extinction is often hard to determine, especially when the last individual dies. Some species might die out before the last one passes away. This can be tricky to figure out, and we usually find out later. Sometimes, a species that was thought to be extinct reappears, like in old fossils. About 99 percent of all species, more than five billion, that have ever lived on Earth are believed to be extinct. Currently, scientists estimate there are around 8.7 million species of eukaryotes globally, but the number could be much higher if we count microorganisms like bacteria. Species appear through a process called speciation, where new types of organisms develop and thrive when they can use resources in a unique way. Species go extinct when they can't survive in changing conditions or when other species outcompete them. The relationship between animals and their environments is well understood. On average, a species lives for about 10 million years before becoming extinct, although some, called living fossils, barely change for hundreds of millions of years. Mass extinctions, when many species disappear at once, are rare. However, individual extinctions happen frequently. Recently, more extinctions have been recorded, and scientists are worried about the high rate of species loss. Many species that become extinct are never studied. Some scientists predict that up to half of the plant and animal species might disappear by 2100. In 2018, a report suggested that the loss of 300 mammal species during the human era would take 5 to 7 million years to recover. A 2019 report by IPBES stated that the amount of wild animal biomass has fallen by 82%, natural ecosystems have lost about half their area, and a million species are at risk of extinction—mostly due to human actions. Twenty-five percent of plant and animal species are threatened with extinction. In June 2019, one million species were at risk of extinction, with at least 571 lost since 1750, but the actual number might be higher. The main cause of extinctions is the destruction of natural habitats through activities like deforestation and converting land for farming. A symbol (†) next to a species name usually means it is extinct.

The Boston National Historical Park shows how Boston played a role in the American Revolution. It became a national park on October 1, 1974. Seven out of eight sites are linked by the Freedom Trail, a walking tour in downtown Boston. All eight places are considered national historic landmarks. Five of the sites are not owned or run by the National Park Service but work together through agreements. The National Park Service manages visitor centers in Faneuil Hall and the Charlestown Navy Yard.

Stuart Leonard Miller (December 26, 1927 – January 4, 2015) was a pitcher in Major League Baseball. He played for the St. Louis Cardinals from 1952 to 1956, the Philadelphia Phillies in 1956, the New York/San Francisco Giants from 1957 to 1962, the Baltimore Orioles from 1963 to 1967, and the Atlanta Braves in 1968. He threw and batted right-handed. Miller played in 16 seasons, winning 105 games and losing 103. He had 1164 strikeouts and 154 saves in 704 games. He was an All-Star for the Giants in 1961. In 1962, he had a high earned run average (ERA) of 4.12. In 1963, he had a better ERA of 2.24 and led the American League in games played, games finished, and saves. He was the closer for the Orioles and was 5th in MVP voting in 1965. Miller and Steve Barber pitched a no-hitter for the Orioles in 1967, but they lost 2-1. In 1967, he allowed Mickey Mantle's 500th career home run. Miller was also known as the "butterfly man" because of his quick and agile pitching. In one memorable All-Star game, Miller's pitching led to Roger Maris and Al Kaline advancing to bases. Stuart Miller had a successful career in baseball.

Priscilla Renea Hamilton, born on September 14, 1988, is an American singer and songwriter. She is with Capitol Records. Her first album, "Jukebox," came out on December 1, 2009. She is most famous for writing or co-writing hit songs like "California King Bed" by Rihanna, "Worth It" by Fifth Harmony, and "A No No" by Mariah Carey.

Mildred Ella "Babe" Didrikson Zaharias (June 26, 1911 – September 27, 1956) was an American athlete. She was very good at golf, basketball, baseball, and track and field. She won two gold medals in track and field at the 1932 Summer Olympics. Later, she played professional golf and won 10 LPGA major championships. People think she was one of the best athletes ever.

Geoff James Nugent, born on February 14, 1977, performs as Jim Jefferies. He is an American-Australian stand-up comedian, actor, and writer. He created and starred in the FX sitcom "Legit" from 2013 to 2014. He also hosted the Comedy Central late-night show "The Jim Jefferies Show" from 2017 to 2019.

Gauri Lankesh was born on January 29, 1962, and died on September 5, 2017. She was an Indian journalist and activist from Bangalore, Karnataka. Gauri worked as an editor for "Lankesh Patrike," a Kannada weekly started by her father. She also created her own weekly newspaper called "Gauri Lankesh Patrike." Gauri was shot outside her home. She was known for criticizing right-wing Hindu extremism. Gauri received the Anna Politkovskaya Award for speaking against right-wing Hindu extremism, supporting women's rights, and opposing caste-based discrimination.

In the creation myths of the Aztecs and other Nahua peoples, the term 'five suns' refers to the idea that the current world came after four previous worlds, which were created and then destroyed. This belief is part of the older mythological and cosmological traditions from central Mexico and Mesoamerica. The Aztec society inherited many of these traditions, but added their own interpretations. According to the late Postclassic Aztecs, there were four previous worlds or 'suns' before the current one. Each of these worlds was destroyed due to the actions of important gods. The current world is the fifth sun, and the Aztecs saw themselves as the 'people of the sun.' They believed their duty was to fight in a cosmic war to provide the sun with 'nourishment,' or blood and hearts. Without this, the sun would disappear. This means the survival of the universe depended on these offerings.
Bank of America Tower can refer to buildings that were previously called the Bank of America Tower.
Ouanne is a town in the Yonne department of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté in central France. There is also a river called Ouanne. The river begins near Ouanne and joins the Loing.

Dimitar Ivanov Berbatov, born on January 30, 1981, is a former Bulgarian football player. He played as a striker and was the captain of the Bulgaria national team from 2006 to 2010. He is the country's top goalscorer. Berbatov was born in Blagoevgrad and started his career with Pirin. In 1998, he joined CSKA Sofia at 17. In January 2001, he was signed by Bayer Leverkusen in Germany. He played in his first Champions League final 18 months later, coming on as a substitute in the 2002 UEFA Champions League final, where Leverkusen lost to Real Madrid 2-1. After five-and-a-half years with Leverkusen, he moved to Tottenham Hotspur in 2006, where he played for two years. In 2009, he joined Manchester United and played in the 2009 Champions League final, where his team lost to Barcelona 2-0. At Manchester United, he won two Premier League titles in 2008-09 and 2010-11 and was the Premier League Golden Boot winner in 2010-11. He moved to Fulham in 2012, then played for Monaco in France, PAOK in Greece, and Kerala Blasters in India before retiring at the end of the 2017-18 season. Berbatov made his debut for Bulgaria in 1999 at 18 and was their captain from 2006 to 2010. He scored 48 goals in 78 matches for his country. He won the Bulgarian Footballer of the Year award seven times, breaking the record set by Hristo Stoichkov.

The saying "the road to hell is paved with good intentions" means that having good intentions can sometimes lead to bad results. An alternative way to say this is "hell is full of good ideas, but heaven is full of actions."
Eclectic is a town in Elmore County, Alabama, United States. It became a town in 1907. In 2010, there were 1,001 people living there. It is part of the Montgomery metropolitan area.
Water Stratford is a village and civil parish near the River Great Ouse in Aylesbury Vale, Buckinghamshire, England. It is roughly west of Buckingham and close to the boundary with Oxfordshire.

graduation means giving a diploma or degree to students. It can also be a ceremony where students become graduates. The day of graduation is called graduation day. The ceremony itself may be known as commencement, convocation, or invocation.
Love Street" is a song by the American rock band The Doors. It is from their 1968 album called "Waiting for the Sun.

This article lists the NHL teams that have played in the playoffs and won series, reached the Stanley Cup Finals, and had Stanley Cup droughts up to the 2019 playoffs. Teams that have never been in the playoffs are listed by their first season in the league. Note: The 2004-05 season was cancelled, so it's not included. Currently, 31 NHL teams play. Eleven of them have never won the Stanley Cup. The Toronto Maple Leafs, one of the original six teams, haven't won in 52 seasons. Four teams have never reached the Stanley Cup Finals. The oldest of these is the Winnipeg Jets/Aztec Coyotes, with 38 seasons. The Maple Leafs have the longest championship drought at 52 seasons. The New York Rangers broke their long drought in 1994 after 53 seasons. The Chicago Blackhawks ended their 47-season drought in 2010, making it the second-longest. In 2010, 2011, and 2012, the Chicago Blackhawks, Boston Bruins, and Los Angeles Kings broke one of the top eleven longest droughts. The Florida Panthers have the longest active series win drought of 23 seasons. The Winnipeg Jets/Aztec Coyotes had the longest drought between series wins, 25 seasons, which ended in 2012. The Buffalo Sabres have the longest active playoff appearance drought of 9 seasons. The Florida Panthers and Edmonton Oilers had the longest playoff droughts of 10 seasons, ending in 2012 and 2017, respectively.

uranium-235 (U) is an isotope of uranium found in about 0.72% of natural uranium. Unlike the more common isotope uranium-238, uranium-235 can sustain a fission chain reaction. It is the only isotope of uranium that occurs naturally. Uranium-235 has a half-life of 703.8 million years. It was discovered in 1935 by Arthur Jeffrey Dempster. When hit by slow neutrons, uranium-235 can absorb them and split into smaller parts, with a cross-section of about 584.3±1 barns. For fast neutrons, the cross-section is smaller, around 1 barn. Most of the time, uranium-235 absorbs neutrons and splits, but sometimes it captures a neutron without splitting to form uranium-236.

Rūsiņš Mārtiņš Freivalds was a Latvian computer scientist and mathematician. He was born in Cēsis in 1942 and studied at Moscow State University. Freivalds became a member of the Latvian Academy of Sciences in 1992. He discovered Freivalds' algorithm for checking matrix products. He taught at the University of Latvia and had students like Daina Taimiņa and Andris Ambainis. Freivalds passed away from a heart attack in Riga in 2016, aged 73.
Hera Hilmarsdóttir, known as Hera Hilmar, was born on December 27, 1988. She is an Icelandic actress. She began acting as a child in the 1990s. She started acting again in 2008.

A foundation is a type of nonprofit organization that gives money and support to other charities through grants. Sometimes, foundations do charitable work directly. There are two main kinds: public charitable foundations, like community foundations, and private foundations, often set up by an individual or family. However, the word "foundation" can also describe organizations that don't give grants to the public.

A nucleosome is the basic unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes. It looks like a thread wrapped around a spool, with a piece of DNA wound around eight histone proteins. These histone proteins form a group called a histone octamer. Each histone octamer consists of two copies each of four types of proteins: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. DNA needs to be compacted into nucleosomes to fit inside the cell nucleus. After nucleosome wrapping, eukaryotic chromatin becomes more complex, eventually forming chromosomes. Nucleosomes may carry inherited information through changes in their histone proteins. The exact position of nucleosomes in the genome is important because it affects how accessible the DNA is to regulatory proteins. Nucleosomes were first seen in electron microscopes in 1974 by Don and Ada Olins. Roger Kornberg suggested their structure in 1974. In 1987 and 1988, Lorch et al. and Han and Grunstein showed that nucleosomes can act as gene repressors. Each nucleosome core particle contains about 146 DNA base pairs wrapped around a histone octamer. These particles are connected by stretches of linker DNA up to about 80 base pairs long. A nucleosome is often considered to be the core particle plus one of these linker regions. Maps showing where nucleosomes are located in the genome are now available for many organisms, including mouse liver and brain. Linker histones like H1 and its forms help compact the DNA, attaching to the linker region. Without linker histones, nucleosomes look like "beads on a string of DNA" under a microscope. In most eukaryotic cells, DNA is packaged by histones, but in mature sperm cells, protamines are used instead to achieve higher packaging. Nucleosomes are also found in archaea, suggesting they are not unique to eukaryotes.

A gauleiter was the leader of a regional Nazi party branch. This leader was in charge of an area called a "gau" or "reichsgau". The word can be singular or plural depending on the situation. Gauleiter was a Nazi party rank, just below the highest rank "reichtsleiter" and the top position "Führer". During World War II, someone could become a gauleiter only if directly chosen by Adolf Hitler.

Raziya al-Din, known as Razia Sultana, ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240. She was the first female Muslim ruler in the Indian subcontinent. Her father, Shamsuddin Iltutmish, made her his heir after being impressed by her performance in 1231-1232 when she helped run Delhi while he was away. However, she faced challenges. Razia's half-brother, Ruknuddin Firuz, became king after their father's death. Shah Turkan, Ruknuddin's mother, tried to kill Razia. During a rebellion, Razia won support from the people and took the throne in 1236. Some nobles opposed her, but she took more power. This upset the Turkic nobles, who didn't want her in charge. In April 1240, she was overthrown by a group of nobles after ruling for less than four years. She married one of the rebels, Ikhtiyaruddin Altunia, tried to get back the throne, but was defeated by her half-brother, Muizuddin Bahram, in October that year. She was killed shortly after.
Deer Park is a city in Hamilton County, Ohio, United States. It is near Cincinnati. In 2010, the city had 5,736 people.

The Jordan National Under-23 football team represents Jordan in international competitions, including the Olympic Games, Asian Games, and other under-23, under-22, and under-21 tournaments. The team is managed by the Jordan Football Association. In 2013, the Jordan Olympic team won the bronze medal in the AFC U-22 Championship in Oman.

Ganesh Chaturthi, also known as Vinayaka Chavithi, is a Hindu festival celebrating the arrival of Lord Ganesha from Mount Kailash with his mother Goddess Parvati. People set up clay idols of Ganesha at home or in temporary stages called pandals. There are prayers, fasting, and singing of religious texts during the festival. People offer sweets like modaka to Lord Ganesha, believed to be his favorite. The festival lasts for ten days, ending with a public procession and immersion of the idols in water. About 150,000 statues are immersed annually in Mumbai. After the immersion, Ganesha is believed to return to Mount Kailash. The festival celebrates Ganesha as the god of new beginnings, remover of obstacles, and god of wisdom and intelligence. It is widely celebrated in India, especially in Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Telangana, Odisha, West Bengal, Gujarat, and Chhattisgarh. In Tamil Nadu, it is usually celebrated privately at home. The festival is also observed in Nepal and by the Hindu community worldwide, including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Malaysia, Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Suriname, other parts of the Caribbean, Fiji, Mauritius, South Africa, the United States, and Europe. At public events, there are also competitions in sports and martial arts.

Indiana University of Pennsylvania (IUP) is a public research university in Indiana County, Pennsylvania. In fall 2019, it had 8,279 undergraduate students and 2,079 postgraduate students, making a total of 10,348 students. IUP is near Pittsburgh. It is run by a local council of trustees and the board of governors of the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education. IUP has smaller campuses in Punxsutawney, Northpointe, and Monroeville. IUP is also accredited by the Middle States Commission on Higher Education.
Vacco is a town in the Mendrisio district of Ticino in Switzerland. It is the last village in the Valle di Muggio.

The 2006 Winter Paralympic Games, also called "IX Giochi Paralimpici Invernali" in Italian, were the ninth Winter Paralympics. They happened in Turin, Italy, from March 10 to 19, 2006. These were the first Winter Paralympic Games held in Italy. They were also the first Paralympics to use the new Paralympics logo.
McIntire is a city in Mitchell County, Iowa, in the United States. In 2010, it had 122 people living there.

Ronald Vaughan Joyce, born on October 19, 1930, and passed away on January 31, 2019, was a Canadian entrepreneur and billionaire. He co-founded Tim Hortons, a doughnut chain, with Tim Horton in 1964. After Tim Horton's death, Ron Joyce played a key role in setting up Tim Horton Children's Camps and the Tim Hortons Children's Foundation. Joyce received many awards for his business success and charity work. He was named a member of the Order of Canada in 1992 for his dedication to helping underprivileged children and youth.

The federal government of Germany, which includes the federal chancellor and cabinet ministers, is the main executive body. The rules for organizing the cabinet, how it is chosen, and when it can be dismissed are written in Articles 62 to 69 of Germany's Basic Law. Unlike in the Weimar Republic, the Bundestag (the federal parliament) can only dismiss the chancellor if they also elect a new one at the same time. This means the whole cabinet, not just individual ministers, would be replaced. The Basic Law was made to prevent another dictatorship and to stop the political problems that happened in the Weimar Republic, where the Reichstag (the parliament) would remove chancellors but fail to choose a new one. If the chancellor loses a vote of confidence but doesn't get a new chancellor elected, they can ask the president to dissolve the Bundestag for a new election or declare a legislative emergency. The president isn't required to follow these requests. Chancellors and cabinet members can also be members of the Bundestag, and most of them are.

Sash!, a German DJ, released his third studio album called Trilenium. It came out on May 22, 2000, through the X-it label. People were not very excited about the album, and it only reached number 13 in the British charts.

Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, was born on April 7, 1853, and died on March 28, 1884. He was the youngest son of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Leopold became Duke of Albany, Earl of Clarence, and Baron Arklow. He had a health problem called haemophilia, which caused his death at the age of 30.

Rose Joan Blondell, born on August 30, 1906, and passed away on December 25, 1979, was an American actress who worked for about 50 years in films and on television. She started her career in vaudeville. After winning a beauty pageant, Blondell began acting in films. She became famous for her funny, sexy roles with Warner Bros. pictures and appeared in over 100 films and TV shows. She was most active in films during the 1930s and early 1940s. During that time, she acted in nine films with Glenda Farrell, playing gold diggers in each. Later in her life, she kept acting in smaller roles. She was nominated for an Academy Award for her role in "The Blue Veil" in 1951. Near the end, she was nominated for a Golden Globe for her role in "Opening Night" in 1977. She also starred in "Grease" in 1978 and "The Champ" in 1979, which was released just before her death from leukemia.

Roderick "Rody" Falesca van Rijnders was from the Netherlands. He was a coxswain. Rody won a silver medal in coxed pairs at the 1968 Summer Olympics with Hadriaan van Nes and Herman Suselbeek. He also won a bronze medal at the European level in 1965.

Bamba is a peanut butter-flavored snack made by the Osem Corporation in Kiryat Gat, Israel. Bamba is a popular snack in Israel. It has been sold since 1964 and people still buy it. Bamba takes up 25% of the snack market in Israel. Other companies also make similar snacks, like Parpar and Shush.

Fruitafossor was a termite-eating mammal that lived in North America during the late Jurassic period, about 150 million years ago. Based on a complete skeleton of an animal about the size of a chipmunk, it was discovered on March 31, 2005, in Fruita, Colorado. Fruitafossor looked like an armadillo or an anteater and likely ate insects, similar to how these animals eat today. However, its skeleton shows it was not related to armadillos, anteaters, or any modern mammals. This means that specializations for eating ants or termites evolved independently many times in mammals, including in Fruitafossor, anteaters, numbats, aardwolves, aardvarks, pangolins, and echidnas.

Samuel Cornelius Phillips was born on January 5, 1923, and died on July 30, 2003. He was an American record producer who was very important in making rock and roll popular in the 1950s. Phillips created Sun Records and Sun Studio in Memphis, Tennessee. At his studio, he produced music by famous artists like Elvis Presley, Roy Orbison, Jerry Lee Lewis, Carl Perkins, Johnny Cash, and Howlin' Wolf. He started Elvis Presley's music career in 1954. In 1969, Phillips sold Sun Records to Shelby Singleton. Phillips was also an early investor in Holiday Inn hotels. He owned and ran radio stations in Memphis, Florence, Alabama, and Lake Worth, Florida. He believed in equal rights and worked to break down racial barriers in the music industry.

Aleksandar Stipčević was born on October 10, 1930, and died on September 1, 2015. He was a Croatian archeologist, librarian, and historian who focused on the Illyrians. His most famous book, "Iliri" (meaning "The Illyrians"), was published in 1974. This book was also translated into English, Italian, and Albanian.
Dillingen is a "landkreis" (district) in Swabia, Bavaria, Germany. It borders the districts of Donau-Ries, Augsburg, and Günzburg, as well as the Heidenheim district in Baden-Württemberg.

Amol is a city and the main town in Amol County, in Mazandaran Province, Iran. In 2006, it had about 197,470 people living in 55,183 families. Amol is by the Haraz River and is close to the Caspian Sea and the Alborz Mountains. It is about west of Tehran and east of the provincial capital, Sari. Amol is an old and important city in Iran. It is known for its history and is famous in literature, such as in the Shahnameh. Amol is a center for industry, culture, and agriculture. It is also important for transportation, tourism, and dairy and meat products. It is sometimes called the "History, Science, and Philosophy City," "City That Does Not Die," and "Hezar Sangar City."

Aberfoyle is a village in Perthshire, Scotland. It is in the Stirling council area. The village is northwest of Glasgow. Aberfoyle's parish name comes from this village. In 2011, the village had 1,065 people.

"Avatar: The Last Airbender" is an American animated TV series created by Michael Dante Dimartino and Bryan Konietzko. It started on February 21, 2005, on Nickelodeon and ended on July 19, 2008. Each season of the show is called a "book," and each episode is a "chapter." There are three main "books" named after the four elements that the main character, Aang, must learn: water, earth, and fire. The first two books have 20 episodes each, and the third has 21. There are also two recap episodes and three short episodes. In the show, some people can control elements like air, water, earth, and fire. These people are called "benders." Not everyone can bend elements, and those who can usually only bend one. The avatar, Aang, is special because he can bend all four elements and talk to spirits. Aang is born in one nation and is reborn in another, following the order of air, water, earth, and fire. The story starts 100 years after the Fire Nation starts a war against the other nations. The Fire Nation wants to find Aang, who is hidden as an airbender. Aang was frozen in ice for 100 years and knows nothing about the war. The series begins when Aang is freed by Katara, a waterbender. The main story follows Aang and his friends—Sokka, Katara, and later Toph and Zuko—as they try to master all elements and defeat the Fire Nation. Zuko, the exiled crown prince of the Fire Nation, is also a major character. Zuko was hurt by his father, the current Fire Lord, and wants to capture Aang to win back his father’s favor and regain his honor.

Delphi (; ) was once called Pytho ( πυθώ ). It was an ancient sanctuary where the Pythia, an oracle, gave advice on important decisions to people from ancient Greece. The ancient Greeks believed the center of the world was in Delphi, marked by a stone monument called the Omphalos. Located on the southwest slope of Mount Parnassus, Delphi overlooks the coastal plain to the south and the Valley of Phocis. Today, it is an archaeological site with a small modern town nearby. UNESCO recognized Delphi as a World Heritage Site because it had a big influence in ancient times. Many important ancient Greek city-states built monuments there, showing their strong connection to Greek culture.

Mather Tower, also known as Lincoln Tower, is a tall building in Chicago. It is at 75 East Wacker Drive in the downtown area, next to the Chicago River. People call it "the inverted spyglass" because of its unique design. It has an 18-story octagonal tower on top of a 24-story rectangular part. This building was the tallest in Chicago when it was completed in 1928. It is very slim, with the smallest floor space per floor among Chicago skyscrapers. Architect Herbert Hugh Riddle designed it for the Mather Stock Car Company, which made train cars for transporting animals. The tower's design was influenced by Chicago's 1923 zoning law, which allowed buildings to be tall as long as the top floor was smaller than the bottom. Mather's founder, Alonzo Mather, was involved in the tower's design, including the octagonal tower. Plans for a second building behind it were cancelled due to the Great Depression. By the 1990s, the building was in bad shape. In 2000, a damaged top part called the "cupola" was removed. Later, the building was restored by Masterworks Development Corporation. Now, the bottom part is a hotel, and the top part is used by a membership company. The tower became a Chicago historic landmark in 2001 and received a national award in 2006.

In telecommunications and computer networks, multiplexing, or muxing, is a way to combine several signals into one signal for sharing on a single medium. This helps use a limited resource more efficiently. For example, many phone calls can use one wire. This method started in the 1870s with telegraphy and is now used widely in communications. In telephony, George Owen Squier developed carrier multiplexing in 1910. The combined signal is sent through a communication channel like a cable. This channel is divided into separate channels for each message or data stream. At the receiving end, a process called demultiplexing separates the original channels. A device that does multiplexing is called a multiplexer (MUX), and one that does demultiplexing is called a demultiplexer (DEMUX or DMX). Inverse multiplexing works the other way around. It splits one data stream into several, sends them over different channels, and then reassembles the original data stream. In computing, I/O multiplexing involves handling multiple input/output events using a single event loop, with system calls like poll and select in Unix.

John Landry "Buddy" Boudreaux was a musician from Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He played saxophone and clarinet. Since 1934, he led and performed in several bands that toured the southern United States. These bands attracted famous performers to Baton Rouge. In 1998, the State-Times newspaper named him "the city's sound of big band." His bands supported many well-known artists, including Andy Williams, Bernadette Peters, and Dionne Warwick. He also opened shows for Tony Bennett, Tony Orlando, and the Beach Boys. The song "My Baton Rouge," co-written by him and his barber, Michael T. Abadie, was declared the city's official song in 1998.
CAPIF is an Argentine organization that belongs to IFPI. IFPI represents the music industry in Argentina. CAPIF is a nonprofit group made up of big and smaller music companies.

In the "The Simpsons" episode "Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish," which is the fourth episode of the show's second season, it aired on November 1, 1990, on the Fox network. In the episode, Bart catches a fish with three eyes in a river near the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. An inspection of the plant shows many safety problems. Mr. Burns tries to become governor to stop the plant from closing. Before the election, Burns has a dinner with the Simpson family on TV to appeal to the common voter. However, Marge sabotages Burns's plan by serving him the head of Blinky, the three-eyed fish. The episode, written by Sam Simon and John Swartzwelder and directed by Wes Archer, was meant to be the season premiere but was replaced with "Bart Gets an F" because Bart was very popular in the early 1990s. The episode includes references to American movies, mainly "Citizen Kane," where Burns acts like the character Charles Foster Kane. Mary Bailey's name is similar to George Bailey's wife from "It's a Wonderful Life." People say the episode is a funny take on politics and the environment. It won an Environmental Media Award in 1991 for the best TV show with an environmental message. Since its first air, Blinky, the three-eyed fish, has been mentioned in news about nuclear waste and mutations. Critics liked the episode for its political satire, and it was the most-watched show on the Fox network that week.

June Gable, born on June 5, 1945, is an American actress. She is famous for playing Estelle Leonard, Joey's agent, in the NBC show "Friends." She also got nominated for a Tony Award for her work on Broadway.
James Rempe, born on November 4, 1947, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, is an American professional pool player. He was inducted into the Billiard Congress of America's Hall of Fame in 2002.
