A rectifier changes alternating current (AC), which flows in both directions, into direct current (DC), which only flows in one direction. This process is called "rectification." Rectifiers come in different forms such as vacuum tube diodes, wet cells, mercury-arc valves, and semiconductor diodes. Early ones used a crystal detector with a small wire touching a crystal of galena. Rectifiers are used in DC power supplies and high-voltage direct current systems. They can also detect radio signals or flames. For smooth DC, an electronic filter like a capacitor or choke may be used. Inverting the process from DC to AC is called an "inverter."

Virginia City is a town in Madison County, Montana, United States. In 1961, it and the surrounding area became a national historic landmark district called the Virginia City Historic District. The town had 190 people in 2010.

Emily Bishop is a fictional character in the British TV show "Coronation Street." She is played by Eileen Derbyshire and is the longest-standing female character, first appearing on December 21, 1960. Derbyshire took a break from the show in 2015 and returned briefly for a short appearance in 2019 to celebrate Ken Barlow's 80th birthday. Emily left the show on January 1, 2016, after 55 years.

A nuclear submarine uses a nuclear reactor for power. Compared to "conventional" (usually diesel-electric) submarines, nuclear submarines have many advantages. They don't need to surface often because nuclear power doesn't rely on air. This allows them to travel much faster for longer periods. Plus, they can go for many years without needing fuel, as modern nuclear subs can run for 25 years without refueling. In contrast, conventional submarines can only stay submerged for a few days at slow speed and a few hours at high speed. Only a few countries have nuclear submarines due to high costs. Some of the worst nuclear accidents have happened with Soviet submarines.

Septimia Zenobia, also known as Bat-Zabbai in Palmyrene, lived from around 240 to 274 AD. She was a queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Legends say she came from a wealthy family and married Odaenathus, the ruler of the city. After Odaenathus died, Zenobia became the leader of her son, Vaballathus, and controlled the region. In 270, she led an invasion that brought much of the Roman East under Palmyrene rule, including Egypt. By mid-271, her empire extended from central Anatolia to southern Egypt, but she still paid homage to Rome. In 272, after Aurelian's campaign, Zenobia declared her son an emperor and she became the empress, breaking away from Rome. The Romans defeated her, and she was taken to Rome and lived there until her death after 274. Zenobia was a learned queen who encouraged learning and was kind to her people, protecting religious minorities. Her story inspired many people over time, and she is seen as a symbol of Syrian pride.
This is a list of rivers in Saint Lucia. The rivers are listed going around the island, starting from the northern part.

Jabalpur, formerly known as Jubbulpore (until 2006), is a city in Madhya Pradesh, India. It is one of the biggest cities in the state. According to the 2011 census, Jabalpur is the third-largest urban area in Madhya Pradesh and the 38th-largest in the country. The city is famous for Dhuandhar Falls and the White Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat. People believe the game of snooker started here. Jabalpur is important for government work, industry, and business. It is also a big place for education. The city has a high court, state government headquarters, and many industries, including four major Indian Ordnance Factories. It is a major trading center and producer of forest products, growing fast. Jabalpur is the main city of Jabalpur district, the second-largest in Madhya Pradesh, and the administrative center of a division. Historically, it was part of the Kalachuri and Rajgond dynasties. In the early 1800s, it became part of British India and was renamed Jubbulpore. It has military bases and is the headquarters for the West Central Railway, Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board, Tropical Forest Research Institute, and army headquarters for five states. The city is also home to the 1 Signal Training Centre.

In chemistry, an ester is a compound made from an acid (organic or inorganic) with a hydroxyl group replaced by an alkoxy group. Typically, esters are created by a reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Glycerides, which are fatty acid esters of glycerol, are important in biology as a major type of lipid, found in animal fats and vegetable oils. Some esters, with a low molecular weight, are used as fragrances in essential oils and pheromones. In DNA, phosphoesters form the backbone. Nitrate esters, like nitroglycerin, are known for their explosive nature. Polyester, an ester, is a key plastic. Esters usually have a sweet smell and are good solvents for plastics, plasticizers, resins, and lacquers. They are also widely used as commercial lubricants.

The division of northern Melbourne was an Australian electoral area in Victoria. It was in the inner northern suburbs of Melbourne and was named that way. It covered parts of Carlton, North Melbourne, and Fitzroy. In July 1906, it was replaced by the Batman division. The division was represented by one member, H. B. Higgins, who was attorney general from 1904 to 1905. Higgins did not run for the Batman division in the 1906 election because he became a justice of the High Court of Australia in 1906.

cultured meat is made by growing animal cells in a lab, not by slaughtering animals. It is a type of cellular agriculture. The idea of cultured meat was introduced by Jason Matheny in the early 2000s. He wrote an important paper about it and helped set up New Harvest, a non-profit that supports research on cultured meat. In 2013, Mark Post, a professor, created the first burger patty made from cells in a lab. Several companies have since shown prototypes of cultured meat, but it isn't available in stores yet. Memphis Meats and SuperMeat say they will sell lab-grown meat in 2020. People haven't tried it yet, so it's not known if they will like it. The process is still being improved, but it could have many benefits, such as being better for health, the environment, and the economy.

John Guillermin, born on November 11, 1925, and died on September 27, 2015, was a British film director, writer, and producer. He worked mostly on big, action adventure films. Some of his famous films include "I Was Monty's Double" (1958), "Tarzan's Greatest Adventure" (1959), "Never Let Go" (1960), "Tarzan Goes to India" (1962), "Waltz of the Toreadors" (1962), "The Blue Max" (1966), "The Bridge at Remagen" (1969), "The Towering Inferno" (1974), "King Kong" (1976), "Death on the Nile" (1978), "Sheena" (1984), and "King Kong Lives" (1986). From the 1980s, he worked on less important projects. His last films were lower budget theatrical releases and TV movies. John Guillermin was known to be very strict and sometimes angry. He often shouted at actors and crew members. This made some producers and actors unhappy. However, his skills in capturing both small and big scenes were excellent.

Wake up! Pope Francis released a music album on November 27, 2015, on Believe Digital. The album has Pope Francis' words and prayers. It includes speeches he made in different places between 2013 and 2015. There is also music of prayers and hymns by Italian artists and producers.
People's Palace can mean:

Blanco County, named after the Blanco River, is in Texas. It had 10, 497 people in 2010. The main town is Johnson City. Texas made Blanco County in 1858 from parts of Burnet, Comal, Gillespie, and Hays counties. Blanco was the county seat from 1858 to 1890, then it changed to Johnson City.
Peoria County is in Illinois, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 186, 494 people. The main city is Peoria. Peoria County is in the Peoria, Illinois metro area.

Belkin International, Inc., is an American company that makes consumer electronics, focusing on connectivity devices. Based in Playa Vista, Los Angeles, California, it sells various products like routers, iPod and iPhone accessories, mobile computing accessories, surge protectors, and network switches. Belkin also offers hubs, USB and computer network cables, KVM switches, racks, and enclosures. The company owns Belkin, Linksys, and Wemo brands, as well as a smart home water management company called Phyn.

Irrigation is the process of giving plants water at the right times. It helps grow crops for farming, keeps gardens healthy, and lets plants grow in dry places when it doesn't rain much. Irrigation also helps protect plants from frost, stop weeds, and stop the ground from becoming too hard. When farming relies only on rain, it's called rain-fed. Irrigation systems are used for many things, like keeping animals cool, stopping dust, sending waste away, and in mining. It's often studied with drainage, which is taking water away from a place. For over 5,000 years, irrigation has been important in farming and has helped many cultures and regions.

X-Men: The Last Stand, also known as X3 or X-Men 3, is a 2006 movie about superheroes. It's the follow-up to X2 from 2003 and the third film in the X-Men series. Brett Ratner directed, and Simon Kinberg and Zak Penn wrote it. Many actors are in it, including Hugh Jackman, Halle Berry, Ian McKellen, and others. The story is partly based on two comic book arcs. It's about a "mutant cure" and the comeback of Jean Grey, which affects mutants and humans. Bryan Singer, who directed the first two films, left to make Superman Returns. James Marsden was in it but left before filming, so his character dies. Matthew Vaughn was hired as the new director but left, replaced by Ratner. Filming lasted from August 2005 to January 2006 with a big budget of $210 million, making it the most expensive film at the time. It had lots of special effects. The movie came out on May 26, 2006, from 20th Century Fox. It made about $459 million worldwide, being the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2006 and the highest at the time for the X-Men series. Reviews were mixed, praising the acting, music, and action scenes but criticizing the script and lack of dynamics.

Rudi van Dantzig was born on August 4, 1933, and passed away on January 19, 2012. He was a Dutch choreographer, company director, and writer. Van Dantzig was very important in making Dutch ballet famous all over the world during the second half of the 20th century.

Parma is a city in northern Italy, in the region of Emilia-Romagna. It is known for its buildings, music, art, ham, cheese, and surrounding countryside. Parma has a university, one of the oldest in the world. The city is split by a stream. The part on the other side of the river is called "oltretorrente." Parma's Etruscan name became the word for a round shield in Roman times. An Italian poet, Attilio Bertolucci, said: "As a capital city, it had to have a river. As a small capital, it got a stream, which is often dry."

A bottle cap seals the top opening of a bottle. It is usually colorful and has the brand's logo. Plastic caps are for plastic bottles. Metal caps with plastic backing are for glass bottles. The metal is usually steel. Some plastic caps have a pour spout. Flip-top caps give controlled dispensing of dry products. Caps for plastic bottles are often made of a different plastic type.

David Wark Griffith, born on January 22, 1875, and died on July 23, 1948, was an American film director. He is considered one of the most important filmmakers of his time. He helped create long movies that could be shown in theaters. His film "The Birth of a Nation" (1915) made people money, but it also caused a lot of arguments because it showed African Americans in a bad way and made the Ku Klux Klan look good. "Intolerance" (1916) was made to answer his critics, but it didn't say sorry for the negative images of African Americans in his movies. Some of Griffith's other films, like "Broken Blossoms" (1919), "Way Down East" (1920), and "Orphans of the Storm" (1921), were also successful. But he often spent too much money on making and promoting his films, which made them fail in the theaters. By the time he made his last big movie, "The Struggle" (1931), he had directed about 500 films. Griffith, along with Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, and Douglas Fairbanks, started a company called United Artists. This allowed them to control their own work and not depend on big movie studios. He was also one of the people who started the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

A mathematical proof is an argument that shows a statement is true based on given assumptions. It uses previous statements, like theorems, and basic rules to build a logical case. Every proof can start with basic rules called axioms. Presenting many cases is not enough; a proof must show the statement is true in all cases. A statement believed true but not proven is called a conjecture or hypothesis. Proofs mix symbols and words, but written proofs are mostly in natural language. Formal proofs, fully in symbols, are studied in proof theory. How proofs are used shows differences between formal and informal math practice, and how math is a language is a topic in math philosophy.

This list shows world heritage sites in France. These sites are either culturally or naturally important, or both. France joined the UNESCO World Heritage Convention in 1975 and can nominate sites for the list. As of now, 44 French sites are on the list. Of these, 39 are cultural, 4 are natural, and 1 is mixed. Three sites are shared between countries. The oldest site was added in 1979, and the most recent in 2019. Five sites were proposed in 1979. France's tentative list includes 37 sites. UNESCO uses different types of sites: cultural, natural, and mixed. They choose sites based on criteria I to VI for culture and VII to X for nature. The dates on the list show when sites were added, and the submission dates are for the tentative list. Each site's number connects to its description on the UNESCO website.

Kimble County is in Texas, on the Edwards Plateau. In 2010, it had 4,607 people. The county seat is Junction. It was created in 1858 and organized in 1876. The county is named after George C. Kimble, who died at the Battle of the Alamo.
Gagny is a town in the eastern part of Paris, France. It is situated near the center of Paris.

The Salt Fork of the Arkansas River is a smaller river that joins the Arkansas River. It is in southern Kansas and northern Oklahoma in the United States. Through the Arkansas River, it is part of the Mississippi River watershed.

Elizabeth Bonnin, born on September 16, 1975, is a presenter from France and Ireland. She works in science, wildlife, and nature shows on TV in Ireland and the UK. She is also a biochemist and wild animal biologist. In the early 2000s, she hosted morning shows and music shows like "Top of the Pops." She is famous for presenting programs such as "Galapagos," "How the Earth Works," "Animals in Love," "Stargazing Live," "Blue Planet Live," "Cats v Dogs: Which is Best?" and "Should We Close Our Zoos?" From 2009 to 2014, she co-hosted BBC's factual series "Bang Goes the Theory." Since 2013, she has co-hosted ITV's "Countrywise." In 2019, she presented "Meat: A Threat to Our Planet?"

Don Ammache, born Dominic Felix Amici on May 31, 1908, and died on December 6, 1993, was an American actor and comedian. After performing in college shows, stock, and vaudeville, he became a popular radio star in the early 1930s. This led to a movie contract with 20th Century Fox in 1935. He was a handsome and charming leading man in 40 films over the next 14 years. He was popular in comedies, dramas, and musicals. In the 1950s, he worked on Broadway and in television. He hosted NBC's "International Showtime" from 1961 to 1965. In his later years, he returned to film work. He had a successful comeback, playing a villain in "Trading Places" (1983) and winning an Academy Award for best supporting actor for his role in "Cocoon" (1985).

Didier Yves Drogba Tébily, born on March 11, 1978, is a retired Ivorian footballer who played as a striker. He was the top scorer and former captain of the Ivory Coast national team. Drogba is well-known for his career at Chelsea, where he scored more goals than any other foreign player and is the club's fourth highest all-time scorer. He was named one of Chelsea's greatest players and was in the Chelsea team of the 2010-2020 decade. Drogba was named African Footballer of the Year twice, in 2006 and 2009. He started his professional career at Le Mans in 1996 and moved to Guingamp in 2001, where he scored 17 goals in 34 matches. He then went to Olympique de Marseille, where he scored 19 goals and helped the club reach the 2004 UEFA Cup final. In 2004, he moved to Chelsea for £24 million, setting a club record. In his first season, he helped Chelsea win their first league title in 50 years. A year later, he won another league title. He was named in the FIFA World XI for 2007. In March 2012, Drogba became the first African player to score 100 Premier League goals. Two months later, he scored in the 2012 FA Cup final, becoming the first player to score in four separate FA Cup finals. He also scored in the 2012 UEFA Champions League final, equalizing in the 88th minute and scoring the winning penalty. After a stint with Shanghai Shenhua in China and Galatasaray in Turkey, where he scored the winning goal in the 2013 Turkish Super Cup, Drogba returned to Chelsea in 2014. He retired at the age of 40 in 2018. Drogba was an Ivorian international from 2002 to 2014, captaining the national team from 2006 until his retirement. He is the nation's all-time top goalscorer with 65 goals from 105 appearances. He led the Ivory Coast to their first FIFA World Cup in 2006 and captained the team at the 2010 and 2014 World Cups. He retired from international football on August 8, 2014. After retiring, he became vice president of Peace and Sport on December 11, 2018.

Robert Ray "Rod" Roddy was an American announcer for radio and TV. He was known for announcing game shows, including "Whew!" and "Press Your Luck" on CBS. He is famous for saying "Come on down!" on "The Price is Right." This phrase is on his gravestone. Roddy took over for the previous announcer, Johnny Olson, on "The Price is Right" in 1986. He stayed as the announcer until he died in 2003 and was the longest-serving announcer on the show until 2020. Roddy also appeared on camera in many episodes of "Press Your Luck" and "The Price is Right." He voiced Mike the Microphone on "Disney's House of Mouse" from 2001 until his death.

Travers was a town in the Val-de-Travers district of the Neuchâtel canton in Switzerland. On January 1, 2009, Travers merged with the towns of Boveresse, Buttes, Couvet, Fleurier, Les Bayards, Môtiers, Noiraigue, and Saint-Sulpice to form the new Val-de-Travers municipality.

Hurricane Dora was the first hurricane to hit Florida's east coast. It was the sixth tropical storm and the second hurricane of the 1964 season. Dora started as a tropical wave near Senegal on August 28. It was upgraded to a tropical storm on September 1 after an airplane flight. Dora then moved northeast and grew stronger. By September 3, it was a Category 1 hurricane. Six hours later, it became a Category 2. The storm intensified more on September 5 and reached its strongest point as a Category 4 with winds of 130 mph. On September 6 at 6 PM, it weakened to a Category 3. Later that day, it became a Category 2 and headed west. On September 7, Dora continued as a Category 2 storm as it approached Florida's east coast. Its movement became erratic, making loops. At 4 AM on September 10, it hit St. Augustine, Florida, with winds of 110 mph. By September 11, it was just a tropical storm over land. Dora moved over southwestern Georgia, then turned east-northeast. Early on September 14, it re-entered the Atlantic Ocean near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and became an extratropical cyclone. The remnants of Dora moved northeast and dissipated off Newfoundland on September 16. Along the coast, tides were very high. Strong winds hit northern Florida, with the highest wind recorded in St. Augustine at 125 mph. In Jacksonville, about 156,000 customers lost electricity, and 19% of phones in Duval County were out of service. Most of the damage in Jacksonville was to older buildings and coastal areas. The city also experienced flooding from the St. Johns River. Heavy rain damaged crops and flooded many roads and bridges, isolating some communities for days. In Florida, 74 houses were flattened and 9,374 received damage. About 50 farm buildings and 423 small businesses were severely damaged or destroyed. Three people died, and damages were about $230 million. In Georgia, about 1,135 homes were damaged, and five were destroyed. Eighteen trailers suffered major damage, and 43 small businesses were destroyed or severely damaged. One person died, and damages were about $9 million. Other states were affected, but the damage was much less. Overall, Hurricane Dora caused $280 million in damage and five deaths.
An icon, from the Greek word for image, is a religious painting in Eastern Christianity. It may also refer to:

The Samsung Galaxy S6 is a type of smartphone. It was made and sold by Samsung Electronics and came after the Galaxy S5. There were actually two versions: the Galaxy S6 and the Galaxy S6 Edge. The main difference was that the Edge had a screen that curved around the sides. Samsung showed these at a big event on March 1, 2015, and they went on sale on April 10, 2015. At another event in August 2015, Samsung added a third version, the Galaxy S6 Edge+, which had a bigger screen and more memory but couldn't control devices with infrared. The S6 had a metal body and glass back, which was different from earlier models. It also had a better camera, a simpler user interface, could charge wirelessly, and supported mobile payments. Critics liked the S6 because it was better built than before and had better displays, performance, and camera. However, some users didn't like that it couldn't be expanded or have the battery removed. The S6 Edge was also criticized for not using its curved screen much, so it cost more but didn't offer much extra. The Galaxy S7 came out in March 2016 and replaced it.

Sir John Elliot was born on May 6, 1898, and died on September 18, 1988. He was a British transport and railway manager. His birth name was John Elliot Blumenfeld. His father was R. D. Blumenfeld, who worked as the news editor of the "Daily Mail." Later, his father became the managing editor of the "Daily Express." In March 1923, Sir John changed his last name to Elliot, his mother's surname, as advised by Lord Beaverbrook.

irredentism refers to movements that claim and seek to regain territory considered lost by the movement's members. They believe this territory belongs to their nation, based on history or legend. Sometimes, disputes arise about the exact boundaries and whether these claims represent expansionism.

The KGB, or Committee for State Security, was the main security agency in the Soviet Union from 1954 to 1991. It continued the work of earlier agencies like the Cheka, NKGB, NKVD, and MGB. The KGB reported to the Council of Ministers and was responsible for internal security, intelligence, and secret police work. Similar agencies existed in each Soviet republic, except for the Russian SFSR. The KGB was treated like a military service, following army laws and regulations. Its main duties included foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence, and protecting government leaders, borders, and communications. The KGB split into the Federal Security Service and the Foreign Intelligence Service of the Russian Federation after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991. In the early 1990s, South Ossetia, with Russian help, created its own KGB, keeping the same name. Belarus also established its own security agency called the State Security Committee.
Tagsdorf is a commune in Haut-Rhin, which is in Alsace, in northeastern France.
Brienzwiler is a municipality in the Interlaken-Oberhasli district, which is in the canton of Bern, Switzerland. It includes the village of Brienzwiler and the settlement of Balmhof.

Parker Brothers was an American toy and game company that became part of Hasbro in 1991. They made over 1,800 games since 1883. Some of their popular games include Monopoly, Clue, Sorry!, Risk, Trivial Pursuit, Ouija, Aggravation, Bop It, and Probe. After Parker Brothers became part of Hasbro, they stopped using the Parker Brothers name. However, in 2017, Hasbro brought back the Parker Brothers brand by releasing new games that are similar to some of their well-known older games.
The epicenter in seismology is the point on the Earth's surface directly above where an earthquake or underground explosion starts. This point is directly above the hypocenter or focus.

Elephant polo is a type of polo played on elephants. It is played in Nepal, Rajasthan (India), and Thailand. Teams from England and Scotland also play. For this game, you use a regular polo ball and sticks made of cane, about six to ten feet long. The playing area is shorter than a usual polo field because elephants move slower. Two people ride each elephant. One person, called a mahout, guides the elephant. The other player directs the mahout and hits the ball. Elephant polo started in Meghauli, Nepal, and Tiger Tops in Nepal is where the world championships take place. In Nepal and Thailand, games follow rules set by the World Elephant Polo Association (WEP). Other countries, like India and Sri Lanka, run their own tournaments. Sri Lanka had an annual tournament in Galle organized by the Ceylon Elephant Polo Association. In 2007, an elephant got angry during a game, hurting two players and damaging the Spanish team's bus. People who care about animal welfare have said the elephants are treated cruelly. This led to games being cancelled, sponsors stopping support, and the removal of elephant polo records from the Guinness Book of World Records. In October 2018, the Thailand Elephant Polo Association said they would stop playing elephant polo matches. They used to host a tournament at the Anantara Hotel Bangkok.
Stapleton can mean: A surname A place name

Lily Chloe Ninette Thomson, born on April 5, 1989, is known as Lily James and is an English actress. She studied acting at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London. Her acting career started in the British TV series "Just William" in 2010. After playing a supporting role in the period drama series "Downton Abbey" from 2012 to 2015, she had a big break as the main character in the fantasy film "Cinderella" in 2015. James then played Natasha Rostova in the period TV series "War & Peace" in 2016. She starred in several films, including "Baby Driver" (2017), "Darkest Hour" (2017), "The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society" (2018), "Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again" (2018), and "Yesterday" (2019).

Barley, also known as "hordeum vulgare," is a type of cereal grain from the grass family. It is grown in many places with cooler climates around the world. People started growing barley a long time ago, around 10,000 years ago, especially in Asia and Europe. Barley can be used for different things, like feeding animals, making beer and alcohol, and eating as a food. It is used in soups and bread in various cultures. Barley grains can also be turned into malt. In 2017, barley was the fourth most grown grain, after maize, rice, and wheat.

In physics, Gauss's law for magnetism is one of the four Maxwell's equations that form the basis of classical electrodynamics. This law states that the magnetic field has no source or sink; it is always a solenoidal vector field. It essentially means that magnetic monopoles, or single magnetic charges, do not exist. Instead, the fundamental entity for magnetism is the magnetic dipole. If magnetic monopoles were found, this law would need to be changed. Gauss's law for magnetism can be expressed in two forms: the "differential form" and the "integral form." Both forms are equivalent due to a mathematical principle called the divergence theorem. The term "Gauss's law for magnetism" is not used everywhere. Sometimes, it is called the "absence of free magnetic poles," and one reference even states it has "no name." It is also referred to as the "transversality requirement," as it demands that the polarization be perpendicular to the direction of propagation for plane waves.
glinde can refer to several places in Germany. See also: glynde.
Fabien Eboussi Boulaga was a philosopher from Cameroon. He was born on January 17, 1934, and died on October 13, 2018.

Michael Francis McCormack, born on August 2, 1964, is an Australian politician. He has been the leader of the National Party and the deputy prime minister since February 2018. McCormack is also in charge of infrastructure, transport, and regional development. Before that, he worked as the minister for defence personnel and minister for veterans' affairs from 2017 to 2018. He became a member of the House of Representatives in 2010, representing Riverina in New South Wales. Before politics, he was a newspaper editor.

Eldorado is a city in Saline County, Illinois, United States. In 2010, it had 4,122 people, and in 1980, the population was higher at 5,198. The city's name used to be spelled "Eldero" or "Elder-redo," combining the last names of its founders: Judge Samuel Elder, his son William, his grandson Francis Marion, and his neighbor Joseph Reed, along with his brother William. Legend says a sign painter changed the name to "Eldorado" on the train depot. This spelling and pronunciation (el-do-ray-doh) stuck. Eldorado is part of the Illinois–Indiana–Kentucky area and is a place where people live but do not work, in the Harrisburg micropolitan area.

vellum is a material made from animal skin, used for writing or printing. It is sometimes called parchment. Vellum, specifically, is usually made from calfskin and considered higher quality than other types of animal skin. It can be used to create pages, scrolls, books, or codices. The term comes from the Latin "vitulinum," meaning "calfskin," and "vélin" in old French. Modern experts prefer to use the term "membrane" due to confusion. Without a lab, it can be hard to identify the animal type. Vellum is smooth and durable but can vary in quality. The production involves cleaning, stretching the skin on a frame, scraping it with a knife, and alternating wetting and drying to create tension. A final finish may involve pumice and treatments with lime or chalk. Modern "paper vellum" is made from synthetic plant material, similar in quality and use. It is used for tracing, technical drawings, plans, and blueprints.

Bihar Muslims are people from the Indian state of Bihar who follow Islam. Most Bihar Muslims belong to the Sunni sect. Even before the Mughal era, all religious leaders in Bihar, like ulemas, mullas, and sufis, were Sunni. However, there are also many Shia Muslims in Patna. These Shia Muslims came from Lucknow in the 1800s.

Morehouse Parish is in Louisiana, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 27, 979 people. The main town is Bastrop. Morehouse Parish was created in 1844. It is part of the Bastrop, LA micropolitan statistical area, which is included in the Monroe–Ruston–Bastrop, LA combined statistical area.

The Virginia Plan, also called the Randolph Plan after its creator, or the large-state plan, suggested a strong national government with three parts and two legislative chambers. James Madison wrote it before the 1787 Constitutional Convention started. This plan was important because it guided the main topics discussed during the convention. It especially proposed that the national legislature should represent states based on population. The Virginia Plan helped large states. In response, the New Jersey Plan was created to support smaller states.
Johnny Rozsa is a photographer based in New York. He takes pictures of fashion, people, and famous individuals.
Bud Brown could mean:

Marina Abramović, born on November 30, 1946, is a Serbian artist. She works in conceptual and performance art, also helps people through philanthropy and film. Her art looks at the body, how long someone can perform, and ideas about men and women. She has been active for over forty years and calls herself the "grandmother of performance art." Abramović is known for involving observers and exploring "pain, blood, and the body's limits."

Sharsheret is a nonprofit organization that helps Jewish women with breast cancer and ovarian cancer. They provide healthcare resources, money help, support groups, and educational programs to thousands of women and their families in the United States. Sharsheret has offices in California, Florida, Illinois, New Jersey, and New York. Their main office is in Teaneck, New Jersey. They focus on young women and Jewish families because Ashkenazi Jews are more likely to have a BRCA gene change. But they also help people from other backgrounds.

The term "orient" means "east" and traditionally includes areas to the east of Europe. It is the opposite of "occident," which means the western world. In English, "orient" is often used to refer to Asia, which is divided into regions like the Near East, Middle East, and Far East. These regions include areas such as West Asia, South Asia, East Asia, and Southeast Asia. The word "oriental" is sometimes used to describe things from the orient. However, because it has a European focus and its meaning has changed over time, some people in North America consider it offensive when used to describe people from East Asian or Southeast Asian countries.

Go-Ahead London is the name used for all bus operations in London by the Go-Ahead Group. This name started in August 2008. Before that, the company used different names and brands. Go-Ahead London is the biggest bus company in London, running 115 bus routes for Transport for London.

Hurricane Gloria was the first big storm to hit northeastern United States since Hurricane Agnes in 1972. It was the first major storm to directly affect New York City and Long Island since Hurricane Donna in 1960. Gloria formed from a tropical wave in the Atlantic Ocean and intensified into a powerful hurricane on September 22, 1985. It hit North Carolina's Outer Banks on September 27, and then landed twice on Long Island and Connecticut on the same day. Gloria became an extratropical storm over New England on September 28. Before hitting the coast, the National Hurricane Center warned parts of the East Coast. Many people evacuated, and Gloria was called the "storm of the century." Its strongest winds stayed east of the center, sparing some areas. But it knocked down trees and power lines, leaving over 4 million people without power. On Long Island, about 1.5 million people lost power, causing the Long Island Lighting Company to be replaced. Six people died because of fallen trees. In North Carolina, high waves damaged homes and caused beach erosion. The storm surge destroyed 48 homes on Long Island and damaged many roofs. Flooding closed highways, and thousands had to leave their homes in Pennsylvania. Crop damage amounted to about $20 million. Total damage in the United States was estimated at $900 million. In Canada, Gloria's remnants caused minor power outages in New Brunswick.

Colusa was formerly known as Colusi, Colusi's, Koru, and Salmon Bend. It is the county seat of Colusa County, California. In 2010, the population was 5,971, up from 5,402 in 2000. The name Colusi comes from the local Coru Native American tribe. In the 1840s, this tribe lived on the opposite side of the Sacramento River.
This list includes NHL players who played at least one game from 1917 to now and have last names starting with "S". The list was last updated for the 2018–19 NHL season.

Student transport means taking children and teenagers to and from schools and school events. They can walk, ride a bicycle, or even ride a horse (for younger students). Older students might drive cars. Family members or caregivers can also go with them. Sometimes, the transport is organized by the school using buses or taxis.

The Shaolin Temple, also called Shaolin Monastery, is a Chan Buddhist temple in Dengfeng County, Henan Province, China. It is said to have been founded in the fifth century. The Shaolin Temple is the main temple of the Shaolin school of Buddhism today. It is located west of the city of Zhengzhou. In 2010, the Shaolin Monastery and its pagoda forest were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the "Historic Monuments of Dengfeng".

The Yakovlev Yak-18 is a two-seater military training plane. It was made in the Soviet Union. It first used a 119 kW (160 hp) Shvetsov M-11FR-1 engine. Service began in 1946. A version was also made in China as the Nanchang CJ-5.

Edward Paul Abbey, born on January 29, 1927, and died on March 14, 1989, was an American writer and essayist. He wrote about nature and criticized how public lands were managed. He is famous for his book "The Monkey Wrench Gang." This book has inspired environmental and eco-terrorist groups. He also wrote a non-fiction book called "Desert Solitaire."

Pärnu is the fourth largest city in Estonia. Tallinn, the capital city, is north of Pärnu. Tartu, Estonia's second largest city, is to the east. Pärnu is in southwestern Estonia, by the coast of Pärnu Bay, which is part of the Gulf of Riga in the Baltic Sea. It is a popular summer holiday destination with many hotels and restaurants, and big beaches. The Pärnu River goes through the city and ends at the Gulf of Riga. Pärnu had an airport.

The national flag of Singapore was adopted in 1959, the year Singapore became self-governing. It was officially recognized as the national flag again when Singapore became fully independent from Malaysia on August 9, 1965. Before Singapore became independent, its flag was the only state flag in Malaysia that was not the usual 1:2 ratio. The flag has two main colors: red on top and white below. In the top left corner, there is a white crescent moon with a white five-pointed star underneath it. The flag symbolizes a young nation that is growing, friendship among people, and good ideas for the country. Boats at sea do not use the national flag as their main flag. Instead, merchant and pleasure boats use a civil ensign with a red background and a white crescent and star emblem in the center. Non-military government boats, like coast guard ships, use a state ensign with a blue background and the national flag in the top left corner, along with a red and white compass design at the bottom. Naval warships use a similar state ensign, but in white with a red compass emblem. There are rules for using and displaying the flag. People can now fly it on vehicles during national holidays and at home throughout the year.

NCAA Division I (D-I) is the highest level of college sports in the United States, run by the NCAA. D-I schools have bigger budgets, better facilities, and give out more athletic scholarships than Division II and III schools. They also compete at the highest level. This used to be called the University Division, but changed to Division I in 1973. Division II and III were created from splitting the College Division. Division I schools offer scholarships and want to compete against each other, while Division III schools do not. For college football, D-I schools are divided into FBS and FCS, with FBS having higher attendance and more scholarships. The FCS has a tournament to decide a national champion. In 2014, D-I had 345 out of 1,066 NCAA schools, with 125 in FBS, 125 in FCS, and 95 without football. Schools moving up to D-I need to join a conference and show they can support it financially.

Varduhi Varderesyan was an Armenian actress. She moved to Armenia in 1946 and finished her studies at the Leninakan Drama Theatre Studio. She then worked at the same theater. From 1958, she was one of the main actresses at the Sundukyan Drama Theatre in Yerevan. In 1988, she was named a People's Artist of the USSR. In 2002, she was honored as an honorary citizen of Yerevan.
Tjako van Schie was born on April 17, 1961, in Coevorden. He is a Dutch pianist and composer. Tjako works as a répétiteur at the Amsterdam Conservatory.

Gladys Cooper, born on December 18, 1888, and passed away on November 17, 1971, was an English actress. Her career lasted for seven decades, from stage performances to films and television. As a teenager, she performed in Edwardian musical shows and silent films before the First World War. From 1917 to 1933, she managed the Playhouse Theatre and acted in many roles there. Starting in the early 1920s, Cooper got praised for her performances in plays by W. Somerset Maugham and others. In the 1930s, she starred in London's West End and Broadway shows consistently. In 1940, she moved to Hollywood and found success in different character roles. She was nominated for three Academy Awards for Best Supporting Actress: for "The Song of Bernadette" in 1943, "My Fair Lady" in 1964, and most famously, "Now, Voyager" in 1942. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, she acted both on stage and in films, continuing to star on stage until her final year.

Anastasia: The Mystery of Anna (also titled Anastasia: The Story of Anna) is a 1986 American, Austrian, and Italian made-for-television movie. It tells the story of Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia. The film was directed by Marvin J. Chomsky. It stars Amy Irving, Rex Harrison (in his last acting role), Olivia de Havilland, Omar Sharif, Christian Bale (in his first film), and Jan Niklas. The movie is based on Peter Kurth's book, "The Riddle of Anna and Anastasia." It was first shown in two parts on television.

Stanisław Karczewski was born on November 14, 1955, in Warsaw. He is a Polish politician and surgeon. Karczewski became a senator in 2005. From 2011 to 2015, he was the deputy marshal of the senate. He served as the marshal of the senate from 2019 to 2015.

Aldgate is a London Underground station in the City of London. It is on the Circle line between two other stations. Aldgate is also the end station for the Metropolitan line. It is in Travelcard Zone 1. Aldgate station opened in 1876, with its entrance on Aldgate High Street. In 1884, another station called Aldgate East opened nearby. Today, Aldgate East is served by the District and Hammersmith & City lines.
Struth is a commune in Haut-Rhin, which is in Alsace, a region in northeastern France.

The Equality Act 2010 is a UK law that aims to combine, update, and add to previous laws about not discriminating. It includes laws like the Equal Pay Act 1970 and the Sex Discrimination Act 1975. This act has the same main goals as EU laws against discrimination but offers extra protection, such as for nationality and citizenship. It covers discrimination in work and daily life based on age, disability, gender, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, and sexual orientation. The act stops employers and service providers from discriminating or harassing people based on these nine characteristics. For disabled people, employers must make reasonable changes to their workplaces. The act mostly applies to the UK except Northern Ireland.
Dawson County is in Montana, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 8, 966 people. The main town is Glendive.

Edward Reed, born on September 11, 1978, was an American safety in the NFL. He played mostly for the Baltimore Ravens. He went to the University of Miami and was a two-time All-American. Reed was drafted by the Ravens in 2002 and played there for 11 seasons before joining the Houston Texans and New York Jets in 2013. He was chosen for nine Pro Bowls, won the 2004 NFL Defensive Player of the Year award, and holds records for the two longest interception returns, at 106 and 107 yards. He also has the most interception return yards in NFL history, with 1,590, and tied for the most postseason interceptions with nine. His 64 regular-season interceptions were the most among safeties when he retired. Reed was called a "ball hawk" because he was so good at catching the ball. He studied game tapes to learn about his opponents and made them throw interceptions. Reed was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2019. After retiring, he became a coach, working as an assistant coach for the Buffalo Bills in 2016 and later as the chief of staff for the Miami Hurricanes football team in 2020.
No fun at all, often abbreviated to NFAA, is a Swedish punk rock band.

Michael Rennie, born Eric Alexander Rennie, was an actor from Britain. He was famous for playing the space visitor Klaatu in the movie "The Day the Earth Stood Still" in 1951. He acted in films and TV shows for over 30 years and appeared in more than 50 films.

An illuminated manuscript is a book where the text is decorated with initial letters, borders, and small illustrations. In simple terms, it means adding pretty designs to the pages. This term traditionally refers to books decorated with gold or silver, but now it covers any beautifully designed or illustrated books from the western tradition. In contrast, books from Asia and ancient America are often called painted, not illuminated. Islamic books can be called illuminated, illustrated, or painted, as they use similar techniques to Western ones. The earliest known illuminated manuscripts date back to 400-600 AD, created in the Ostrogothic kingdom and the Eastern Roman Empire. Their importance lies in both their artistic beauty and their role in keeping written history alive. Monks in ancient times preserved many old texts, helping to save literature from disappearing. During the Middle Ages, most illuminated manuscripts were religious. From the 13th century, more non-religious texts started to be illustrated. Most of these books were codices—bound books, replacing scrolls. Only a few survive on papyrus, which doesn’t last as long as parchment. Parchment was usually made from calf, sheep, or goat skin, with vellum being the best quality. By the late Middle Ages, some books were written on paper. Early printed books sometimes had spaces for drawings, or were decorated with gold letters, but the invention of printing led to fewer illuminated manuscripts. By the early 16th century, they were made in much smaller numbers, mostly for wealthy people. Many illuminated manuscripts from the Middle Ages still exist today. They are important as they are the best surviving examples of medieval painting. In fact, they are often the only known paintings from certain periods and regions.

The turnip, also known as the white turnip (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa), is a root vegetable grown in many places with a white, fleshy part. The word "turnip" comes from "turn" meaning it is rounded, and "neep," which comes from the Latin "napus," the plant's name. Small, tender turnips are eaten by people, while bigger ones are used for animal feed. In parts of England, Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall, and Eastern Canada (Quebec, Newfoundland, and the Maritimes), "turnip" or "neep" can also mean rutabaga. Rutabaga is a larger, yellow root vegetable in the same plant family as turnips and is also called swede, which comes from "Swedish turnip."

The Butler, directed by Lee Daniels and written by Danny Strong, is a 2013 American historical drama. It is based on a Washington Post article by Wil Haygood and tells the story of Eugene Allen, a real-life African-American White House butler who worked for 34 years. The movie follows Cecil Gaines, played by Forest Whitaker, who also worked as a White House butler and witnessed many important political and social events in the 20th century. Other stars include Oprah Winfrey, John Cusack, and Jane Fonda. Laura Ziskin, who passed away on June 12, 2011, produced the film. It was released on August 16, 2013, and received mostly positive reviews. Critics praised the cast but criticized the historical accuracy, especially the portrayal of President Reagan. The movie earned over $176 million worldwide with a budget of $30 million.

Highlands is a town in Orange County, New York, United States. It is located on the eastern border of the county. The population was 12,492 as of the 2010 census. West Point, which includes the United States Military Academy, is nearby along the Hudson River. The military reservation covers a large part of the town.

Mr. Men is a series of children's books by Roger Hargreaves, starting in 1971. In 1981, he also wrote Little Miss books with female characters. From 1978, there was another series called Timbuctoo with animal characters. After Mr. Hargreaves died in 1988, his son Adam started writing new Mr. Men and Little Miss stories, like "Mr. Cool," "Mr. Rude," "Mr. Good," "Little Miss Scary," "Little Miss Bad," and "Little Miss Whoops." Each book introduced a main character with one big personality trait to teach a simple lesson. Mr. Men and Little Miss characters often appeared in other stories. By 2015, there were 85 different Mr. Men and Little Miss characters. The books were very popular with colorful illustrations. They sold over 100 million copies in 28 countries. All the characters come from a pretend town called Tickle Town.
lion-sur-mer is a town in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.
66 is the number that comes after 65 and before 67. This number is used in many ways.

Timothy Mackenzie Gunn, born on July 29, 1953, is an American fashion consultant, TV personality, actor, voice actor, and author. He taught at Parsons School of Design from 1982 to 2007 and was the fashion design chair there from 2000 to 2007. After that, he worked as the chief creative officer for Liz Claiborne, which is now called Kate Spade & Company. Gunn became famous as a mentor on the TV show "Project Runway" over 16 seasons. His popularity from "Project Runway" led to two new shows: "Tim Gunn's Guide to Style" on Bravo and "Under the Gunn" on Lifetime. He also wrote five books. As an executive producer, Gunn mentored young designers on "Project Runway." He also voiced Baileywick, a character in "Sofia the First," a Disney Junior show, and narrated the sitcom "Mixology."
Wilkes County is the name of two counties in the United States.

Stopover is a small community in Pike County, Kentucky, United States. It is located at the intersection of Kentucky Route 194 and Kentucky Route 2062, east of Phelps. Stopover had a post office with the zip code 41568. The town got its name because the first postmaster, who owned the local general store, often told people to "stop over and see" him. Stopover has a small country store and four churches: Shepard Memorial Presbyterian Church, Stopover Church of God, Stopover Freewill Baptist Church, and Camp Creek Pentecostal Church.

Antonio de Cabezón was born on March 30, 1510, and died on March 26, 1566. He was a Spanish composer and organist during the Renaissance period. Blind from childhood, he became famous as a performer. He worked for the royal family. He was one of the most important composers of his time and the first major Iberian keyboard composer.
Unionville is a city in Appanoose County, Iowa, United States. In 2010, it had 102 people living there.

John Robert Lewis, born on February 21, 1940, and died on July 17, 2020, was an American leader who fought for civil rights. He was in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1987 until his death. He was a key person in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee from 1963 to 1966. Lewis was one of the six main leaders who organized the 1963 March on Washington. He played important roles in the civil rights movement to end segregation. A member of the Democratic Party, Lewis was elected to Congress in 1986 and served 17 terms in the House of Representatives. Because he had served for so long, he became the leader of the Georgia congressional team. His district included most of Atlanta. Lewis was a leader in the Democratic Party, working as a chief deputy whip from 1991 and as senior chief deputy whip from 2003. He received many honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

In a theocracy, a deity is seen as the highest ruler, guiding human leaders who handle daily government tasks. In ancient Rome, emperors and some family members were considered to have divine approval. The government officially honored living emperors with special treatment, acknowledging their rule as approved by the gods. As emperor, one should respect traditional gods and customs.

Edward Vincent Bracken was an American actor born on February 7, 1915, and died on November 14, 2002. He became famous for his comedy roles. In 1944, he starred in two popular movies: "Hail the Conquering Hero" and "The Miracle of Morgan's Creek." Both movies are still preserved. He also performed in plays, like "Too Many Girls," which was in 1939. Later in his career, Bracken acted in "National Lampoon's Vacation" in 1983, "Oscar" in 1991, and "Rookie of the Year" in 1993.

The Lexington Barbecue Festival is a one-day food event held in October in Lexington, North Carolina, known as the "barbecue capital of the world." Each year, it draws around 200,000 visitors to the uptown Lexington area. They come to taste food from up to 20 local restaurants, dozens of food vendors, and many other vendors. The annual event is featured in a book called "1,000 Places to See in the USA & Canada Before You Die." In 2012, U.S. News and World Report ranked Lexington as the fourth-best city for barbecue.

Flavio Cotti was born on October 18, 1939, in Prato-Sornico. He is a Swiss politician. Cotti became a member of the Federal Council of Switzerland on December 10, 1986, and left his position on April 30, 1999. He belongs to the Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland. While in office, he was the president of the confederation twice—first in 1991 and again in 1998.

kmfdm, originally called "No Pity for the Majority," is a German industrial band formed by Sascha Konietzko in 1984 for a performance art project. Early members included drummer En Esch and vocalist Raymond Watts, who joined and left the band multiple times. The band recorded in Germany before Konietzko and Esch moved to the U.S., where they gained more success with Wax Trax! records. Günter Schulz joined in 1990 and stayed until 1999 when the band broke up. Konietzko revived kmfdm in 2002 on Metropolis Records. By 2005, a consistent lineup included Lucia Cifarelli, Jules Hodgson, Steve White, and Andy Selway. Konietzko and Cifarelli moved back to Germany in 2007, while the others stayed in the U.S. Hodgson and White left between 2015 and 2017, leaving a working trio. Over 20 studio albums and many singles were produced, selling over two million records worldwide. Critics see kmfdm as one of the first bands to bring industrial music to mainstream audiences. The band's music includes heavy metal guitar, electronic music, samples, and both male and female vocals, covering styles like industrial rock and electronic body music. kmfdm is politically active, often against violence, war, and oppression. The band tours after major releases and interacts with fans both online and at concerts. Members have also worked under other names like Watts' Pig, Konietzko's Excessive Force, and Esch and Schulz's Slick Idiot.

Alexain is a small town in the Mayenne department, which is in northwestern France. It is 20 kilometers northwest of Laval and 14 kilometers from Mayenne. The nearest towns are La Bigottière, Placé, and Saint-Germain-d'Anxure.

Islam Bibi was a female police officer in Afghanistan's Helmand province. She was the top-ranking policewoman in Afghanistan at the time of her death. Bibi fought for feminism and led operations against the Taliban. She faced many death threats and was assassinated on July 4, 2013.

The common toad, also known as the European toad, or simply the toad (Bufo bufo), is found in most of Europe, except Ireland, Iceland, and some Mediterranean islands. It also lives in parts of western Asia and a small area in northwest Africa. These toads are part of a group of closely related toads. During the day, toads stay hidden. They become active at night when they hunt for small insects. Toads move slowly, taking short hops or walking. Their skin is gray and has lumpy bumps. Usually, toads are alone. But during the breeding season, many toads gather near breeding ponds. Male toads compete to mate with females. Toads lay eggs in strings in the water, and the eggs turn into tadpoles. After growing in the water for several months, tadpoles develop legs and change into tiny toads. These juveniles leave the water and stay on land for the rest of their lives. The common toad is listed as "least concern" by the IUCN, but it is declining in some areas. Toads are threatened by loss of their habitats, especially drainage of breeding sites. Some toads also die on roads when they migrate. Toads have long been linked to witchcraft in popular culture.

HTC Corporation, also known as High Tech Computer Corporation or Hongda International Electronics Co., Ltd., is a company based in Xindian District, New Taipei City, Taiwan. HTC was founded in 1997 and started by making laptops. It then began making smartphones using Windows Mobile. HTC joined a group called the Open Handset Alliance and helped develop the Android operating system. HTC's first Android phone was the Dream, sold by T-Mobile under the name T-Mobile G1. However, competition from Apple and Samsung reduced HTC's smartphone market share to just 7.2% by April 2015. HTC has been making losses. In 2016, HTC started working on virtual reality with Valve, creating the HTC Vive. After working with Google on the Pixel smartphone, HTC sold half of its design and research team and some smartphone-related ideas to Google in 2017 for a billion dollars.

Tanah Merah MRT station is an above-ground Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station on the East West Line in Bedok, Singapore. It is where the East West Line and the Changi Airport Branch Line meet. Tanah Merah station is unique because it has more tracks than most stations. The middle track serves the Changi Airport Branch Line, which stops at Changi Airport. Tanah Merah in Malay means 'red earth,' named after the red cliffs once visible from the sea. In 2017, the station was given a new code 'CG' to help distinguish it from other services, though this code isn't shown on signs. In 2019, it was announced that the station will move to the Thomson–East Coast Line by 2040. The Changi Airport Branch Line will no longer operate.

Redhill MRT station is an above-ground train station on the East West Line (EWL). It is in Bukit Merah, Singapore. The station is on Tiong Bahru Road, near Jalan Tiong. On the EWL, it is between Tiong Bahru and Queenstown stations. Redhill MRT station opened on March 12, 1988, when the MRT line was extended from Outram Park station to Clementi.

Los Ángeles is the capital of the Bío Bío province, in the commune of the same name. It is located in the center-south of Chile, between the Laaja and Biobío rivers. In 2012, it had 186,671 people. Los Ángeles' municipality has the highest rural population of any municipality in Chile. To the north of the city is Salto del Laaja. About 100 kilometers east is the high Antuco volcano in the Andes. The city helps visitors access nearby Laguna del Laaja National Park. Los Ángeles has an airport called María Dolores.

Flushing is a city in Genesee County, Michigan. The population was 8,389 in 2010. It is considered a suburb of Flint. Flushing is part of the Survey Area of Flushing Charter Township but has its own administration. The city began as a mill town in the mid-1830s. Its location along the Flint River, the county's largest river, was key to its development. The river's water power was important in choosing the settlement areas during the 19th century. Besides its water power, the area was also good for farming. The town was originally going to be called Dover, but that name was already used in Michigan. Charles Seymour, Sr., who used to live in Flushing, New York, named the town after the village there.

A provincial city in Vietnam is often called a city. It is a second-level division in Vietnam and is divided into 713 units, including urban districts, districts, and towns, which all have the same status. By decree no. 42/2009/ND-CP, cities are officially classified as Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3. These cities only belong to provinces as the second-level units. At the third level, cities are divided into wards and communes.

Justin Raimondo, born Dennis Raimondo on November 18, 1951, and passed away on June 27, 2019, was an American author. He worked as the editorial director for AntiWar.com. Raimondo considered himself a conservative-paleo-libertarian.

Arshile Gorky, born Vostanik Manoug Adoian on April 15, 1904, and died on July 21, 1948, was an Armenian-American painter. He spent most of his life as an American citizen. Gorky is known for having a big influence on abstract expressionism. Along with Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock, and Willem de Kooning, he is considered one of the strongest American painters of the 20th century. His artworks were likely inspired by his experiences with suffering and loss, including those from the Armenian genocide.

Evan Rachel Wood, born on September 7, 1987, is an American actress, model, and musician. She has won a Critics' Choice Television Award and been nominated for three Primetime Emmy Awards and three Golden Globe Awards for her work in film and television. Wood started acting in the 1990s. She appeared in TV shows like "American Gothic" (1995-1996) and "Once and Again" (1999-2002). At age nine, she starred in the film "Digging to China" (1997) and got praise for her role as Tracy Freeland in "Thirteen" (2003), a movie about a troubled teenager. She kept acting in smaller movies like "Pretty Persuasion" (2005), "Down in the Valley" (2005), "Running with Scissors" (2006), and "Across the Universe" (2007). In 2008, she acted in bigger movies such as "The Wrestler," "Whatever Works," and "The Ides of March." In 2009, she was on TV in "True Blood," playing a vampire named Sophie-Anne LeClair. She also acted in the TV series "Mildred Pierce" (2011), where she was nominated for a Golden Globe and Emmy Award for best supporting actress. Currently, Wood stars as the android Dolores Abernathy in the HBO show "Westworld" (2016-present). She won a Critics' Choice award and got more Golden Globe and Emmy Award nominations for this role. She also voiced Queen Iduna in the Disney movie "Frozen II" (2019).
Marcel Dupré, born on May 3, 1886, and died on May 30, 1971, was a French organist, composer, and teacher.

Burnout Paradise is a 2008 racing game. It was made by Criterion Games and published by Electronic Arts for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Windows. It was also available on the PlayStation Store and Xbox Live Marketplace. It was added to Greatest Hits and Platinum Hits titles and became backward compatible with Xbox One in November 2016. This was the first game in the Burnout series for Windows. The game is set in a fictional city called Paradise, where players can race in different types of races. You can also compete online in game modes like "Cops and Robbers." New features like a day cycle and motorcycles were added through free updates. The game received positive reviews, with scores of 88% from aggregate sites. It won several awards in 2008. A remastered version, Burnout Paradise Remastered, was released for PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Windows in 2018. Online service for the original game ended in August 2019. A remastered version for Nintendo Switch was released in 2020.

Walter Perry Johnson, nicknamed "Barney" and "The Big Train," was a right-handed pitcher in Major League Baseball. He played for the Washington Senators from 1907 to 1927. After his playing career, he became the manager of the Senators from 1929 to 1932 and later of the Cleveland Indians from 1933 to 1935. Johnson is often considered one of the best pitchers in baseball history. He set several pitching records that still stand today, such as 110 shutouts, 417 wins, and 531 complete games. He also held the record for most strikeouts, with 3,508, for nearly 56 years until 1983. Johnson was the first player in the 3,000 strikeout club, which was not surpassed until 1974. He led the league in strikeouts 12 times, including eight consecutive seasons, and is the only pitcher to have over 400 wins and more than 3,500 strikeouts. Johnson was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame as one of the "first five" members. Known for his gentle nature, he is remembered as an example of good sportsmanship and friendly competition.

Asian Americans are people with Asian ancestry living in America. The term covers various groups from East Asia, South Asia, or Southeast Asia, as defined by the U.S. Census Bureau. This includes people who identify as "Asian" or specific groups like Chinese, Filipino, Indian, Japanese, Korean, or Vietnamese. It does not include people from West Asia, who are considered Middle Eastern Americans. In 2018, Asian Americans made up 5.4% of the U.S. population, rising to 6.5% when including multiracial individuals. Asian migration to parts of what is now the United States began in the 17th century, but large-scale immigration started in the mid-19th century. During the 1880s to 1920s, immigration laws from the U.S. stopped many Asian groups, almost completely halting Asian immigration to the mainland. After these laws were changed in the 1940s to 1960s, Asian immigration increased quickly. Census data from 2010 shows that Asian Americans are one of the fastest-growing minority groups in the U.S.

Ali Hassan Mwinyi was born on May 8, 1925, in Kivure, Pwani Region, Tanzania. He is a Tanzanian politician who was the second president of Tanzania from 1985 to 1995. Before being president, he was an interior minister and vice president. Mwinyi was also the chairman of the ruling party, the Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), from 1990 to 1996. During Mwinyi’s presidency, Tanzania started moving away from the socialist policies of Julius Nyerere. He eased import restrictions and promoted private businesses. Multi-party politics were introduced during his second term under pressure from international donors. He was known as Mzee Rukhsa and supported changes in morals, beliefs, and values without breaking the law. Many believe that under Mwinyi, Tanzania transitioned from Nyerere’s failed socialist policies, which harmed the economy. His administration was key in making decisions that led to economic liberalization and short-term growth.

Samsun is a city on Turkey's north coast with about 1.4 million people. It is the capital of Samsun province and a major Black Sea port. Samsun has two universities, several hospitals, shopping malls, manufacturing, sports facilities, and an opera. It is also where Mustafa Kemal Atatürk began the Turkish War of Independence in 1919.

Haute-Ajoie is a municipality in the district of Porrentruy, in the canton of Jura, Switzerland. It was created on January 1, 2009, by combining the former municipalities of Chevenez, Damvant, Réclère, and Roche-d'Or. On January 1, 2018, the former municipality of Rocrut merged into Haute-Ajoie.
Garden Valley is a town in Jackson County, Wisconsin, United States. In 2000, it had 406 people. North Branch is an unincorporated community within the town.

The University of Idaho (U of I or UIDaho) is a public research university in Moscow, Idaho. It is the state's land-grant and main research university. U of I was Idaho's only university for 71 years until 1963. Its law school started in 1909 and was first approved by the American Bar Association in 1925. The university began on October 3, 1892, with 40 students. Its first graduation in 1896 had four students: two men and two women. Today, more than 12,000 students are enrolled, mostly at the Moscow campus. U of I offers 142 degree programs, from accounting to wildlife resources, including bachelor's, master's, doctoral, and specialist degrees. It also provides 30 certificates. Its 4 and 6-year graduation rates are the highest among public universities in Idaho. The university spends over $100 million on research, generating 74% of all research funding in the state. As a land-grant and leading research institution, U of I has the largest campus in Idaho. Located in the rolling Palouse hills, it sits about 1,300 feet above sea level. The university's sports teams are called the Idaho Vandals and compete in NCAA Division I. Besides the main Moscow campus, U of I has campuses in Coeur d'Alene, Boise, and Idaho Falls. It also runs a research park in Post Falls and numerous extension offices statewide.

Hurricane Isaac was the last tropical storm of the 2006 Atlantic hurricane season. It started from a tropical wave that entered the Atlantic Ocean on September 18. This wave turned into a tropical depression on September 27, southeast of Bermuda. The depression became a tropical storm just 12 hours later. But high wind and cool water temperatures made the storm weaker. Isaac became a Category 1 hurricane and hit Newfoundland as a tropical storm. The effects were small, mainly just strong winds, rough waves, and some rain.

The Christian Community is a religious group that considers itself a Christian denomination. However, other Christian churches do not recognize it as such. It was started in 1922 in Switzerland by Lutheran theologians and ministers, led by Friedrich Rittelmeyer. They were inspired by Rudolf Steiner, who founded anthroposophy. These groups are independent financially and have local and international administrative bodies. There are about 100,000 members worldwide. The main office is in Berlin, Germany. The Christian Community is run by a "Circle of Priests." They have leaders called coordinators. There is a first coordinator, who works with two second coordinators. On a regional level, there are third coordinators called lenkers. Additionally, there is a group of priests called a synod.

The International Baccalaureate (IB), formerly known as the International Baccalaureate Organization (IBO), is a non-profit foundation based in Geneva, Switzerland. It was founded in 1968. The IB offers four educational programs: the IB Diploma Programme and the IB Career-Related Programme for students aged 15 to 19, the IB Middle Years Programme for students aged 11 to 16, and the IB Primary Years Programme for children aged 3 to 12. Schools need to be authorized by the IB to teach these programs. In 2007, the organization changed its name and logo to reflect new arrangements. Now, "IB" can refer to the organization, any of the four programs, or the diplomas or certificates awarded at the end of a program.

In music theory, a diatonic scale is a seven-note scale that includes five whole steps (whole tones) and two half steps (semitones). The two half steps are always separated by two or three whole steps. This arrangement ensures that all the half steps are spread out as much as possible, at least two whole steps apart. The seven notes in any diatonic scale can also be created by using a chain of six perfect fifths. For example, the seven natural notes in the C-major scale can be found by stacking perfect fifths from F. Any group of seven consecutive natural notes, like C–D–E–F–G–A–B, and any of its shifts, forms a diatonic scale. Modern keyboards have white keys that form a diatonic scale, but moving the scale requires pressing some black keys too. A diatonic scale can also be seen as two four-note groups (tetrachords) separated by a whole step. Originally, "diatonic" meant one of the three types of scales used by ancient Greeks. In modern music theory, a scale is called diatonic if it meets the above conditions. Some seven-note scales, like the harmonic minor or melodic minor, are sometimes called diatonic but do not meet these conditions.

The national football team of Ireland represents the country in men's international football. It is managed by the Football Association of Ireland (FAI). The team first played in the 1924 Summer Olympics, reaching the quarter-finals. From 1924 to 1936, they were known as the Irish Free State. From 1936 to 1950, they were called Éire or Ireland by the FAI. In 1953, FIFA decided that for competitive matches, the FAI team should be called the Republic of Ireland, while the IFA team was named Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland could use the name Ireland in the Home International Competition until 1984. In 1949, the Republic of Ireland became the first country outside the United Kingdom to defeat England at Goodison Park, Liverpool. They also reached the quarter-finals in the 1964 European Nations' Cup, losing to Spain. Under Jack Charlton's leadership, the team had its most successful period. They reached their highest FIFA world ranking at sixth in August 1993. They qualified for UEFA Euro 1988, making their first appearance at the UEFA European Championship and reaching the quarter-finals of the 1990 FIFA World Cup for the first time. They also made it to the last 16 in the 1994 World Cup. Mick McCarthy, who succeeded Charlton, missed out on the next three major tournaments but qualified for the 2002 World Cup, reaching the last 16. Martin O'Neill continued this success at UEFA Euro 2016. The team's home stadium is the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, but they sometimes play in other stadiums across the country. The current coach is Stephen Kenny, and the team captain is Séamus Coleman.

Antonio Montana is a fictional character and the main character from the 1983 movie "Scarface." Al Pacino plays him in the film, and André Sogliuzzo voices him in a 2006 video game. The character shows how someone can go from being poor to rich. Montana has become a famous movie character and is known as Scarface because of a large scar on his face. In 2008, he was named the 27th greatest movie character by "Empire" magazine. His story is partly based on Tony Camonte, the main character from the original book and the 1932 film. The character is also inspired by Al Capone. The movie's director, Oliver Stone, named Montana's last name after his favorite NFL quarterback, Joe Montana. There is also a prequel novel called "Scarface: The Beginning" written by L. A. Banks.

Sea glass and beach glass are similar, but they come from different types of water. Sea glass is glass found on beaches near salty water. It becomes frosted because of weathering. People can collect sea glass for hobbies and use it to make jewelry. Beach glass comes from fresh water and is less frosted. Sea glass takes a long time—about 20 to 40 years, sometimes even 100 years—to get its special texture and shape. This process is called "drift glass" because of how the sea moves the glass along the beach. People often use the terms "sea glass" and "beach glass" interchangeably.

Alan Harrison Berg was born on January 1, 1934, and died on June 18, 1984. He was an American lawyer and host of a talk radio show in Denver, Colorado. Berg often talked openly and had strong opinions. He liked to ask challenging questions on his show. On June 18, 1984, Berg was killed by people from a white nationalist group called The Order. Members of The Order wanted to hurt famous Jewish people, including Berg. Two people involved, David Lane and Bruce Pierce, were found guilty of breaking civil rights laws. They were not charged with murder. Lane was sentenced to 190 years in prison, and Pierce to 252 years.

Balltown is a city in Dubuque County, Iowa, United States. It is part of the Dubuque, Iowa, metropolitan area. In 2010, the population was 68, down from 73 in 2000. Balltown has Breitbach's Country Dining, the oldest restaurant and bar in Iowa. It was founded in 1852 and rebuilt twice by the community after it burned down in 2007 and 2008.

Ell is a small town in western Luxembourg, in the canton of Redange. It is close to the border with Belgium. The town of Ell has 340 people living there. Other towns in the same area are Colpach-bas, Colpach-haut, and Roodt.

Tabaré Ramón Vázquez Rosas was born on January 17, 1940. He is a Uruguayan politician who served as Uruguay's 41st president from 2015 to 2020. He was also Uruguay's 39th president from 2005 to 2010. Vázquez is a doctor and an oncologist. He belongs to the left-wing Broad Front coalition. Vázquez first became president in 2005 after being elected in 2004. He left the presidency in 2010 when José Mujica became the new president. Vázquez was elected again in 2015 and left in 2020, when Luis Alberto Lacalle Pou took office.

A volcanic plug, also known as a volcanic neck or lava neck, is formed when magma hardens inside a volcano's vent. If rising magma with gases gets trapped above it, pressure builds up, sometimes causing a big, explosive eruption. Erosion from glaciers can expose the plug on one side, leaving a steep slope on the other. This results in a landform called a crag and tail. If the plug survives, erosion can remove the surrounding rock, leaving the plug standing alone as a unique land feature.

Saint Kitts and Nevis, officially called the Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis, is an island country in the West Indies. It is the smallest country in the Western Hemisphere both in size and population. Queen Elizabeth II is the head of state, just like in other Commonwealth realms. The capital, Basseterre, is on the larger island of Saint Kitts. The smaller island of Nevis is southeast of Saint Kitts, across a narrow channel. Historically, Anguilla, now a British dependency, was part of Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla but chose to separate and remains a British overseas territory. To the north-northwest are Sint Eustatius, Saba, Saint Barthélemy, Sint Maarten, and Anguilla. To the east and northeast are Antigua and Barbuda, and southeast is the small uninhabited island of Redonda (part of Antigua and Barbuda) and Montserrat. Saint Kitts and Nevis were among the first islands in the Caribbean to be colonized by Europeans. Saint Kitts hosted the first British and French colonies in the Caribbean, earning the nickname "the mother colony of the West Indies." It was the last British territory in the Caribbean to gain independence in 1983.
Sensational spelling is when a word is故意用非标准的方式拼写，以制造特别的效果。

Anzonico was a former municipality in the Leventina district of Ticino in Switzerland. On April 1, 2012, it joined the municipality of Faido along with the former municipalities of Calpiogna, Campello, Cavagnago, Chironico, Mairengo, and Osco.

ZDF is the second German television, officially called "Second German Television." It is based in Mainz, Rhineland-Palatinate. ZDF is a public service television that operates as an independent nonprofit. It was founded by all German federal states. ZDF gets money from licence fees and advertisements. The broadcaster is famous for its news programme "Heute," which started in 1963, and "Wetten, dass..?" an entertainment show that began in 1981 and ended in 2014. Thomas Bellut became the director general in 2011.

Sugar is a sweet, soluble carbohydrate used in food. Table sugar, also called granulated or regular sugar, is sucrose, made from glucose and fructose. Simple sugars, like glucose, fructose, and galactose, are single molecules. Compound sugars, or disaccharides, like sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), and maltose (two glucose molecules), are made from two simple sugars.
