An anticyclonic storm is a weather storm. The winds around the storm move in the opposite direction to the winds above an area with low pressure.

Usury is the practice of lending money in an unethical way, making the lender richer unfairly. In some cases, it means charging very high interest rates that are not allowed by law. A person who does this is called a usurer or a loan shark. In many ancient societies, such as ancient Christian, Jewish, and modern Islamic societies, charging any interest on a loan was considered wrong. For example, in ancient India, laws prevented the highest castes from lending money. Similarly, ancient religious texts from Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam criticize lending with interest. Throughout history, many countries, like ancient Greece and Rome, banned loans with any interest. Even when loans with interest were allowed, they were strictly regulated. In medieval Europe, the Catholic Church and other churches thought charging interest was sinful, including using money for a fee. The main idea is that usury involves unethical lending practices, and many cultures and religions have condemned it.

Wenatchee is a city in north-central Washington and is the largest city and county seat of Chelan County. In 2010, it had 31,925 people. By 2019, it was estimated to have 34,360 people. Wenatchee is at the meeting point of the Columbia and Wenatchee rivers, near the Cascade Mountains. It is on the west side of the Columbia River, opposite East Wenatchee. The river forms the border between Chelan and Douglas County. Wenatchee is the main city of the Wenatchee–East Wenatchee metropolitan area, which includes all of Chelan and Douglas counties, with about 110,884 people. The "Wenatchee Valley area" usually refers to land between Rocky Reach and Rock Island Dam on both sides of the Columbia River, including East Wenatchee, Rock Island, and Malaga. The city was named after the nearby Wenatchi Indian tribe. "Awenatchela" means "people at the source of a river." Wenatchee is known as the "Apple Capital of the World" because of its many orchards. It is also sometimes called the "Buckle of the Power Belt of the Great Northwest." This term comes from the series of hydroelectric dams on the Columbia River, with Rock Island Dam being in the middle, labeled the "buckle." This phrase appears at the top of Wenatchee's newspaper, the "Wenatchee World," but is not commonly used elsewhere.

Charles Beauvau, Prince of Craon, lived from September 10, 1720, to May 21, 1793. He was the 2nd Prince of Craon in 1754 and a Marshal of France in 1783. He was a French nobleman and general. He was the son of Marc de Beauvau and brother to Madame de Boufflers. He was also an uncle to the poet Stanislas de Boufflers.

Mikhail Nikolayevich Zadornov (July 21, 1948, in Jūrmala, Latvian SSR, USSR – November 10, 2017, in Moscow, Russia) was a Soviet and Russian stand-up comedian and writer. His father, Nikolai Zadornov, was a famous writer from Riga. His mother, Elena Matusevich (1909-1992), came from an old noble family with roots in the Polish King Stephen Bathory. As a child, Zadornov listened to his father reading him adventure and suspense stories and poems before bedtime. Zadornov’s parents wanted him to be an engineer, so he went to an engineering school. Mikhail Zadornov studied at Moscow Aviation Institute. However, in the early 1980s, he began a career as a humorist and later jokingly remembered his engineering education.

Samuel Willenberg, known as Igo, was born on February 16, 1923, and died on February 19, 2016. He was a Polish survivor of the Holocaust, an artist, and a writer. Willenberg worked as a "Sonderkommando" at the Treblinka extermination camp during World War II. He was part of a planned revolt in August 1943. About 300 people managed to escape, and around 79 are known to have survived the war. After the war, Willenberg went to Warsaw and joined the Warsaw Uprising. He was the last known survivor of the August 1943 Treblinka prisoners' revolt. Like many other survivors, Willenberg moved to Israel. He received Poland's highest honors, including the "Virtuti Militari" and the Commander's Cross of the Order of Merit, given by President Lech Kaczyński. His book "Revolt in Treblinka" was published in Hebrew, Polish, and English between 1986 and 1991. He also created sculptures and paintings.

Richmond is a town in Washington County, Rhode Island. In 2010, it had 7,708 people. The town includes villages like Alton, Arcadia, Barberville, Carolina, Hillsdale, Kenyon, Shannock, Tug Hollow, Usquepaug, Wood River Junction, Woodville, and Wyoming. The students in Richmond go to school in the Chariho Regional School District.
Saint- Jean- sur- Veyle is a town in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Adobe Dreamweaver is a web development tool made by Adobe Inc. It was created in 1997 by Macromedia and continued to be developed until Macromedia was bought by Adobe in 2005. Dreamweaver can be used on Mac OS and Windows. After Adobe bought Macromedia, new versions of Dreamweaver followed W3C standards better. Recent versions have improved support for technologies like CSS, JavaScript, and server-side scripting languages and frameworks such as ASP, ColdFusion, and PHP.

Zalmoxes is an extinct type of dinosaur from Romania. It belongs to a group called rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaurs. The first dinosaur named was called Mochlodon robustum in 1899 by Franz Nopcsa. Later, in 1915, Nopcsa changed the name to Rhabdodon robustum. In 1990, George Olshevsky corrected the name to Rhabdodon robustus. In 2003, a new species of Zalmoxes was named Zalmoxes shqiperorum, named after the Albanian word for Albanians. The name Zalmoxes comes from a Dacian god called Zalmoxis, and robustus means strong or robust.
Jalal Dabagh was born in 1939. He is a Kurdish politician and writer/journalist.

Golf Mill Shopping Center, also called Golf Mill Center, is a shopping mall in Niles, Illinois. It is at 239 Golf Mill Center. The mall has a lot of shops. It covers an area of more than 100,000 square feet. Sterling Retail Services manages the mall. The center is near the intersections of Golf Road, Milwaukee Avenue, and Greenwood Avenue. It has over 100 small stores and four big department stores. There's also an AMC movie theater, two grocery stores, a sports fitness center, and an office tower.

Wikimania is the official yearly conference of the Wikimedia Foundation. At the conference, people talk and discuss topics like Wikipedia, other wikis, open-source software, free knowledge, and free content. They also discuss social and technical aspects related to these topics. Since 2011, the "Wikimedian of the Year" award winner is announced at Wikimania. This award was known as "Wikipedian of the Year" until 2017. The next Wikimania will be in Bangkok, Thailand, in 2021. The planned event for August 2020 was delayed because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Saint-Trivier-de-Courtes is a village in Ain, which is in eastern France.

Giuseppe Zamberletti was born on December 17, 1933, and died on January 26, 2019. He was an Italian politician. Zamberletti helped found Italy's Civil Protection service. He became the first minister of Italy's Civil Protection in 1981.

Alanis Nadine Morissette, born on June 1, 1974, is a singer, songwriter, record producer, and actress from Canada. She is known for her emotional mezzo-soprano voice. Morissette started her career in Canada in the early 1990s with two dance-pop albums that weren't very successful. Later, she moved to Los Angeles to work with a record company. In 1995, she released "Jagged Little Pill," a rock-oriented album that sold over 33 million copies and is her most famous work. Her next album, "Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie," came out in 1998. Morissette took control of her creative work and producing for her later albums, including "Under Rug Swept" (2002), "So-Called Chaos" (2004), "Flavors of Entanglement" (2008), and "Havoc and Bright Lights" (2012). Her ninth album, "Such Pretty Forks in the Road," was released in 2020. Morissette has sold more than 75 million records worldwide and is known as the "queen of alt-rock angst" by Rolling Stone.

Shah Azizur Rahman was a politician from Bangladesh. He served as the prime minister. But he faced a lot of controversy because he worked with the Pakistan army against the movement for Bangladesh's independence.

A parameter, from ancient Greek, means "beside" or "additional" measurement. Generally, it's a feature that helps describe or classify a system, like an event, project, or object. Parameters are important for understanding or assessing a system's condition. In different fields such as math, computer programming, engineering, statistics, logic, and linguistics, parameters have specific meanings. Sometimes, people use "parameter" instead of "limit" or "boundary" incorrectly, possibly due to mixing it up with "perimeter."

A mirage is a natural optical effect where light bends, making distant objects or the sky seem misplaced. The word "mirage" comes from the Latin "mirari," meaning "to look at" or "to wonder at." Mirages can be categorized as inferior, meaning lower, and superior, meaning higher, with a special kind called "fata morgana," which creates multiple, stacked images that change quickly. Unlike a hallucination, a mirage is real and can be filmed because light rays actually bend to create the false image for the viewer. However, what the image looks like depends on how the human brain interprets it. For example, on land, inferior mirages can easily look like reflections of water from a small pond or lake.

Tom Pevsner was born on October 2, 1926, and passed away on August 18, 2014. He was a British film assistant director and producer, working for over 40 years. Tom was the second of three children born to Sir Nikolaus Pevsner, an architectural historian from Russia. In 1933, the family moved to the UK to avoid the Nazi regime in Germany. Tom served in the British army from 1944 to 1948. After that, he studied modern languages at the University of Cambridge and was part of the St John's College film society. He edited "The Cambridge Review" and worked at the Film Finance Corporation after graduation. Tom Pevsner worked on famous films like "The Ladykillers" (1955), "The Longest Day" (1962), and "The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes" (1970) as an assistant director. He also produced "Dracula." He worked as an associate and then as an executive producer on all James Bond films from "For Your Eyes Only" to "GoldenEye." His work on the Bond series was recognized in "Spectre," where character Q mentions the Pevsner hotel. Tom Pevsner died in 2014 at the age of 87. He was honored in the "In Memoriam" tribute during the 87th Academy Awards broadcast on February 22, 2015.

Richard Church Thompson was an American artist who made cartoons. He was famous for a comic strip called "Cul de sac" and an illustrated poem "Make the Pie Higher." In 2010, he won a big award called the Reuben Award. He was born on October 8, 1957, and passed away on July 27, 2016.

Nelson Mandela Bridge is in Johannesburg, South Africa. It is one of five bridges that cross railway lines west of Johannesburg Park Station. The first bridge is the Johan Rissik Bridge next to the station. Nelson Mandela Bridge was finished in 2003 and cost 38 million rand to build. Its purpose was to connect two business areas, Braamfontein and Newtown, and help improve the city center. The bridge is part of Johannesburg's M27 route.

The Hateful Eight, sometimes called the H8ful Eight, is a 2015 American western movie directed by Quentin Tarantino. It stars Samuel L. Jackson, Kurt Russell, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Walton Goggins, Demian Bichir, Tim Roth, Michael Madsen, and Bruce Dern. They play eight strangers who seek shelter from a blizzard in a stagecoach stop after the American Civil War. Tarantino announced the movie in November 2013. He thought of it as a novel and a follow-up to his previous film, Django Unchained (2012), but decided to make it a standalone. After the script leaked in January 2014, he canceled the project and instead did a live reading at the United Artists Theater in Los Angeles. Later, he resumed work on the film. Filming started on December 8, 2014, near Telluride, Colorado. Italian composer Ennio Morricone wrote the original score, which was his first and only score for a Tarantino film in 34 years, and his first significant Hollywood score since 2000. The film was distributed by The Weinstein Company in the U.S. and was first released on December 25, 2015, in a limited 70 mm film release. It expanded widely on December 30, 2015. Critics liked Leigh's performance and Morricone's score. The movie made $155.8 million. Estimates of the budget range from $44 million to $62 million. Morricone won his first Academy Award for Best Original Score and a Golden Globe for his work. The film also got Oscar nominations for Best Supporting Actress (Leigh) and Best Cinematography (Robert Richardson). In 2019, it was re-released as a four-part miniseries on Netflix called "Extended Version." This was Tarantino's last film with The Weinstein Company, as he ended his relationship with them in October 2017 due to allegations of sexual abuse against Harvey Weinstein.

Mason is a city in Michigan, the U.S. It is named after the state's first governor, Stevens T. Mason. As of the 2010 census, the city's population was 8,252. Mason is also the county seat of Ingham County. Interestingly, Mason is the only city in the U.S. that serves as a county seat even though the state capital is in a different city. The capital city, Lansing, is also in Ingham County. However, many county offices and courtrooms are located in Lansing instead of Mason.
Ambleny is a commune in the Aisne department, which is in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France. People who live in Ambleny are called "amblenois" or "amblenoises".

Natural Steps is a small town in Pulaski County, Arkansas, United States. It is near Little Rock, 18 miles northwest, along the Arkansas River. In 2010, it had 426 people. Today, Natural Steps is a small farming area with a few businesses. Some natural rock steps, part of a geologic formation, are still there. These steps are used as markers by river runners but are not open for public viewing.

The cochlea is part of the inner ear and helps with hearing. It is a spiral-shaped cavity in the bony labyrinth. In humans, it makes 2.75 turns around its axis, the modiolus. The organ of corti is an important part of the cochlea. It is the sensory organ for hearing and is found along the partition that separates the fluid chambers in the cochlea. The name "cochlea" comes from this description.

Myrtle Kay Thompson Cagle was born on June 3, 1925, and passed away on December 22, 2019. She was an American pilot and part of the Mercury 13 group of female astronauts. She taught people how to fly airplanes as a flight instructor. She also wrote about aviation in North Carolina.

In American history, the fire-eaters were pro-slavery Democrats in the southern United States before the Civil War. They wanted the southern states to separate and form a new country. Robert Barnwell Rhett from South Carolina was an important leader in this group. Some fire-eaters wanted to start the Atlantic slave trade again, which was banned in 1808.

Daniel Michael Devito Jr., born on November 17, 1944, is an American actor, comedian, director, producer, and screenwriter. He became famous for playing a taxi dispatcher named Louie De Palma in the TV show "Taxi" from 1978 to 1983. This role earned him a Golden Globe and an Emmy award. He also acts as Frank Reynolds in the TV series "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia" which is still on air. In movies, he starred in films like "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest" (1975), "Terms of Endearment" (1983), "Throw Momma from the Train" (1987), "Twins" (1988), and "Matilda" (1996). He has also voiced characters in movies such as "Space Jam" (1996) and "The Lorax" (2012). Devito and Michael Shamberg created Jersey Films. Stacey Sher later joined them. Their company made famous movies like "Pulp Fiction," "Garden State," and "Freedom Writers." Devito also owned Jersey Television, which made the show "Reno 911!" with him and his wife, Rhea Perlman, in the 1996 film "Matilda," based on Roald Dahl's book. Devito was a producer nominated for an Academy Award for "Erin Brockovich." His small height comes from a rare condition called multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, which affects bone growth.
The division of Reid is an electoral area in New South Wales, Australia.
Auguste Chabaud was a French painter and sculptor. He lived from October 3, 1882, to May 23, 1955.

The 1978 FIFA World Cup, held in Argentina from June 1 to 25, was the 11th FIFA World Cup. Argentina won, beating the Netherlands 3-1 in extra time in the final. The final took place at Estadio Monumental, River Plate's home stadium, in Buenos Aires. This was Argentina's first World Cup title, making them the fifth team (after Uruguay, Italy, England, and West Germany) to both host and win the tournament. Argentina, the Netherlands, and Brazil finished as top three teams. Iran and Tunisia made their first World Cup appearances. This was the last World Cup with 16 teams; from the next one in Spain, FIFA increased the number to 24. The official ball was the Adidas Tango.

Healesville Sanctuary, formerly called Sir Colin Mackenzie Sanctuary, is a zoo that focuses on native Australian animals. It is in Healesville, a rural area of Victoria, Australia. The sanctuary has a history of breeding native animals. It is one of only two places that have successfully bred platypuses, the other being Sydney’s Taronga Zoo. It also helps with breeding endangered helmeted honeyeaters. The zoo is in a natural bushland setting. Visitors can walk through paths that lead to different habitat areas, where they can see wallabies, wombats, dingoes, kangaroos, and over 200 types of native birds. Guided tours, bird shows, and information areas are available for visitors.
Pré-en-pail was a former commune in the Mayenne department of northwest France. On January 1, 2016, it became part of a new commune called Pré-en-pail-Saint-Samson.

The French national aeronautical and astronautical association is called 3AF or AAAF. It is based in Paris and was formed in 1971 from two earlier groups: AFITAE, which started in 1945, and SFA, which began in 1955. 3AF brings people together who are interested in aerospace. They represent these people's viewpoints and help develop scientific and technological knowledge related to aerospace and its history. Members are mainly technicians, engineers, and researchers. Industrial partners include large companies like Alcatel Space, EADS, and Arianespace. 3AF also has honorary members. 3AF is part of the Confederation of European Aerospace Societies (CEAS), along with other groups like the German association DGLR, Britain's Royal Aeronautical Society (RAeS), and Italy's AIDA.

Fermentation is a process that changes organic materials through enzyme action. In biochemistry, it specifically means extracting energy from carbohydrates without oxygen. In food production, it generally means using microorganisms to make changes to foods or drinks that are desirable. The science of fermentation is called zymology. In microorganisms, fermentation mainly produces energy from organic nutrients in the absence of oxygen. People have been using fermentation to make foods and drinks since ancient times. For example, it makes pickled foods sour, like cucumbers, and produces lactic acid. It's also used to make alcoholic drinks like wine and beer. Fermentation happens in animals' digestive systems, including humans.

Arif-ur-Rehman Alvi, born on August 29, 1949, is a Pakistani politician. He became the 13th president of Pakistan on September 9, 2018. Before this, he was a member of Pakistan's National Assembly from June 2013 to May 2018 and again from August to September 2018. Alvi is from the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf party. He was chosen as Pakistan's president on September 4, 2018, after a presidential election.

Maynard Elliott Solomon, born on January 5, 1930, is a co-founder of Vanguard Records and a former music producer. Recently, he has written biographies about Viennese classical composers. He wrote an influential biography about Beethoven and an award-winning collection of essays. He also wrote a biography about Mozart. Additionally, Solomon was the first to openly suggest that Schubert might have been gay, in a scholarly setting.
Lancaster can mean: A city A county

Potsdam is the biggest city in Brandenburg, a state in Germany. It is next to Berlin, the capital of Germany, and part of the Berlin/Brandenburg area. Potsdam is by a river called Havel, southwest of Berlin. Potsdam was a royal place for Prussian and German kings until 1918. The city’s design shows ideas from the Enlightenment. It combines architecture and nature to create a picturesque and natural environment. Potsdam has many lakes and is known for its cultural sites, especially the palaces and parks of Sanssouci, the biggest World Heritage site in Germany. The 1945 Potsdam Conference was held at Cecilienhof Palace. In the southeast of Potsdam is Babelsberg, a film studio that started in the 1930s and is now a major film production center in Europe. The Babelsberg film studio is the oldest large film studio in the world. In the 19th century, Potsdam became a science center. Today, it has three colleges, the University of Potsdam, and over 30 research institutes.

Ray Milton Dolby was an American engineer and inventor, born on January 18, 1933, and died on September 12, 2013. He invented a noise reduction system called Dolby NR. At Ampex, he helped develop the video tape recorder. He also founded Dolby Laboratories.

Michael Gregory Rowe, born on March 18, 1962, is an American TV host and narrator. He used to be an opera singer. He is famous for hosting "Dirty Jobs" on the Discovery Channel and "Somebody's Got to Do It" for CNN. Currently, he hosts a series called "Returning the Favor" on Facebook. In this show, he finds people doing good deeds and returns the favor to them. He also hosts a podcast named "The Way I Heard It with Mike Rowe." This podcast tells short stories made for curious people who don't have much time. Rowe has narrated shows like "Deadliest Catch," "How the Universe Works," and "Shark Week" on the Discovery Channel, the Science Channel, and National Geographic. He has also appeared in Ford Motor Company commercials. In June 2020, the Discovery Channel announced "Dirty Jobs: Rowe’d Trip," four episodes to air in mid-July 2020, described as a mix of a reunion, a road trip, and a look-back-special.

Joe Osborn was born on August 28, 1937, and died on December 14, 2018. He was an American bass guitar player. Joe worked as a session musician in Los Angeles with the Wrecking Crew in the 1960s to 1980s. He also worked in Nashville with the A-Team of studio musicians during the same time period.
Buhler is a city in Reno County, Kansas, United States. In 2010, the city had 1,327 people.

Screaming Trees was an American rock band formed in Ellensburg, Washington, in 1985. The band members were Mark Lanegan (vocalist), Gary Lee Conner (guitar), Van Conner (bass), and Mark Pickerel (drummer). Later, Barrett Martin replaced Pickerel. The band played hard rock and had psychedelic influences, and was linked to the grunge genre. They made seven studio albums, five EPs, and three compilations. Screaming Trees was one of the first grunge bands, along with others like Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Nirvana, and Soundgarden. The band gained fame during the early 1990s grunge movement and was very successful. They had one top ten hit. Screaming Trees stopped making music for a long time due to difficulties making a follow-up album to "Dust." They officially broke up in 2000.

Hedemora is a town in Dalarna County, Sweden. It has 7,273 people living there in 2010. Despite being small, it is called a "city" because of its history. It is the oldest city in the county. Hedemora is from people like Jonas Nilsson, Kerstin Thorborg, Martin Matsbo, Bertil Norman, and Ulf Stenlund. The diesel engines made in Hedemora are used in many ships. For example, they are in Collins class submarines in the Royal Australian Navy and in Archer class submarines in the Republic of Singapore Navy. Clifftop Games, an independent game developer from Hedemora, created games like Kathy Rain and Whispers of a Machine.

The Indian roller (Coracias benghalensis) is a bird in the roller family. It is found in western Asia and the Indian subcontinent. It is not considered in danger and is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List. Another roller, the Indochinese roller, was once considered the same species but is now separate. Males perform flying shows during breeding season. Indian rollers are often seen perched on trees and wires in open areas like grasslands and scrub forests. The largest population is in India, and some Indian states consider it their state bird.

The 1963 Atlantic hurricane season had one of the deadliest storms on record: Hurricane Flora. The season started on June 15 and ended on November 15. It usually includes most Atlantic storms during these months. There were nine named storms that year. The first storm, Hurricane Arlene, formed between the Cape Verde islands and the Lesser Antilles on July 31. It caused some damage to Bermuda, with strong winds resulting in about $300,000 in damage (1963 USD). Other storms like Beulah, Debra, and a unnamed storm did not hit land. Hurricane Cindy hit Texas in September, causing wind damage and floods. Three people died and about $12.5 million in damage was reported. Hurricane Edith went through the Lesser and Greater Antilles, causing 10 deaths and around $43 million in damage, mostly on Martinique. The worst storm of the season was Hurricane Flora. It was a Category 4 hurricane and caused heavy rain and flooding in the Greater Antilles, especially in Cuba. At least 7,193 people died, and about $773.4 million in damage was caused. Flora is among the deadliest hurricanes in the Atlantic. Hurricane Ginny formed in October and moved erratically offshore the southeastern United States. Eventually, it hit Nova Scotia, causing at least three deaths and $400,000 in damage in the U.S. The last storm, Tropical Storm Helena, caused five deaths and over $500,000 in damage on Guadeloupe. Overall, the storms in this season caused at least 7,214 deaths and about $830.1 million in damage.

Vicente Trueba Pérez was born on October 16, 1905, in Sierra Pando, Torrelavega, Cantabria, and he died on November 10, 1986. He was a Spanish professional road racing cyclist. He is famous for winning the King of the Mountains award at the Tour de France. This means he won the overall classification in the mountains classification of the Tour de France. He also came in sixth place in the overall Tour de France rankings.
Septèmes-les-Vallons is a town in the Bouches-du-Rhône area of southern France. It is about 10. 7 kilometers or 6. 5 miles north of Marseille's center.

In music, a chord progression is a sequence of chords. This sequence is the base of harmony in Western music, from classical to modern times. It is also the foundation of popular music like pop and rock, and traditional music such as blues and jazz. In these types of music, the chord progression guides the melody and rhythm. In tonal music, chord progressions show or challenge the key of the song. In classical music theory, they are usually written with Roman numerals, like i-vi-ii-v. In popular and traditional music, chord progressions are often named with the chord's name and quality. For example, in C major, this would be written as C major–A minor–D minor–G major. In rock and blues, musicians use Roman numerals to transpose songs easily. The 12-bar blues is often based on i, iv, and v chords. So, it might be written as i–i–i–i, iv–iv–i–i, v–iv–i–i. Using Roman numerals allows a band leader to instruct musicians to play the same chord progression in any key. For instance, in C major, it would be C–C–C–C, F–F–C–C, G–F–C–C; in G major, it would be G–G–G–G, C–C–G–G, D–C–G–G. Chord progressions can be simple or complex. Pop and rock songs from the 1980s to 2010s often have simple progressions. Funk focuses on the groove and rhythm, sometimes using just one chord for a whole song. Some jazz-funk songs use just two, three, or four chords. Punk and hardcore punk use only a few chords. Meanwhile, bebop jazz songs can have complex progressions with one or two chord changes per bar.
Lourscheid is a town in the Trier-Saarburg district, in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany.

The Denisovans were an extinct species of ancient human who lived in Asia during the early Stone Age, possibly until around 30,000 to 14,500 years ago in Papua New Guinea. We know very little about them, but most of what we understand comes from studying their DNA. Scientists call them "homo denisova," "h. altaiensis," or "h. sapiens denisova." The first Denisovan was found in 2010 from a young girl's finger bone in Denisova Cave in Siberia. Her DNA showed they were closely related to Neanderthals, who also lived in the cave at times but may not have lived there together. Other Denisovan bones were later found in the same cave and in a cave in China. Denisovans lived in different environments, like forests, tundras, mountains, and jungles. They likely had dark skin, eyes, and hair, with a strong Neanderthal appearance. But they also had larger molars, similar to some ancient humans and apes. Denisovans mated with modern humans. About 3 to 5 percent of the DNA of people from Melanesia and Aboriginal Australians comes from Denisovans. They may have mated with Neanderthals as well, with around 17 percent of the Denisovan DNA coming from Neanderthals. A mix of Denisovan and Neanderthal was found, nicknamed "Denny." Additionally, 4 percent of Denisovan DNA is from an unknown ancient human species that split from modern humans over a million years ago.

Questacon, the national science and technology center, is in Canberra, Australia, by Lake Burley Griffin. It has over 200 interactive exhibits about science and technology. Questacon also has many programs for children to love science.

Peter Neville Luard Pears, born on June 22, 1910, and died on April 3, 1986, was an English singer. He worked closely with the composer Benjamin Britten for almost forty years, as both a personal and professional partner. Pears started his singing career slowly and was unsure about his path. However, meeting Britten in 1937 helped him focus on singing. After partnering with Britten, Britten composed many songs and operas tailored for Pears's voice, with Pears performing in more than ten of Britten's operas. In concerts, Pears and Britten were famous for their performances of songs by Schubert and Schumann. They also recorded many of Britten's works made for Pears. Together, they performed a wide range of music by different composers. Pears sang music from different eras, from the Tudor period to modern times. With Britten, he co-founded the Aldeburgh Festival in 1947 and the Britten-Pears School in 1972. After Britten passed away in 1976, Pears kept working at the festival and the school, where he directed singing. Pears had a special voice that some people liked, and he was very good at singing many types of music.

Edgar Lawrence Doctorow, born on January 6, 1931, and passed away on July 21, 2015, was an American writer. He was famous for writing historical fiction. He wrote twelve novels and three collections of short stories, plus one play. His notable novels include "Ragtime" (1975), "Billy Bathgate" (1989), and "The March" (2005). These novels placed fictional characters in real historical settings with real historical figures and used various storytelling methods. His stories were known for their creativity. Doctorow was praised for his bravery and imagination. Several of his works were made into films, such as "Welcome to Hard Times" (1967), "Daniel" (1983), "Billy Bathgate" (1991), and "Wakefield" (2016). His best-known film adaptation was "Ragtime" (1981) and its Broadway musical (1998), which won four Tony Awards. Doctorow received many writing awards, including three National Book Critics Circle Awards and the American Academy of Arts and Letters Gold Medal for Fiction. Former President Barack Obama called him one of America's greatest novelists.

Roger Mayweather was born on April 24, 1961, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. He was an American boxer and trainer who fought from 1981 to 1999. Mayweather won two world championships: he had the WBA and Lineal Super Featherweight titles from 1983 to 1984, and the WBC Light Welterweight title from 1987 to 1989. He also had the IBO Light Welterweight title in 1994 and the IBO Welterweight title from 1994 to 1995. Roger was the son of Bernice (Ambrose) and Theartha Mayweather. He was part of the Mayweather boxing family, which includes his brother Floyd Mayweather Sr. and Jeff Mayweather. His nephew, Floyd Mayweather Jr., is also a boxer. Roger trained Floyd Mayweather Jr. from 2000 to 2012. Under Roger's guidance, Floyd became one of the biggest names in boxing and one of the best boxers ever.

Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas is a 1997 American animated musical fantasy film. It came out directly to video. The movie is a sequel to the 1991 Disney film Beauty and the Beast. It sold 7.6 million VHS copies in 1997. This is the first follow-up to the original Beauty and the Beast film, with the next one being Belle's Magical World in 1998.
Charmes-sur-Rhône is a village in Ardèche, which is in southern France.

Aberdeen (in Lakota, "ablíla") is a city in South Dakota. It is the county seat of Brown County and is located northeast of Pierre. As of the 2010 census, Aberdeen had 26,091 people, making it the third-largest city in the state after Sioux Falls and Rapid City. Aberdeen is part of the Aberdeen micropolitan area, which includes Brown and Edmunds counties and had a population of 40,602 in 2010. The city is considered a college town, as it is home to Northern State University and Presentation College.
Anicadu is a village that is about 4 km from Mallapally town. It is in the Pathanamthitta district.

Cranbrook is a city in southeast British Columbia, Canada. It is located on the west side of the Kootenay River where it meets the St. Mary's River. Cranbrook is the biggest town in the area known as the East Kootenay. In 2016, Cranbrook had 19,259 people, and the total population of the town and nearby areas was 26,083. Cranbrook is where the Regional District of East Kootenay has its main office. It is also where several provincial offices are located, including those for the Rocky Mountain Forest District. The city has a museum called the Canadian Museum of Rail Travel, which shows old train cars from the 1900s and 1920s.

The Swedish Bandy Association is the governing body for bandy in Sweden. It organizes men's leagues like Elitserien and Allsvenskan, and women's league Damallsvenskan. The association also manages the men's and women's national teams. It was created on April 5, 1925, in Stockholm and moved from Katrineholm. Bandy came to Sweden in 1895 when Clarence von Rosen, an all-round athlete, learned about the game during a visit to Great Britain. He started Stockholm Hockeyklubb, the first bandy club in Sweden. In 1905, bandy was organized within the Swedish Ballgame Association, then in 1906 within the Swedish Football Association. On April 5, 1925, the Swedish Bandy Association was formed, representing 49 clubs. Since 1931, the association has regularly arranged national leagues in Sweden. The title of Swedish Bandy Champions goes to the winners of the final, played in March. Until 2013, the association consisted of 23 district associations, which were then replaced by six larger districts for better administration: Central Sweden, North, Stockholm, Småland, South West, and Västergötland. The association was one of the founding members of the Federation of International Bandy in 1955.
Launay-Villiers is a commune in Mayenne department, which is in western France.
Cher is a department in the Centre-Val de Loire region of France. It is named after the Cher River.

kfum örebro is a YMCA association in örebro, Sweden. It was established in 1890. In 1990, the club won the Swedish women's juniors national volleyball championship. From 1996 to 2001, the club won the Swedish national women's volleyball championship for six years in a row. The men's floorball team played in the Swedish top division during the 1990s.

Nuclear weapons testing, uranium mining, and nuclear power have often caused discussions in Australia. The country has had an anti-nuclear movement for a long time. This movement began in 1972-73 when there was debate about French nuclear tests and in 1976-77 when discussions were held about mining uranium in Australia. Several groups were formed in the mid-1970s, such as the Movement Against Uranium Mining and Campaign Against Nuclear Energy (CANE), which worked with other environmental groups like Friends of the Earth and the Australian Conservation Foundation. In 1983, the new Labor government didn't stop uranium mining as promised, which was a setback for the movement. However, by the late 1980s, uranium prices fell, and costs for nuclear power rose, so the anti-nuclear movement seemed to succeed. CANE stopped operating in 1988. Around 2003, people started supporting nuclear power as a way to fight global warming. The Australian government became more interested. However, anti-nuclear campaigners and some scientists argued that nuclear power couldn't replace other energy sources and that mining uranium might produce a lot of greenhouse gases. As of 2015, Australia had no nuclear power plants but five uranium mines. Four were in South Australia, and one was in the Northern Territory. The Olympic Dam mine in Roxby Downs was underground. The Beverley, Four Mile, and Honeymoon mines were in-situ leach mines, and Ranger was an open pit mine. Most of the uranium mined in Australia was exported. Australia had no nuclear weapons or nuclear-powered ships.

Glasgow Central is one of two main train stations in Glasgow, Scotland. It opened on August 1, 1879, by the Caledonian Railway. There are 20 stations managed by Network Rail, and Glasgow Central is the northern end of the West Coast Main Line, serving inter-city trains between Glasgow and England. The other main station is in the city center. Glasgow Central had almost 33 million passengers in 2017-18, making it the twelfth-busiest railway station in Britain and the busiest in Scotland. Network Rail says over 38 million people use it each year, with 80% being passengers. The station is a protected Category A listed building. In Simon Jenkins' book, "Britain's 100 Best Railway Stations," Glasgow Central was one of only ten stations to get five stars. In 2017, it had a customer satisfaction score of 95.2%, which was the highest in the UK.

Aerogel is a very light, synthetic material made from a gel where the liquid is replaced by a gas. It is very lightweight and does not conduct heat well. People also call it "frozen smoke," "solid smoke," "solid air," "solid cloud," or "blue smoke" because it looks like smoke or clouds and is translucent. It feels like fragile foam when touched. Aerogels can be made from different substances. Samuel Kistler created the first one in 1931 as part of a bet with Charles Learned. Aerogels are made by drying the liquid in a gel slowly without causing it to shrink. The first aerogels were made from silica, but later Kistler worked with aerogels from alumina, chromia, and tin dioxide. Carbon aerogels were developed in the late 1980s. Aerogels are not a single type of material but a group of materials with a similar structure.

James Albert Smith Leach, born on October 15, 1942, is an American academic and former politician. He was the ninth chair of the National Endowment for the Humanities from 2009 to 2013. Leach was also a U.S. Representative from Iowa from 1977 to 2007. He taught as the John L. Weinberg visiting professor of public and international affairs at Princeton University's Woodrow Wilson School. He also worked as the interim director of the Institute of Politics at the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University from September 2007 to September 2008. Leach was a Republican member of the U.S. House of Representatives for 30 years, from 1977 to 2007. He represented Iowa's 1st district until 2003, then the 3rd district until 2007. In Congress, he led the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services from 1995 to 2001 and was the chair of the Asian and Pacific Affairs subcommittee of the House Committee on International Relations from 2001 to 2006. He also started and co-chaired the Congressional Humanities Caucus. In 2006, Leach lost his re-election bid to Democrat Dave Loebsack. Notably, he introduced the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act in 1999, an important banking law from the 20th century.

edinburgh trams is a tramway in edinburgh, scotland, run by edinburgh trams ltd. It runs from york place in the new town to edinburgh airport with 16 stops. Work started in june 2008 and opened on may 31, 2014, after delays. In 2003, the project was estimated to cost £375 million. By 2008, when contracts were signed, the cost had risen to £521 million. The final cost, after delays, was £776 million. The scheme became profitable after two years and met more riders than expected. In march 2019, the council agreed to extend the line to newhaven. The extension is expected to be ready by early 2023.

Quarten is a municipality in the constituency of Sarganserland, in the canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland. It is located above Lake Walensee. The municipality includes Quarten itself and the settlements of Oberterzen, Unterterzen, Quinten, Mols, Murg, and parts of Tannenbodenalp.

In aesthetics, the uncanny valley describes how people feel when something looks almost human but not quite. It suggests that objects resembling humans imperfectly can make people feel strange and uncomfortable. This feeling is called "uncanny" or "eeriness." The term "valley" refers to a dip in how much someone likes a replica of a human, compared to a fully human-like one. Examples include robots, 3D computer animations, and realistic dolls. As virtual reality, augmented reality, and photorealistic animations become more common, people sometimes experience unease when something seems almost real but isn't quite there. The uncanny valley theory suggests that objects appearing almost human might make viewers feel cold and eerie.

Andre Kirk Agassi, born on April 29, 1970, is an American retired tennis player who was the world's number one in singles. He won eight Grand Slam titles and a 1996 Olympic gold medal. He also came in second in seven other Grand Slam tournaments. During the open era, Agassi was the first male to win four Australian Open titles. Novak Djokovic later broke this record in 2015, and Roger Federer did so in 2017. Agassi was the second male, after Rod Laver, and the fifth in history to achieve the career Grand Slam. He was the first to achieve the career golden slam, which includes a career Grand Slam and an Olympic gold medal, and the only man to win both. He also won 17 ATP Masters Series titles and was part of the winning Davis Cup teams in 1990, 1992, and 1995. Agassi was number one in the world rankings in 1995 but faced personal issues in the mid-to-late 1990s, dropping to 141st in 1997. He returned to number one in 1999 and had his best years from 1999 to 2003. He was nicknamed "the punisher" during his career. Agassi retired on September 3, 2006, after losing in the third round of the U.S. Open to Benjamin Becker. He has a foundation that has raised over $60 million for at-risk children in southern Nevada. The foundation opened the Andre Agassi College Preparatory Academy in Las Vegas in 2001. Agassi has been married to tennis player Steffi Graf since 2001.

Lothar Herbert Matthäus, born on March 21, 1961, is a German football manager and former player. He led West Germany to victory in the 1990 FIFA World Cup and was named European Footballer of the Year. In 1991, he became the first player to win FIFA World Player of the Year, and remains the only German to do so. Matthäus played in five FIFA World Cups (1982, 1986, 1990, 1994, 1998), more than any other outfield player. He also holds the record for the most World Cup games played (25). He was the captain of the West German team that won the 1990 World Cup in Italy and the German squad in the 1994 World Cup in the U.S. He won UEFA Euro 1980 and participated in UEFA European Championships in 1984, 1988, and 2000. In 1999, at age 38, he was again voted German Footballer of the Year, having won the award in 1990. Matthäus is the most-capped German player, retiring with 150 appearances (83 for West Germany) over 20 years and 23 goals. He is part of the FIFA 100 list of the greatest living football players, chosen by Pelé. Diego Maradona called him the best rival he ever had, saying this is enough to define him in his book "I Am the Diego." Matthäus was a versatile and complete player, considered one of the greatest midfielders of all time. Known for his good passing, understanding of the field, timely tackling, and powerful shooting, he often played as a box-to-box midfielder late in his career.
Karl-Josef Rauber, born on April 11, 1934, is a cardinal in the Catholic Church. He worked as a papal nuncio from 1982 until he retired in 2009.

Dwight Lyman Moody, known as D. L. Moody, was an American preacher and publisher who lived from February 5, 1837, to December 22, 1899. He founded several institutions including Moody Church, Northfield School, now called Northfield Mount Herman School, and the Moody Bible Institute. One of his famous sayings was "faith makes all things possible, love makes all things easy." Moody gave up his successful business selling shoes to focus on spreading his faith. During the American Civil War, he worked with the YMCA and Christian Commission helping Union soldiers. In Chicago, he created a major Christian center that is still active today. He worked with singer Ira Sankey to travel across the United States and the British Isles. Moody's lively speeches talked about God's love and friendship, kindness, and forgiveness instead of warning about hell and punishment.

Stephanie Murphy was born as Đặng Thị Ngọc Dung on September 16, 1978. She is an American politician from Florida. Murphy belongs to the Democratic Party. She became a member of the United States House of Representatives for Florida's 7th congressional district in 2016, after beating the incumbent, John Mica. The 7th district includes parts of Orlando and includes cities like Winter Park, Maitland, Sanford, and Altamonte Springs. Murphy is the first Vietnamese-American woman, and the second Vietnamese-American overall (after Republican Joseph Cao from Louisiana), to be elected to Congress.

Patrick Head was born on June 5, 1946. He co-founded and was the former engineering director of the Williams Formula One team. For 27 years, Head was the technical director at Williams Grand Prix Engineering. He was responsible for many innovations in Formula One racing. Head was in charge of designing and building Williams cars until May 2004, when his role was taken over by Sam Michael.

Jizya is a yearly tax historically collected from permanent non-Muslim subjects in Islamic states. It was a financial charge on non-Muslims, known as dhimmis. Only adult, free, sane male dhimmis had to pay this tax, while women, children, the elderly, sick, disabled, monks, hermits, slaves, and Musta'mins—non-Muslims living temporarily in Muslim lands—were exempt. Those who joined the military were also exempt, as were those too poor to pay. The Quran and Hadiths mentioned jizya but did not specify its amount. Early Islamic rulers likely adapted existing tax systems from previous empires, such as the Byzantine and Sasanian. The application of jizya varied over Islamic history. Together with kharāj, a similar tax, it provided a main source of revenue for some Islamic states, like the Ottoman Empire and Indian Muslim sultanates. Jizya was usually a fixed annual amount based on the payer’s financial capability. Historically, jizya was seen as a protection fee for non-Muslims, exemption from military service, permission to practice non-Muslim faiths with some autonomy, and proof of submission to the Muslim state. Some viewed it as a sign of humiliation for non-Muslims in Muslim states, while others saw it as a source of revenue. The term jizya is found in the Quran, referring to a tax from "People of the Book," specifically Jews and Christians. Other religions, like Zoroastrians and Hindus, later also paid jizya. In the Indian subcontinent, this practice ended by the 18th century and almost vanished in the 20th century. No Islamic state now imposes this tax, though some extremist groups, like the Pakistani Taliban and ISIS, have tried to revive it. Some modern Islamic scholars argue that non-Muslims should still pay jizya, giving different reasons. For example, Sayyid Qutb saw it as punishment for polytheism, while Abdul Rahman Doi viewed it as a counterpart to zakat paid by Muslims. Khaled Abou El Fadl, a moderate, argues that the dhimma system, which includes jizya, is not appropriate for modern nation-states and democracies.

Saint-Sauveur-en-Puisaye is a town in the Yonne department, which is in Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, in central France. In the early 1970s, the Château de la Folie, located north of the village (halfway to Mézilles), was used for one of the "Maharishi’s Science of Creative Intelligence" projects. People from all over the world came to live there to learn and practice transcendental meditation. They worked to renovate the buildings to turn the château into a meditation center. There were plans to create a meditation campus in the fields between the château and the Etang de la Folie, near the D7 road. However, the project was abandoned in the mid-1970s for unknown reasons.

Rodney Stephen Steiger, born on April 14, 1925, and died on July 9, 2002, was an American actor. He was famous for playing unique, often volatile characters. He was considered "one of Hollywood's most charming and dynamic stars." Steiger was closely connected with method acting, deeply embodying his roles, which sometimes caused disagreements with directors and co-stars. In 1954, he played Marlon Brando's mobster brother, Charley, in "On the Waterfront." In 1964, he starred as Sol Nazerman in "The Pawnbroker," a bitter Jewish Holocaust survivor. For his performance in "The Pawnbroker," he won the Academy Award for Best Actor. In 1967, he played a police chief in "In the Heat of the Night," opposite Sidney Poitier. This film also won five Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Actor for Steiger. Steiger was born in Westhampton, New York, to a vaudevillian father. He had a hard childhood, fleeing from his alcoholic mother at 16. After serving in World War II in the South Pacific, he started his acting career in 1947 with television roles. In 1953, he starred as the title character in the TV play "Marty," earning critical acclaim. He made his stage debut in 1946 and appeared in several plays, including "An Enemy of the People" (1950), "Night Music" (1951), "Seagulls Over Sorrento" (1952), and "Rashomon" (1959). Steiger's film debut was in "Teresa" in 1951. He appeared in films like "The Big Knife" (1955), "Oklahoma!" (1955), "Across the Bridge" (1957), and "Al Capone" (1959). After his role in "The Pawnbroker," he played a Russian politician in "Doctor Zhivago" (1965). "In the Heat of the Night" (1967) won him five Academy Awards, including Best Actor. The film also praised his performance as a Mississippi police chief who respects an African-American officer, Sidney Poitier. In the 1970s, Steiger focused on European productions. He portrayed Napoleon Bonaparte in "Waterloo" (1970), a Mexican bandit in "Duck, You Sucker!" (1971), and Benito Mussolini in "The Last Days of Mussolini" (1975). In 1979, he played a disturbed priest in "The Amityville Horror." In the 1980s, heart problems and depression affected his career, leading him to accept roles in low-budget B-movies. One of his final roles was as Judge H. Lee Sarokin in "The Hurricane" (1999), which reunited him with director Norman Jewison. Steiger was married five times and had a daughter, opera singer Anna Steiger, and a son, Michael Steiger. He passed away on July 9, 2002, in Los Angeles due to complications from surgery for a gallbladder tumor, at the age of 77. His wife at the time was Joan Benedict Steiger.

Suelli, in the Sardinian language called Sueddi, is a municipality in South Sardinia, Italy. It is located north of Cagliari. As of December 31, 2004, the population was 1,179, and it covers an area of unknown size. Suelli borders the municipalities of Gesico, Mandas, Selegas, Senorbì, and Siurgus Donigala.
remetschwil is a town in the area of baden, in the canton of aargau, in switzerland.

Suseok, also known as viewing stones or scholar's stones, refers to small naturally occurring rocks in Korea. These rocks are traditionally valued, similar to Chinese gongshi and Japanese suiseki. Suseok can be any color. Their size varies, ranging from very small, less than one kilogram, to much larger, weighing hundreds of kilograms. The term also includes rocks placed in traditional Korean gardens.

Glynis Johns, born on October 5, 1923, is a retired British actress, dancer, pianist, and singer. She was born in Pretoria, South Africa, while her parents were performing. Glynis Johns is famous for creating the role of Desirée Armfeldt in the Broadway show "A Little Night Music." She won a Tony Award for this role. She also played Winifred Banks in the Walt Disney movie "Mary Poppins," and sang songs written for her, including "Send in the Clowns" and "Sister Suffragette." She was nominated for an Oscar for her role in the 1960 film "The Sundowners." Glynis Johns is known for her deep, husky voice and her cheerful personality.
Manuele Blasi, born on August 17, 1980, is a former Italian football player who played as a midfielder.

Ketchikan is a city and the main town in the Ketchikan Gateway Borough of Alaska. It is the largest town in southeastern Alaska. The downtown area is a historic district. In 2010, Ketchikan had 8,050 people and was the fifth-largest city in Alaska. Including nearby smaller places, the population was 13,477. In 2017, Ketchikan's population was estimated at 13,754. Ketchikan became a city in 1900, making it the oldest city in Alaska. It is on Revillagigedo Island, named in 1793 by Captain George Vancouver. Ketchikan got its name from Ketchikan Creek, which flows through the town. The creek's name means "thundering wings of an eagle" or "the river belonging to kitschk" in Tlingit.

Teulada, which means "tegula" in Latin, is a municipality in the province of South Sardinia, in the Italian region of Sardinia. It is located southwest of Cagliari. One of the areas in Teulada, called Sant'Isidoro di Teulada, might be where an ancient Roman city named Bithia (also called Biotha and Biora) was located. During World War Two, on November 27, 1940, there was a short naval battle. The British ship HMS Newcastle and three other British cruisers fought with several Italian Navy ships near Cape Spartivento.

Joe Perry, born on September 10, 1950, is a musician and songwriter. He is the lead guitarist and a founding member of the rock band Aerosmith. Aerosmith is very popular and has sold over 150 million albums worldwide and 70 million in the U.S. alone. They are known as one of the best rock bands in America. Perry has his own band called Joe Perry Project. He also plays with Alice Cooper and Johnny Depp in a band called Hollywood Vampires. Perry was ranked 84th among the greatest guitarists of all time by Rolling Stone. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Aerosmith in 2001. In 2013, Perry and his songwriting partner Steven Tyler got a special award from ASCAP and were inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. In October 2014, a book about his life was published.

The Torres Strait is a waterway between Australia and the island of New Guinea. It is about wide at its narrowest part. To the south is Cape York Peninsula, which is the northernmost part of Australia. To the north is the western part of Papua New Guinea. The strait is named after navigator Luis Vaz de Torres, who sailed through it in 1606.

George Washington's first inauguration as the first U.S. president took place on Thursday, April 30, 1789, on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City. He became the first president for a four-year term. Robert Livingston, the New York Chancellor, gave Washington the oath of office. This event marked the start of the U.S. executive branch under the 1787 Constitution. John Adams became vice president on April 21, 1789, when he began his duties as the Senate's presiding officer.

Landshut is a town in Bavaria, in the southeast of Germany. It is located near the River Isar and is the capital of Lower Bavaria, one of seven administrative regions in Bavaria. Landshut is also the main city in its surrounding area, with over 70,000 people living there. It is the largest city in Lower Bavaria, followed by Passau and Straubing. It is also called "City of the Three Helmets" because of its coat of arms. Landshut is known for a big medieval festival called the Landshuter Hochzeit. Due to its closeness to Munich and the Franz Josef Strauss International Airport, Landshut has become a good place for business investments. The town has a strong industrial economy and has one of the lowest unemployment rates in East Bavaria.

Leon Jackson, born on December 30, 1988, is a Scottish singer. He won the fourth season of the British talent show "The X Factor" in 2007. After winning, Jackson starred in a web series called "Leon's Life," which was online from 2007 to 2008. His first album, "Right Now," came out in 2008 and was the 75th best-selling album in the UK that year. It had the singles "Don't Call This Love," "Creative," and "Stargazing." Jackson's first single, "When You Believe," was a cover of a song originally sung by Whitney Houston and Mariah Carey, and was written by Stephen Schwartz. It sold over 400,000 copies and was the 92nd best-selling single of the 2000s in the UK. It was also the third best-selling single in 2007. In 2007, Jackson had the best-selling single by a British male artist, beating singers like Mika, Take That, and Mark Ronson. His single "When You Believe" sold more than Leona Lewis's "Bleeding Love" and Rihanna's "Umbrella," which were in the first and second positions, respectively. As of 2016, Jackson had one UK number one single, two UK top ten singles, and one UK top five album. He spent a total of thirteen weeks in the UK singles charts top 75 with his three charted singles and nine weeks in the UK album charts top 75 with his debut album. His winning single "When You Believe" is currently the seventh best-selling "X Factor" winners single. His debut album ranks as the eighth best-selling debut album from an "X Factor" winner.

Dara Singh Randhawa, born Dedar Singh Randhawa, was an Indian wrestler, actor, and politician. He began acting in 1952. He was the first athlete to be chosen for the Rajya Sabha, India’s upper house. He worked as a Hindi and Punjabi film producer, director, and writer. He acted in films and on television. He is famous for never losing a wrestling match worldwide and later becoming a popular movie star. He played Hanuman in the 1976 film "Bajrangbali" and in "Ramayan," a series by Ramanand Sagar. In 2018, WWE inducted him into their Hall of Fame.

Todor Stoyanov Burmov (14 January 1834 – 7 November 1906) was a leading Bulgarian conservative politician and the first prime minister of independent Bulgaria. He studied at the Kiev Theological Academy and taught in Gabrovo and edited a newspaper. During Ottoman rule, Burmov and Gavril Krastevich were part of a moderate group that wanted an independent Bulgarian Orthodox church linked to Constantinople. This was opposed by stronger nationalists wanting full separation. Burmov was close to Alexander of Bulgaria and became prime minister on July 17, 1879, despite the weak conservative position. His government tried to stabilize the new country by putting Varna and other areas under martial law due to unrest. The government failed because conservatives lacked support in the assembly and fell in the same year. After leaving office, Burmov stayed active in politics. He worked as finance minister in the governments of Leonid Sobolev and Archbishop Kliment Turnovski. Later, he returned to journalism and joined Dragomir Tsankov's Progressive Liberal Party.

Pinhais is a municipality in Paraná state in Brazil. In 2018, it had 130,789 people. Pinhais became a separate municipality from Piraquara in 1992. It is part of the Curitiba metropolitan region. Pinhais is the smallest municipality in Paraná by area. The Autódromo Internacional de Curitiba and the ExpoTrade Arena are in Pinhais.
Ganbareh" is a song by the German group Sash! It came out on June 24, 2002, through Virgin Records. It was their first single from their fourth album, "S4! Sash!

A parody mass is a musical setting of the mass, usually from the 16th century, that uses parts of another pre-existing piece of music, like a fragment of a motet or a secular song, as its main melody. Unlike the other major types of Renaissance mass composition—cantus firmus and paraphrase mass—this one doesn’t mean humor. Often, non-religious songs were used, but sacred music was also common. The term "imitation mass" is suggested because "parody" was misunderstood from a 16th-century text. During the Renaissance, parody masses were very popular; Palestrina wrote many of them. In 1562, the Council of Trent banned secular material in church music. In Italy, they followed these rules closely, but in France and Germany, they ignored them. A parody mass uses a polyphonic fragment, while a paraphrase mass uses just one voice. Techniques include adding or removing voices, adding new fragments, or using the fragment at the beginning of each part. Pietro Cerone advised starting each main section with the source's beginning and using subsidiary ideas freely. Early examples include Josquin des Prez's "Missa malheur me bat," "Missa mater patris," and "Missa fortuna desperata," and Antoine Brumel's "Missa de dringhs." By the mid-16th century, most masses used this technique.

Zifeng Tower, also known as Greenland Center-Zifeng Tower or Greenland Square Zifeng Tower, used to be called Nanjing Greenland Financial Center. This very tall building was finished in 2010. It has 89 floors in total. The first 41 floors have shops and offices. Floors 49 to 71 have a hotel, many restaurants, and a public observation deck on the 72nd floor. The tower's shape helps separate these different parts. It is now the tallest building in Nanjing and in the province of Jiangsu. It is the 11th tallest in China and the 20th tallest in the world. The building was designed by the firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, led by Adrian Smith. The tower takes up 18,721 square meters. The Nanjing Greenland Intercontinental Hotel is inside the tower.

Jealousy is feeling insecure, afraid, or concerned about having less than others. It can make you feel angry, resentful, inadequate, helpless, or disgusted. In the past, jealousy and envy had different meanings, but now they are often used the same way. Jealousy happens in many relationships and even in very young babies. Some say it's a natural feeling in all cultures, while others think it's culture-specific. Jealousy can be about suspicion or reacting to something. It is often a mix of strong feelings. Researchers study jealousy, identifying what causes it. Sociologists show how cultural beliefs influence jealousy. Biologists also find unconscious factors affecting jealousy. Artists and writers have long explored jealousy in their work, and religious leaders have offered views on it based on their beliefs.

The Foucault pendulum is a simple device named after French physicist Léon Foucault. It was created to show that the Earth is rotating. This pendulum was first shown in 1851 and was the first experiment to provide clear evidence of the Earth's rotation. Today, Foucault pendulums can be found in science museums and universities as popular displays.

John Singer Sargent, born on January 12, 1856, and died on April 14, 1925, was an American artist living in Europe. He was famous for painting portraits, especially of rich and famous people from the Edwardian era. He made about 900 oil paintings and over 2,000 watercolors, along with many sketches. Sargent traveled widely, painting in places like Venice, the Tyrol, Corfu, the Middle East, Montana, Maine, and Florida. He was born in Florence to American parents and trained in Paris. He later moved to London, where he spent most of his life. Sargent gained international fame as a portrait painter. His painting "Portrait of Madame X" at the Paris Salon in the 1880s caused a scandal, which led him to move to England. There, he continued his successful career. From the start, Sargent showed great skill, especially in his brushwork. His formal portraits were grand, while his informal works showed influence from impressionism. In his later years, he grew unsure about formal portrait work and focused on murals and outdoor painting. Art historians didn't pay much attention to artists who painted royalty and famous people until the late 20th century.

Proposition 64, also known as the Adult Use of Marijuana Act (AUMA), was a 2016 vote where Californians decided to make cannabis legal. Its full name is the Control, Regulate and Tax Adult Use of Marijuana Act. People approved it with 57% support. It became a law on November 9, 2016. Recreational cannabis sales began in California in January 2018.

David Wayne Parks was an American football player who played as a wide receiver and end. He was born on December 25, 1941, and passed away on August 8, 2019. Parks was chosen first in the 1964 NFL draft from Texas Technological College (now known as Texas Tech University). He was named to three Pro Bowls and was an All-Pro two times. In 1965, he won the "triple crown" of receiving by leading the NFL in receptions, receiving yards, and touchdowns. In 2008, he was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame.

Bradford interchange is a transport center in Bradford, West Yorkshire, England. It has a railway station and a bus and coach station next to each other. The interchange was designed in 1962 and opened on January 14, 1973. It is used by most city center bus services and National Express coaches. The railway station, one of two in the city center (the other is not mentioned), is served by Northern trains. It also marks the end of the Grand Central services from London King's Cross.
" When the tigers broke free" is a Pink Floyd song by Roger Waters. The song talks about the death of his father, Eric Fletcher Waters. Eric Waters died in the Battle of Anzio during World War II.

Neon Trees is an American rock band from Provo, Utah. They gained national attention in late 2008 by opening for The Killers on several tours. Soon after, they were signed by Mercury Records. In 2010, they released their first album, "Habits." Their first single, "Animal," became very popular, reaching No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 1 on the Alternative Songs chart.

Elbert D. Glover is a researcher and writer about tobacco addiction and helping people stop smoking. He teaches at the University of Maryland College Park School of Public Health. His job title is professor and chair of the department of behavioral and community health.

Margaret Jobeth Williams, born on December 6, 1948, is an American actress and TV director. She was nominated for an Academy Award in 1994 for directing a short film called "On Hope." Since 2009, she has been the president of the Screen Actors Guild Foundation. Williams became well-known for her roles in movies like "Stir Crazy" (1980), "Poltergeist" (1982), "The Big Chill" (1983), "The Day After" (1983), "Teachers" (1984), and "The Accused" (1986). She was nominated for three Emmy Awards. The first was for her acting in the TV movie "Adam" (1983), the second for the TV miniseries "Baby M" (1988), and the third for a guest role in the sitcom "Frasier" (1993-1994). She also acted in the TV series "The Client" (1995-1996) and had regular roles in "Dexter" (2007) and "Private Practice" (2009-2011).

Versigny is a town in the Aisne department, which is in Hauts-de-France, a region in northern France. It belongs to the Communauté de Communes des Villes d'Oyse. Versigny is located between Saint-Quentin, Laon, and Chauny.

Forgetting Sarah Marshall is a 2008 American romantic comedy. It was directed by Nicholas Stoller and stars Jason Segel, Kristen Bell, Mila Kunis, and Russell Brand. Justin Bomboko Lokumba was born on September 22, 1928, and died on April 10, 2014. He was a Congolese politician and important leader. Bomboko was the foreign minister for the Congo. Bomboko also held the position of foreign minister three times: from 1960 to 1963, 1965 to 1969, and again in 1981. He died in Brussels, Belgium, at the age of 85, after a long illness.
Anthony Lane is a British journalist. He writes about movies for The New Yorker magazine.

Meccano is a model construction system created in 1898 by Frank Hornby in Liverpool, United Kingdom. It uses metal strips, plates, angle girders, wheels, axles, gears, and plastic parts connected with nuts and bolts. You can build working models and mechanical devices with it. Meccano has a factory in Calais, France. In 2013, it was bought by a Canadian toy company called Spin Master. In 1913, a similar construction set was introduced in the United States under the name Erector. In 2000, Meccano bought the Erector brand and became available worldwide.

Red is the color at the end of the light spectrum, next to orange and opposite violet. Its wavelength is about 625 to 740 nanometers. Red is a primary color in both RGB and CMYK models and its opposite color is cyan. Reds include bright, yellow-tinted scarlet and vermillion, and range from light pink to dark burgundy. Red was one of the first colors used in prehistoric art, made from ochre. The ancient Egyptians and Mayans used red for ceremonies, and Roman generals were colored red after victories. In China, red was used for early pottery and later for palace gates and walls. During the Renaissance, nobles and wealthy people wore bright red clothes made from kermes and cochineal. The 19th century brought synthetic red dyes, replacing older ones. Red became the color of revolution, like the Russian and Chinese flags after their revolutions. Red is linked to blood, making it historically related to sacrifice, danger, and bravery. In modern surveys, it is also seen as a color for heat, activity, passion, love, anger, and joy. In Asia, especially China and India, red symbolizes happiness and good fortune.

Timothy J. Davlin was the mayor of Springfield, Illinois, from April 2003 until his suicide in December 2010. He was 53 years old at the time. The mayor's job is supposed to be non-partisan, but Springfield usually follows party lines, including mayoral races. Both main political parties in Sangamon County support candidates. Davlin was supported by the Democratic Party.
José Francisco "El Nene" Sanfilippo was born on May 4, 1935. He was an Argentine football player who played as a striker.

Leishmania is a type of trypanosome that causes leishmaniasis. These are spread by sandflies. In the Old World, sandflies in the genus "Phlebotomus" transmit the disease. In the New World, sandflies in the genus "Lutzomyia" do this. At least 93 sandfly species worldwide can carry and spread the disease. Leishmania primarily infects vertebrates, including hyraxes, canids, rodents, and humans.

Mycoplasma genitalium, or Mgen, is a small, harmful bacterium that can be passed through sex. Medical reports say it is becoming more common. It can become resistant to antibiotics, including azithromycin, which was once a good treatment. Mgen was found in humans in 1981 and named in 1983. It can make both men and women sick and increase the risk of HIV. Mgen can cause urethritis in both genders and cervicitis and pelvic inflammation in women. It often has symptoms like chlamydia and is found more frequently than chlamydia and gonorrhoea in some people. Its entire genetic code was published in 1995, with 475 genes. It was thought to have the smallest genetic code until 2003. In 2008, the first synthetic genome was made from Mgen. In 2014, a protein called protein M from Mgen was described.

Huáscar Inca (Quechua: "Waskar Inka", 1503–1532) was the sapa Inca, or ruler, of the Inca empire from 1527 to 1532. He became leader after his father, Huayna Capac, and his brother, Ninan Cuyochi, both died from smallpox while fighting near Quito.

Jacques Dupont was born on June 19, 1928, and passed away on November 4, 2019. He was a French cyclist who won medals in the Olympics and races. A combat sport is a competitive contact sport involving one-on-one combat. In many of these sports, a contestant wins by scoring more points or by disabling their opponent. Some common combat sports include mixed martial arts, boxing, wrestling, judo, and kickboxing.

The Zitter Forest is in the Eifel region, in the German district of Euskirchen (North Rhine-Westphalia) and in the Belgian province of Liège (Wallonia). It's between Hellenthal (north), Dahlem (east), Kronenburg (south), and the Belgian village of Büllingen (west). The Zitter Forest is part of the Hohes Venn–Eifel nature park. To the north, the Eifel National Park borders it; to the south, the Kyll river does. The sources of the Olef, Urft, and Kyll rivers are in the Zitter Forest, which is mostly wooded and has hills like Weissstein (692 m, with ski slopes), Bärbelkreuz (662.8 m), Hühnerhöhe (659.9 m), and Kamberg (637.8 m). Villages like Giescheid, Miescheid, Neuhaus, Ramscheid, and Udenbreth in the northern part of the Zitter Forest belong to the highest parishes in the Rhineland. The Zitter Forest is one of the last homes for wildcats in Germany. A big tower called the Eifel-Bärbelkreuz transmission tower is also in this forest.

The 2011 Daytona 500, the 53rd race, happened on February 20, 2011, at Daytona International Speedway in Daytona Beach, Florida. It was the first race of the 2011 NASCAR Sprint Cup season. Trevor Bayne, racing for Wood Brothers Racing, won. Carl Edwards came in second, and David Gilliland, Bobby Labonte, and Kurt Busch were third to fifth. Bayne led before the last restart and kept winning his first cup race and Wood Brothers' fifth Daytona 500 win. The race had 16 cautions and 74 lead changes by 22 different drivers. After the race, Carl Edwards was first in the drivers' championship with 42 points, one more than David Gilliland and Bobby Labonte. A flat lens has a flat shape that lets it create images without distortion. It can have very large openings. Sometimes, the term flat lens is used for lenses that bend light in a special way. Flat lenses need a material that can bend light nearly 180 degrees over a wide angle. Recently, scientists made flat lenses using metasurfaces.

An LC circuit, also known as a resonant circuit, tank circuit, or tuned circuit, consists of an inductor (L) and a capacitor (C) connected together. It can act as an electrical resonator, similar to a tuning fork, storing energy that oscillates at the circuit's resonant frequency. LC circuits are used to generate signals at a specific frequency or to pick out a signal at a specific frequency from a complex signal, a function called a bandpass filter. They are important parts in many electronic devices, especially in radio equipment. In these devices, they are used in circuits like oscillators, filters, tuners, and frequency mixers. An LC circuit is an ideal model, assuming no energy loss due to resistance. However, any real circuit will have some energy loss because of small resistance in the components and wires. The goal is usually to make the circuit oscillate with minimal damping, so resistance is kept as low as possible. While all real circuits have some losses, studying the ideal circuit helps understand and develop physical intuition. For a circuit that includes resistance, see the RLC circuit.

Ottawa is the capital city of Canada. It is located on the south bank of the Ottawa River in eastern Ontario. Ottawa borders Gatineau, Quebec, and forms part of the Ottawa-Gatineau area and the National Capital Region. As of 2016, the city had 934,243 people and 1,323,783 in the larger metropolitan area, making it the fourth-largest city and fifth-largest metropolitan area in Canada. In June 2019, the population was estimated to be over a million. Ottawa was founded as Bytown in 1826 and became Ottawa in 1855. It is now the political center of Canada. The city's size grew through several annexations and a major change in 2001. The name "Ottawa" comes from the Algonquin word "Odawa," meaning "to trade." Ottawa has a very educated population and is home to many important institutions like the National Arts Centre, the National Gallery, and several national museums.
Der er et yndigt land" is a Danish national anthem often translated as "There is a lovely country.

Young Frankenstein is a 1974 American comedy horror movie. Mel Brooks directed it and Gene Wilder plays the main character, a descendant of Dr. Victor Frankenstein. Peter Boyle acts as the monster. Other actors include Teri Garr, Cloris Leachman, Marty Feldman, Madeline Kahn, Kenneth Mars, Richard Haydn, and Gene Hackman. Wilder and Brooks wrote the screenplay. This film is a funny version of the classic horror movie about Frankenstein. It parodies the 1930s Universal Pictures adaptations of Mary Shelley’s novel. Many props, like lab equipment, were created by Kenneth Strickfaden for the 1931 film. To make it look old, Brooks filmed the movie in black and white and used 1930s-style credits and scene changes. The music was composed by John Morris, who often worked with Brooks. The movie was very popular and well-liked by critics. It ranked number 28 on Total Film’s list of the 50 greatest comedy films, number 56 on Bravo’s list of 100 funniest movies, and number 13 on the American Film Institute’s list of the 100 funniest American movies. In 2003, it was chosen for preservation in the Library of Congress National Film Registry because it’s important culturally, historically, or aesthetically. Brooks later turned it into a stage musical with Thomas Meehan. On its 40th anniversary, Brooks said it was his best film as a writer-director, even though it wasn’t his funniest.
