The Pharaoh hound is a hunting dog from Malta. In Maltese, it is called "xoc-xoc," which means "rabbit dog." This dog is used for hunting rabbits in Malta's rocky areas. The Pharaoh hound is part of the "spitz and primitive" group classified by the Fédération cynologique internationale. It resembles other Mediterranean breeds in this group, such as the Cirneco dell'Etna, the Podenco Andaluz, the Podenco Canario, the Podenco Ibicenco, and the Portuguese Podengo. It is the only Maltese dog breed recognized internationally.

Rabbi Baruch Mordechai Ezrachi is a well-known rabbi and a leader of non-Hassidic Lithuanian Jews. He is the head teacher at Ateres Yisrael yeshiva in Bayit Vegan, Jerusalem. The RSA is a London-based British organization that aims to find practical solutions to social problems. It was founded in 1754 by William Shipley and given a royal charter in 1847. King Edward VII allowed it to use "royal" in its name in 1908. The shorter name and RSA acronym are used more often. Notable past members include Charles Dickens, Benjamin Franklin, Stephen Hawking, Karl Marx, Adam Smith, Nelson Mandela, David Attenborough, William Hogarth, John Diefenbaker, and Tim Berners-Lee. Today, RSA has members from 80 countries around the world. RSA gives out three medals: the Albert Medal, the Benjamin Franklin Medal, and the Bicentenary Medal. Winners include Nelson Mandela, Sir Frank Whittle, and Professor Stephen Hawking. RSA members are creative thinkers who contribute to knowledge, as shown by the first use of "sustainability" in the environmental sense in the RSA Journal in 1980.

Tokyo is the capital and largest city of Japan. It is located at the head of Tokyo Bay on Japan's main island, Honshu. Tokyo is Japan's political and economic center, where the emperor and national government work. In 2019, it had about 13.9 million people. The Greater Tokyo area has more than 37.3 million people, making it the world's largest urban area. Tokyo used to be a fishing village called Edo. In 1603, it became the main political center when the Tokugawa family took control. By the 1700s, Edo was one of the world's largest cities with over a million people. In 1868, after the Tokugawa rule ended, the imperial capital moved to Edo, which was renamed Tokyo, meaning "Eastern Capital." Tokyo was destroyed by a big earthquake in 1923 and bombing during World War II. After 1950, it rebuilt and grew quickly, leading Japan's economic recovery. Since 1943, Tokyo has managed the 23 special wards, some towns, and two island groups. Tokyo is the world's largest urban economy and has 36 of the Fortune Global 500 companies. It's a leading business and finance center, with a strong rail system. Notable areas include Chiyoda, where the Imperial Palace is, Shinjuku, the main administrative area, and Shibuya, a business and shopping center. Tokyo has hosted major events like the 1964 Summer Olympics and three G7 summits.

The Chaldean Catholic Church uses the East Syriac rite in Syriac for its services. It is a part of Syriac Christianity and is in full agreement with the Catholic Church. Led by the Chaldean Catholic Patriarch of Babylon, the church has its headquarters in Baghdad, Iraq, at the Cathedral of Mary, Mother of Sorrows. The U.S. Department of State reported in 2018 that Chaldean Catholics make up about 67% of Christians in Iraq. The 2019 European Asylum Support Office guidance on Iraq confirms this information.

Racewalking, or race walking, is a long-distance event in athletics. Unlike running, one foot must always touch the ground. Race judges check this. Racewalking events are usually on roads or running tracks. The distances can be up to 62 miles (100 km). In the Summer Olympics, both men and women compete in 20 km race walks. Men also compete in a 50 km race walk. These events happen on the roads. At the World Athletics Championships, there are 20 km and 50 km race walks for men and women. The IAAF World Race Walking Cup, started in 1961, has 10 km race walks for juniors, plus 20 km and 50 km events. The IAAF World Indoor Championships once had 3000 m and 5000 m race walk events but stopped them in 1993. Major championships often include 20 km race walks. Racewalking came from long-distance competitive walking in Britain, called pedestrianism. By the mid-1800s, it had most of its current rules. Since the mid-20th century, Russian and Chinese athletes have been very successful. Europe and parts of Latin America have produced other top walkers. To run fast in racewalking, athletes take shorter steps, like very fast 800 m runners.

Timpani, or kettledrums, are drums in the percussion family. They have a stretched membrane called a head over a large bowl, usually made of copper. Modern timpani can be quickly tuned to specific pitches using a foot-pedal. They are played with specialized sticks called timpani sticks. These drums were originally used in military bands but became common in classical orchestras by the late 1700s. Today, timpani are found in many types of music groups, such as concert bands, orchestras, and even some rock bands. In Italian, the plural of timpano is timpani, but in English, both terms are used. A player of timpani is called a timpanist.

Orangeburg County is in South Carolina, U.S. The 2010 census showed its population was 92, 501. Orangeburg is the county seat. Orangeburg County was formed in 1769. Jasonville is a city in Greene County, Indiana, United States. As of the 2010 census, it had 2,222 people. It is the westernmost part of the Bloomington, Indiana, metropolitan area. It is about 15 miles closer to Terre Haute than to Bloomington.

Alejo Carpentier y Valmont, born on December 26, 1904, and died on April 24, 1980, was a Cuban novelist, essayist, and musicologist. He was very influential in Latin American literature during its famous "boom" period. Born in Lausanne, Switzerland, Carpentier grew up in Havana, Cuba. He strongly considered himself Cuban. He traveled a lot, especially in France, South America, and Mexico, where he met important cultural and artistic figures. Carpentier cared about Latin American politics and often supported revolutionary movements, like Fidel Castro's communist revolution in Cuba in the mid-20th century. Because of his left-wing beliefs, he was sometimes in trouble and had to leave his country for some time. Carpentier knew a lot about music and wrote about it. He wrote a detailed book about Cuban music. He used musical ideas and writing techniques in his stories. He often included African-Cuban influences and cultural aspects in his works. Although Carpentier wrote in many genres, including journalism, radio plays, and academic essays, he is best known for his novels. He was one of the first writers to use magical realism, a technique called "lo real maravilloso," to explore the fantastical qualities of Latin American history and culture. His most famous novel, "El reino de este mundo" (The Kingdom of This World), was about the Haitian revolution in the late 18th century and showed the use of magical realism. Carpentier also used the "new world baroque" style, inspired by French Surrealism. His travels to Europe and other parts of Latin America helped him understand more about Latin American identity. His writings included elements of Latin American political history, music, social issues, and art. These works had a big impact on younger writers in Latin America and Cuba, such as Lisandro Otero, Leonardo Padura, and Fernando Velázquez Medina. Carpentier died in Paris in 1980 and was buried in Havana's Colon Cemetery with other Cuban artists and politicians.

On March 27, 2014, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 68/262. This resolution was made in response to Russia's annexation of Crimea. The title of the resolution is "Territorial Integrity of Ukraine." The resolution is not binding. It was supported by 100 United Nations member states. These states affirmed their commitment to Ukraine's territorial integrity, based on internationally recognized borders. The resolution also stated that the 2014 Crimean referendum was invalid. Eleven nations voted against the resolution. Fifty-eight countries abstained. Additionally, 24 countries were not present when the vote took place. The resolution was introduced by Canada, Costa Rica, Germany, Lithuania, Poland, and Ukraine. Before this resolution was adopted, the United Nations Security Council had seven meetings to address the Crimean crisis. However, they could not reach an agreement, as Russia vetoed a draft resolution sponsored by 42 countries.

Forbing is a community in Caddo Parish, Louisiana, United States. It is part of the Shreveport–Bossier City area.

Saydabad district is in Maidan Wardak province, Afghanistan. It is known for its pleasant climate, with hills, streams, and orchards. Saydabad city is the capital of the district. The district had many people from Kabul visiting as a retreat until the late 2000s when fighting increased. Saydabad has the most people in the province, with 114,793 residents. Nigel David Short, born on June 1, 1965, is an English chess grandmaster. He also writes articles, teaches, and comments on chess games. Since October 2018, he has been FIDE's vice-president. Short became a grandmaster at 19 years old. In January 1988 to July 1989, he was the world's third-ranked chess player by FIDE. In 1993, he was the first English player to compete in the World Chess Championship. That year, he played against Garry Kasparov in London. Kasparov won the match with a score of 12½ to 7½.

Nicole Sinclair was born on July 26, 1968. She is a British politician. She used to lead the We Demand a Referendum party. She worked as a member of the European Parliament for the West Midlands from 2009 to 2014. In June 2009, Sinclair was elected as an MEP as a candidate from UK Independence Party. Later, she left the Europe of Freedom and Democracy group, which UKIP was part of in the European Parliament. She did this because she believed some group members had extreme right-wing views, such as being against homosexuals and migrants. From January 2010 to September 2012, Sinclair was an independent MEP. During this time, she started the We Demand a Referendum party. In 2014, she lost her election. In her statement, she said: "My employers have decided, and it seems I was not successful in being re-elected as an MEP for the West Midlands region." Sinclair was the first ever transgender British parliamentarian.

In physics, a shock wave, or shock, is a disturbance that travels faster than the speed of sound in the medium. Like other waves, it carries energy and moves through a medium. However, it has sudden, significant changes in pressure, temperature, and density. In supersonic flows, an expansion fan, or Prandtl-Meyer expansion fan, can cause additional expansion. This expansion wave may meet and interact with the shock wave, creating interference. When a supersonic aircraft passes, a sonic boom is produced by constructive interference. Unlike solitons, which do not lose energy quickly, a shock wave loses its energy rapidly over distance. As a shock wave goes through matter, energy is conserved but the matter becomes more disordered, or increases in entropy. This means less energy can be used to do work, and creates drag on fast-moving objects. Shock waves are irreversible processes.

Lewis Collins, born on May 27, 1946, and passed away on November 27, 2013, was an English actor who performed in films and theater. His most famous role was playing 'Bodie' in the British TV show "The Professionals" from the late 1970s to the early 1980s.

Summerland has 11,615 people and is a town on the west side of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, Canada. It is between Peachland to the north and Penticton to the south. Kelowna, the biggest city nearby, is to the north, about 70 kilometers away, accessible by Highway 97. Vancouver is about 320 kilometers to the west. Summerland is known for "bottleneck drive," a route that connects several wineries.

Northeastern University (NU or NEU) is a private research university in Boston, Massachusetts, founded in 1898. It offers undergraduate and graduate programs on its main campus in Boston. The university also has smaller campuses in Charlotte, North Carolina; Seattle, Washington; San Jose, California; San Francisco, California; and in Toronto, Vancouver, and Portland, Maine. In 2019, NEU bought a college of humanities in London, England. About 18,000 undergraduate students and 8,000 graduate students are enrolled. NEU is a very active research university. The university has a special program called co-op, which combines classroom learning with real-world work experience. There are over 3,100 partners worldwide. Nearly all undergraduate students take part in this program. More than 76% of students receive financial aid, and the university gave out $296.2 million in scholarships in 2019-2020. Northeastern’s sports teams, called the Huskies, play in the NCAA Division I and are part of the Colonial Athletic Association. The men's and women's hockey teams play in Hockey East, while the rowing teams compete in their own leagues. The university's men's track and field team won back-to-back championships in 2015 and 2016. In 2013, the men's basketball team won its first regular season championship, the men's soccer team won its first CA title, and the women's ice hockey team won a record 16th Beanpot championship. The men's hockey team won the Beanpot in 2018, 2019, and 2020.

Esther Salas was born on December 29, 1968. She is a judge in the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey, based in Newark, New Jersey. She worked as a United States Magistrate Judge of the same court from 2006 to 2011. In 2011, she became a United States District Judge. Salas is the first Hispanic woman to serve as both a United States Magistrate Judge and a United States District Judge in the District of New Jersey.

Trapani is a city and "comune" on Sicily's west coast in Italy. It is the capital of the Trapani province. Trapani was founded by the Elymians. Today, it is an important fishing port and the main entrance to the nearby Egadi islands.

Christian Karembeu, born on December 3, 1970, is a former French professional footballer. He is now a strategic advisor for Olympiacos. During his career, he played for Nantes, Sampdoria, Real Madrid, Middlesbrough, Olympiacos, Servette, and Bastia. He was also successful with the French national team. He was born in New Caledonia, an overseas territory, and was a key player in winning the 1998 FIFA World Cup in France. He also played in France's UEFA Euro 2000. He is part of a group based in Paris planning to add a Pacific island team to the A-League.

Abdullah bin Abdulaziz Al Saud was king of Saudi Arabia and custodian of the two holy mosques from 2005 until his death in 2015. He became king after his half-brother King Fahd died. Like Fahd, Abdullah was one of King Ibn Saud's many sons. Abdullah had important jobs in politics. He became mayor of Mecca in 1961 and commander of the Saudi Arabian National Guard. He was also deputy defense minister and crown prince when Fahd became king in 1982. Abdullah was the real ruler of Saudi Arabia after Fahd had a serious illness in 1995 until he became king in 2005. During his time as king, Abdullah worked closely with the United States and the United Kingdom. He allowed women to vote and compete in the Olympics. He kept things the same during protests in Saudi Arabia during the Arab Spring. A BBC report in 2013 suggested Saudi Arabia could get nuclear weapons from Pakistan. Abdullah also helped resolve a disagreement between Pakistan's former prime minister Nawaz Sharif and general Pervez Musharraf. Abdullah had two crown princes who died before him. He named his defense minister, Salman bin Abdulaziz, as the new crown prince. Abdullah had many wives and children. He was very rich, with a fortune of about $18 billion. Abdullah died in 2015, three weeks after being hospitalized for pneumonia. He was succeeded by his half-brother, Salman.

A community is a group of people who share common values, beliefs, or traditions. They might live in the same place, like a town or neighborhood, or connect online. Communities are defined by strong relationships that go beyond family. These relationships help shape their practices, roles, and identities in social institutions like family, work, or government. Communities can be small, like a neighborhood, or large, like a country or global online groups. The English word "community" comes from Latin, meaning "shared" or "common." People in a community often share goals, beliefs, resources, and concerns, which makes them feel connected.
Laigné was a small town in the Mayenne department of France, in the northwest part of the country. On January 1, 2018, Laigné joined with the town of Prée-d'Anjou to form a new town.

Shaw is a city in Bolivar and Sunflower counties, Mississippi, United States. It is in the Mississippi Delta region. The city's name comes from an old Indian tribe nearby. In 2010, the population was 1,952.

Cantabria is an autonomous community in northern Spain with its capital city, Santander. It is part of a historic region and is bordered on the east by the Basque Country, on the south by Castile and León, on the west by Asturias, and on the north by the Cantabrian Sea. Cantabria is known as part of "Green Spain," a region between the Bay of Biscay and the Cantabrian Mountains, because of its lush vegetation due to a wet and mild oceanic climate. Atlantic winds, stopped by the mountains, influence the climate. On average, it rains about this much each year. Archaeological sites from the Upper Paleolithic period are found here. The most significant site is Altamira Cave, which dates back to around 37,000 BC. It and nine other Cantabrian caves were declared UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Cantabria became a modern province on July 28, 1778, in Puente San Miguel, Reocín. July 28 is celebrated as a holiday for its institutions. The region gained its own self-governing institutions on December 30, 1981, with the approval of the Organic Law of the Autonomy Statute of Cantabria.

James John Benzelock was born on June 21, 1947. He played ice hockey as a right winger. He was chosen fifth overall in the 1968 NHL draft by the Minnesota North Stars. However, he never played in the National Hockey League. Instead, he played 166 games in the World Hockey Association with the Alberta Oilers, Chicago Cougars, and Quebec Nordiques. Most of his career was in minor professional leagues like the CHL, IHL, and Nahl.

Imperia Tower is a complex in Moscow, Russia, located on plot 4 of the Moscow International Business Center. It includes a 60-story skyscraper and a 14-story building under construction. The 60-story skyscraper was built from 2001 to 2002, stopped in 2003, and was restarted in 2006, completing in 2011. Construction of the 14-story building began in 2013 and is expected to finish in 2018.

Chess Records was an American record company started in 1950 in Chicago. It mainly released blues and rhythm and blues music. Over time, it expanded to soul music, gospel, early rock and roll, and some jazz and comedy recordings. They were on the Chess label and on Checker, Argo/Cadet, and Cadet Concept labels. Today, all Chess records are owned by Universal Music Group and managed by Geffen Records. Founded by two Jewish brothers from Poland, Leonard and Phil Chess, the company made and released many important rock singles and albums. Musician and critic Cub Koda said Chess was "America's greatest blues label." Chess had different offices on Chicago's South Side, first at two locations on South Cottage Grove Ave. Their most famous location was 2120 S. Michigan Avenue, where the Rolling Stones recorded in 1964. The Stones recorded there again in 1965 and 1967. The building was called Ter-Mar Studios but was commonly known as Chess Studios. It is now the home of Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation. In the mid-1960s, Chess moved to a bigger space, the former Revere Camera Company building at 320 E. 21st Street. Leonard Chess died in 1969, and the brothers sold the company soon after.

Raspberry is a color like the color of raspberries. The first time "raspberry" was used as a color name in English was in 1892. In 2018, a book about the "raspberry" color was published by Coloratura.

Chondrostei is a group of fish that have some bone tissue but are mainly made of cartilage. Their ancestors were bony fish with fully developed bones. Chondrostei fish share some features with elasmobranchs, such as having spiracles, a heterocercal tail, and no scales. However, they are more similar to teleosts according to the fossil record. The 52 living species in this group are divided into two orders: acipenseriformes (sturgeons and paddlefishes) and polypteriformes (reedfishes and bichirs).

Retalhuleu is a department in southwestern Guatemala. It goes from the mountains to the Pacific Ocean. Its area is 1,856 square kilometers. In 2018, the department had 326,828 people. The capital city is Retalhuleu. The K'iche' Maya people are the largest indigenous group. Retalhuleu has some pre-Columbian ruins, like Takalik Abaj.

Typesetting is about arranging letters and symbols to create text. In older systems, physical types were used, while in digital systems, these are replaced by digital equivalents. Letters and symbols are chosen based on how a language is written and then arranged for viewing. To do typesetting, you need fonts. Fonts and typefaces are often mistaken for each other, but they are not the same. A key impact of typesetting is that it made it easier to identify the author of a work. This was problematic for people who copied without permission.

"Color of Night" is a 1994 American erotic mystery film. It was made by Cinergi Pictures and released in the U.S. by Hollywood Pictures. The movie was directed by Richard Rush and stars Bruce Willis and Jane March. Other actors include Ruben Blades, Lesley Ann Warren, Brad Dourif, Lance Henriksen, Kevin J. O'Connor, and Scott Bakula. "Color of Night" didn't do well at the box office. It was even given the worst film award of 1994. But surprisingly, it was one of the most rented films on home video in 1995. "Maxim" magazine said it had the best sex scene in film history. In 2018, Kino Lorber, with permission from Disney, released a special Blu-ray edition of the film. This version includes a commentary by the director, Richard Rush.
Stora Vikå is a place in Nynäshamn municipality, Stockholm county, Sweden. In 2010, it had 651 people living there.

Marie Eugene Francois Thomas Dubois was born on January 28, 1858, and died on December 16, 1940. He was a Dutch scientist who studied very old human ancestors and rocks. Dubois is famous for finding "Pithecanthropus erectus," which is also called "Java man." Before Dubois, some human ancestor fossils had been found, but Dubois was the first person to look for them on purpose.

Charles Frederick "Karch" Kiraly, born on November 3, 1960, is an American volleyball player, coach, and broadcaster. In the 1980s, he was a key player on the U.S. national team that won gold medals in the 1984 and 1988 Olympic Games. He later won another gold medal in 1996, which was the first Olympics to include beach volleyball. He is the only person, male or female, to win Olympic gold medals in both indoor and beach volleyball. Kiraly played college volleyball for UCLA, where his teams won three national championships under coach Al Scates. Currently, he coaches the United States women's national volleyball team.

Snap! is a German eurodance group formed in 1989 by producers Michael Münzing and Luca Anzilotti. Over the years, the group has changed its lineup. They have included American singers, songwriters, and rappers like Thea Austin, Turbo B, and Penny Ford. Snap! is famous for their songs "The Power" and "Rhythm Is a Dancer." Both songs reached number one in many countries.

Glass frogs are a type of frog in the Centrolenidae family, which belongs to the order Anura. Most glass frogs are lime green, but some have see-through belly skin. You can see their insides, like their heart and digestive system, through this skin. That’s why they are called glass frogs. Glass frogs live mainly in trees and only come down during mating season.

Benthos refers to the group of animals living on, in, or near the bottom of bodies of water like seas, rivers, lakes, or streams. This community exists in underwater environments from tidal pools to the deep ocean floor. Many creatures adapted to the pressure of deep water cannot live in the upper parts of the water. Pressure increases about one atmosphere for every 10 meters of depth. In the deep ocean, where sunlight does not reach, the primary energy source is organic matter from the upper water layers that sinks down. This decaying matter forms the basis of the benthic food chain, and most creatures in this zone are scavengers or break down dead plant and animal matter. The term "benthos" was first used by Haeckel in 1891, coming from the Greek word meaning "depth of the sea." In freshwater biology, it describes organisms living at the bottom of lakes, rivers, and streams. Another term, "benthon," is sometimes used but is redundant.

Monday is the day between Sunday and Tuesday. According to the international standard ISO 8601, it is the first day of the week. In some countries, it is the second day of the week. Monday comes from old English "mōnandæg" and middle English "monenday". This name originally means "day of the moon".

Development started in 1994 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. Due to delays and technical issues, Square switched to pre-rendered video, moving production to the PlayStation. Veterans from the "Final Fantasy" team, including Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yoshinori Kitase, and Nobuo Uematsu, worked on it. This game was the first to use full motion video and 3D computer graphics, with 3D character models over 2D backgrounds. "Final Fantasy VII" included more science fiction elements and a more realistic look. Gameplay stayed similar to previous games but added new features like materia, limit breaks, and new mini-games. Over 100 people worked on it with a big budget for development and marketing. With a large promotional campaign, it was both a commercial and critical success. It is widely seen as a landmark game and one of the most influential and greatest video games of all time. It won many game of the year awards and helped sell more PlayStation consoles, popularizing console role-playing games worldwide. Praise was given for its graphics, gameplay, music, and story. However, the English version was criticized. Its success led to better versions on other platforms, a multimedia sub-series called "Compilation of Final Fantasy VII," and the ongoing high-definition "Final Fantasy VII Remake," which came out in 2020.

Melide is a town in the Lugano district of Ticino, in Switzerland. It is very close to Monte San Salvatore mountain and sits right by Lake Lugano. A causeway in Melide to the east helps people cross to Bissone and allows a north-south highway. Melide is famous for the Swissminiatur museum, which shows miniature versions of famous Swiss buildings.

Ullared is a small place in Falkenberg municipality, Halland county, Sweden. In 2010, it had 791 people living there. The village has a big store called Gekås. Gekås is the largest store in Sweden and Scandinavia. Because the store is so big and has low prices, people often use "Ullared" and "low prices" interchangeably. Many stores offering lower prices were set up in the village since the early 1990s.

The Durrells, known as The Durrells in Corfu in North America, is a 26-episode British comedy-drama series. It is based on Gerald Durrell's three autobiographical books about his family living on Corfu from 1935 to 1939. The show started on April 3, 2016, and ended on May 12, 2019. Simon Nye wrote the series, and Steve Barron and Roger Goldby directed it. Christopher Hall produced it, with Lee Morris and Sally Woodward Gentle as executive producers. Lee Durrell, widow of Gerald Durrell and director of the Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, acted as a consultant. The series was filmed partly at Ealing Studios and Twickenham Studios in London.

Reading Rainbow was an American educational TV show for kids that aired on PBS Kids from July 11, 1983, to August 28, 2009. It had 155 half-hour episodes over 21 seasons. The show encouraged kids to read and recommended books from the library. An iPad and Kindle Fire app with the same name was launched in 2012, becoming the top educational app in 36 hours. It featured books and on-location stories, and ended with reruns until August 2009. It was the third-longest-running kids' show on PBS, after Sesame Street and Mister Rogers' Neighborhood. The show used stereo sound and ended in 2006, but the app continued to be popular. In 2014, a Kickstarter campaign raised $5.4 million to make the app available on more devices and provide free access to disadvantaged classrooms.

Paul Anthony Samuelson was an American economist born on May 15, 1915, and died on December 13, 2009. He won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1970. The Swedish Royal Academy said he had improved economic theory more than any other economist of his time. Samuelson was considered the top academic economist of the 20th century by The New York Times. Samuelson was a very influential economist of the 20th century. In 1996, President Bill Clinton honored him with the National Medal of Science for his contributions to economics for over 60 years. Samuelson believed math was important for economists and wrote a book called "Foundations of Economic Analysis." He also wrote the best-selling economics book, "Economics: An Introductory Analysis," which has been published in 40 languages and sold nearly 4 million copies. Poterba, a former head of MIT's economics department, said Samuelson left a big legacy as a researcher and teacher. Samuelson started college at the University of Chicago when he was 16 during the Great Depression. He got his PhD from Harvard at 23 and became an assistant professor at MIT at 25. He became a full professor at 32 and was later named MIT's highest faculty honor, the Institute Professor. Samuelson worked at MIT and helped make its economics department famous by bringing in other well-known economists like Robert Solow, Franco Modigliani, Robert Merton, Joseph Stiglitz, and Paul Krugman. All of them won Nobel Prizes. Samuelson advised Presidents John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson and worked for the US Treasury and President's Council of Economic Advisers. He and Milton Friedman, from the Chicago School, wrote weekly columns for Newsweek, representing different economic views.

Richard Benaud, born on October 6, 1930, and passed away on April 10, 2015, was an Australian cricketer. After retiring from international cricket in 1964, he became a well-respected cricket commentator. Benaud was a test cricket all-rounder, combining leg spin bowling with aggressive lower-order batting. He helped bring Australia back to the top of world cricket with fellow bowling all-rounder Alan Davidson in the late 1950s and early 1960s. In 1958, he became Australia's test cricket captain until 1964. He was the first player to reach 200 wickets and 2,000 runs in test cricket, achieving this in 1963. Cricket writer Gideon Haigh said Benaud was "perhaps the most influential cricketer and cricket personality since World War II." According to Sri Lankan cricket writer Harold de Andrado, Benaud was one of the greatest cricket personalities as a player, researcher, writer, critic, author, organizer, adviser, and student of the game.

"The Loud House" is an American animated comedy show created by Chris Savino. It first aired on Nickelodeon on May 2, 2016. The show is about Lincoln Loud. He is the middle child and the only boy in a house with many girls. He often talks directly to viewers, explaining the crazy situation and relationships in the family.

Most of Japan's old provinces had one or more "ichinomiya." These gave rise to place names, like the city of Ichinomiya in Aichi. Shrines of lower rank are called "ninomiya" (second), "sannomiya" (third), "shinomiya" (fourth), and so on.

Jed Allan Brown, born on March 1, 1935, and known as Jed Allan, was an American actor and TV host. He was famous for his roles as C.C. Capwell in "Santa Barbara," Don Craig in "Days of Our Lives," Rush Sanders in "Beverly Hills, 90210," Scott Turner in "Lassie," and Harold Johnson in "The Bay." He was also known for hosting "Celebrity Bowling." He passed away on March 9, 2019.

Gliese 667 cc, also called GJ 667cc, HR 6426cc, or HD 156384cc, is an exoplanet located in the habitable zone of a red dwarf star named Gliese 667 c. Gliese 667 c is part of a triple star system. The exoplanet is about 23. 62 light-years away, in the constellation of Scorpius. Scientists found Gliese 667 cc by measuring the star's movement using the radial velocity method, which involves observing changes in the star's spectrum due to the planet's gravitational pull.

Neumarkt is a "landkreis" (district) in Bavaria, Germany. It borders several districts: Nürnberger Land, Amberg-Sulzbach, Schwandorf, Regensburg, Kelheim, Eichstätt, and Roth. These districts surround Neumarkt in a clockwise direction, starting from the north.

Caryophyllaceae, also known as the pink family or carnation family, is a group of flowering plants. In the APG III system, it belongs to the Caryophyllales order and includes 33 other families like amaranthaceae and polygonaceae. This family is quite large, with over 80 genera and around 2,600 species. Mostly found in temperate climates, a few species grow on tropical mountains. Well-known plants in this family include pinks and carnations, firepinks, and campions. Many species are grown as ornamental plants, and some are widespread weeds. Most species grow in the Mediterranean and surrounding regions of Europe and Asia. The family has fewer genera and species in the southern hemisphere, but it includes the Antarctic pearlwort, which is one of the only two flowering plants found in Antarctica. The name "Caryophyllaceae" comes from "caryophyllus," an old word for "dianthus."

Terrel Howard Bell was the secretary of education under President Ronald Reagan. He served as the second secretary of education, after Shirley Hufstedler. He was born on November 11, 1921, and died on June 22, 1996.

Oberstrass is a quarter in district 6 of Zürich. It used to be its own municipality until it joined Zürich in 1893. Oberstrass has 9,494 people living there. One of two funiculars in the city is located in Oberstrass. The funicular, originally built as the Rigiblick restaurant in 1901, was turned into a theater called Rigiblick in 1984.

Hemphill is a city in Sabine County, Texas, United States. In 2010, it had 1,198 people. Hemphill is the main city in Sabine County. It is on State Highway 87, where State Highway 184 meets it. The city is surrounded by Sabine National Forest and Toledo Bend Reservoir.

Carla Bozulich, born on December 24, 1965, is an American musician from Los Angeles. She is the lead singer and founder of The Geraldine Fibbers and Evangelista. She was also a founding member of Ethyl Meatplow and Scarnella. The Geraldine Fibbers made two albums for Virgin Records. Their first album, "Lost Somewhere Between the Earth and My Home," was described as "a country feedback masterpiece" by Vice. In 2006, Bozulich started Evangelista. Her first Evangelista album, "Evangelista," was released by Constellation Records and was their first release by a non-Canadian artist. In 2007, The Sunday Times called "Evangelista" "a vivid inner darkness which shames rock's weeping millionaires." For the albums "Hello, Voyager" (2008), "Prince of Truth" (2009), and "In Animal Tongue" (2011), Bozulich used the name Evangelista. Some consistent members of the band include Tara Barnes (bassist), Dominic Cramp (keyboardist/sampler), Nels Cline (guitarist), Jessica Moss (violinist), Nadia Moss (organist), Ches Smith (drummer), and a multi-instrumentalist and co-producer. Godspeed! You Black Emperor contributed to arranging, recording, and collaborative songwriting. The line-up of Evangelista changes for each performance or recording. "Hello, Voyager" features 14 musicians. In 2014, Constellation released "Boy," an album under Bozulich's name as a solo artist. Her latest album with Constellation, "Quieter," came out in May 2018 and includes previously unreleased recordings. Bozulich has also worked with other projects like collaborations with Francesco Guerri, Novitarian/Sarah Lipstate, and Devin Sarno.
Arkelstorp is a small place in Kristianstad municipality, Skåne county, Sweden. By the end of 2010, it had 768 people living there.

A leaf blower, also called a blower, is a gardening tool that blows air out through a nozzle to move leaves and grass cuttings. It can be powered by electricity or gasoline. Older gasoline models usually had two-stroke engines, but newer models now use four-stroke engines to help reduce air pollution. Leaf blowers come in different types. Handheld models are easy to use, while backpack models with a handheld wand are more comfortable for long periods. Some larger units with wheels are pushed like a lawnmower. They can also vacuum leaves and small twigs into a bag. This makes them a blower vac.

Sheyi Emmanuel Adebayor, born on February 26, 1984, is a professional footballer from Togo who plays as a striker. He has played for several clubs, including Arsenal, Manchester City, Tottenham Hotspur, and Crystal Palace in England, and Metz in France. He also played for Monaco in Monaco, Real Madrid in Spain, Istanbul Başakşehir and Kayserispor in Turkey, and Olimpia Asunción in Paraguay. In 2008, he was chosen as African Footballer of the Year while playing for Arsenal. In 2020, he joined Olimpia Asunción, becoming the most famous signing and the highest-paid player in Paraguay’s history. Adebayor played for the Togo national team at the 2006 FIFA World Cup in Germany, which was the country's first and only appearance in the World Cup. In January 2010, his national team bus was shot at on the way to the 2010 Africa Cup of Nations in Angola. He retired from the national team after this incident. In 2013, he returned to the Togo team for the 2013 African Cup of Nations in South Africa, helping them reach the quarter-finals. He is currently Togo's all-time top goalscorer with 32 goals.

Andrzej Wojciech Suski, born on December 24, 1941, is a retired Polish Roman Catholic prelate. He was born in Płock. Suski became a priest in 1965. He was an auxiliary bishop of Płock from 1986 to 1992. In 1992, he became the bishop of Toruń. He retired in November 2017.

RMJM is a large architecture and design company. They offer services like architecture, development management, engineering, interior and landscape design, consultancy, master planning, product design, advisory services, and urban design. RMJM works with many types of clients in sectors such as mixed-use, education, healthcare, energy, residential, government, and hospitality. Specific services are provided by divisions like RMJM Sport, RMJM Healthcare, RMJM DX, and RMJM PIM. RMJM was founded in 1956 by architects Robert Matthew and Stirrat Johnson-Marshall. Their first offices were in London and Edinburgh. Since its start, RMJM has promoted modern and contemporary architecture inspired by global cultures.

Herbert "Herb" Gray Eser, born on May 25, 1931, and died on April 21, 2014, was a famous Canadian politician. He was a member of parliament for Windsor West for 40 years, from 1962 to 2002. This made him the longest-serving member of parliament in Canadian history. Gray also worked as a cabinet minister under three different prime ministers and was deputy prime minister from 1997 to 2002. He was Canada's first Jewish federal cabinet minister. He was one of the few Canadians given the honorific "the Right Honourable" not because of his position but for other reasons.
Bodcaw is a town in Nevada County, Arkansas, United States. In 2000, it had 154 people. It is part of the Hope micropolitan area.
Serres-Morlaàs is a town in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, which is in southwestern France.

Pauline Hanson's One Nation, also called One Nation or One Nation Party, is a political party in Australia. It was created in 1997 by Pauline Hanson, David Ettridge, and David Oldfield after Hanson was removed from the Liberal Party of Australia. She was not chosen as a candidate because of comments she made about Indigenous Australians. Hanson was an independent member of parliament for a year before starting One Nation. No One Nation member has ever been elected to the House of Representatives. However, one candidate was elected to the Senate in 1998 and four in 2016. In state politics, One Nation did better. In 1998, they won 22% of the vote in Queensland and 11 seats. David Oldfield was elected to the New South Wales Legislative Council but left the party. Three members were elected to the Western Australian Legislative Council in 2016. At the 2016 election, they got 4.3% of the vote in the Senate. In Queensland, they got 9.2% of the vote. Pauline Hanson, Malcolm Roberts, Brian Burston, and Rod Culleton were elected to the Senate. Hanson serves a six-year term; the others serve three years. Culleton lost his seat in 2017 after becoming bankrupt. In 2017, a court said Culleton's election was invalid due to a criminal conviction. Peter Georgiou took his place. Mark Latham, a former Labor Party leader, joined One Nation in 2018 and won a seat in 2019. The party has a strong nationalist stance. Hanson and others deny the party is racist. Hanson says criticism is not racism; real racism is when people get help just because of their skin color. A 2001 study showed One Nation had no formal ties to racist groups but had informal ties with some. These groups include the League of Rights, Australians Against Further Immigration, the Confederate Action Party, National Action, and several militia groups. In 2019, a member of the militant group True Blue Crew was linked to an One Nation candidate.

Interstate 69 (I-69) is a highway in the United States. Currently, it is made up of ten separate parts. The original continuous path goes from Indianapolis, Indiana, to Port Huron, Michigan, at the Canada–U.S. border. Other parts go southwest to the Mexican border in Texas. Some sections near Corpus Christi, Houston, Mississippi, Memphis, and Evansville have been built or upgraded and marked with signs as I-69. A section in Kentucky uses the state's existing parkway system and a part of I-24. This was approved in 2008, but only a small part is marked. The total length is about 1,700 miles. I-69 came from combining corridors 18 and 20 of the National Highway System in 1991. It includes existing roads like I-94 between Chicago and Port Huron and some connecting roads. Other proposed parts include extending I-530 from Pine Bluff, Arkansas, upgrading U.S. Route 59 from Texarkana, Texas, and adding routes in southern Texas to serve Laredo, Pharr, and Brownsville. In 2007, I-69 was chosen by the U.S. Department of Transportation as one of six key corridors, making it eligible for extra federal funding and quicker planning. However, the funding was stopped, causing some states to pause construction indefinitely.

An observation deck is a raised platform for viewing. It is usually on a tall building, like a skyscraper or observation tower. Sometimes, it is protected from the weather. Some decks have coin-operated telescopes for seeing faraway things.

Khufu, also known as Cheops to the ancient Greeks, was a king in ancient Egypt. He was the second pharaoh of the fourth dynasty, ruling in the first part of the Old Kingdom period around 2600 BC. Khufu took over from his father, Sneferu. People believe he built the Great Pyramid of Giza, one of the ancient wonders. There is only one fully preserved statue of Khufu, a small ivory figurine found in Abydos in 1903. Most information about his rule comes from writings from around 300 BC by ancient Egyptian and Greek historians. These writings show Khufu in a negative light, while his cultural influence lasted long into the Old Kingdom and the New Kingdom.

Selena etc. was a store in South Texas, offering clothes and beauty services. It was started by the famous singer Selena. Selena etc. opened in Corpus Christi in 1994. Another store was opened in San Antonio at about the same time, both with beauty salons. Selena also made clothes with designs inspired by Latin American styles, which became her signature look. She earned over $5 million from these stores. A planned store in Mexico was never opened after Selena's death in 1995. The San Antonio store closed by 1999. After Selena died, her husband Chris Pérez took over the business. In 2009, the Corpus Christi store closed. Chris Pérez sold the store for $165,000. The store had a beauty salon and sold Selena's things, jewelry, hats, and accessories. After that, the remaining items were sold at the Selena museum nearby.

Cardi B, born Belcalis Marlenis Almánzar on October 11, 1992, is an American rapper, songwriter, TV personality, and actress. She grew up in the Bronx, New York. Cardi B became famous after her posts and videos went viral on Vine and Instagram. She was on a TV show called from 2015 to 2017, helping her music career. Cardi B made two mixtapes before signing with Atlantic Records in 2017. Her first album, "Invasion of Privacy," was very successful, topped charts, and won awards. It was her first album to top the Billboard 100. Her songs "Bodak Yellow," "I Like It," and "Girls Like You" also became number-one hits. Her song "Wap" helped her achieve more record-breaking hits. Cardi B has won many awards, including a Grammy and multiple Billboard Music Awards. She is recognized as one of the most influential female rappers and is the highest-certified female rapper in the music industry.
Gothenburg Cathedral is in Gothenburg, Sweden's second-largest city. It is where the bishop of the Gothenburg diocese works in the Church of Sweden.
William Thomas Hart was born on February 4, 1929. He is a senior judge in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.

Kahuta tehsil is one of the eight subdivisions of Rawalpindi district in Punjab, Pakistan. The nearby tehsil of Kallar Sayedan used to be part of Kahuta, but later became a separate tehsil. The name Kahuta comes from the local tree "koh," which has leaves like olives, and "boota." Over time, "koh boota" was shortened to Kahuta.

Richard John Hadlee, born on July 3, 1951, is a former New Zealand cricketer. He is considered one of the best fast bowlers and all-rounders in cricket history. Hadlee was given an MBE in 1980 and became a knight in 1990 for his contributions to cricket. He was the chairman of New Zealand's board of selectors. In December 2002, Wisden chose him as the second greatest test bowler of all time. In March 2009, Hadlee was honored as one of the twelve local heroes, and a bronze statue of him was revealed outside the Christchurch Arts Centre. On April 3, 2009, he was inducted into the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame. Richard Hadlee is the most famous player from the Hadlee cricket family.

Japan surrendered to the Allies on August 15, 1945, and signed the formal surrender on September 2. This ended World War II. By July 1945, Japan's navy could no longer fight, and an invasion was likely. The United States, Britain, and China asked Japan to surrender without conditions, threatening destruction if they didn't. Japan's leaders secretly asked the Soviet Union to help negotiate better terms privately. However, the Soviets were preparing to invade Japanese-held areas. On August 6, the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. The next day, the U.S. president warned Japan to surrender. On August 8, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria. The following day, the U.S. dropped a second atomic bomb on Nagasaki. Emperor Hirohito then ordered Japan to accept the Allied terms. He announced this on August 15 in a radio address. After some secret talks, Japan signed the surrender document on September 2 on a U.S. battleship. The war officially ended in 1952, when a peace treaty took effect.

Kathleen Rachel Makinson, born White, lived from February 15, 1917, to October 18, 2014. She was an Australian physicist. Makinson became the first woman to hold the position of chief research scientist at CSIRO, Australia's research organization.

Heian-kyō was a former name for the city now known as Kyoto. It was the official capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, from 794 to 1868, with a short break in 1180. In 794, Emperor Kanmu moved the imperial court to Heian-kyō from nearby Nagaoka-kyō. This marked the start of the Heian period in Japanese history. Heian-kyō was built like the Tang Dynasty capital Chang'an (modern-day Xi'an). The city stayed the main political center until 1185, when the Minamoto clan defeated the Taira clan in the Genpei War. After this, the government moved to Kamakura and established the Kamakura Shogunate. Even though power was controlled by the samurai class for three different shogunates, Heian-kyō remained the location of the imperial court and seat of power. So, it stayed the official capital. Even after the imperial court moved to Tokyo in 1868, Kyoto is still seen as the official capital because there is no law making Tokyo the capital. Kyoto celebrated its 1200th anniversary in 1994 with various events.

The globe artichoke, also called French artichoke or green artichoke in the U.S., is a type of thistle grown for food. Its edible part is the flower bud before the flower blooms. This bud is a cluster of small, yet-to-bloom flowers with many leaves, and an eatable base. When the buds open, the plant becomes tough and not very tasty. Another kind, the cardoon, is also a thistle from the same species. It's a plant that grows in the Mediterranean. Both wild and cultivated versions exist.

Sportverein Grödig is an Austrian football club from Grödig. The team plays in the Austrian Regional League West, which is the third level of Austrian football. Grödig were pushed down from the Austrian Bundesliga at the end of the 2015-16 season. They went down two levels to the Regional League West because of money problems.

Singapore began sending athletes to most summer Olympics starting in 1948. That year, it was a separate British crown colony, just over three months before the 1948 summer Olympics began. The country kept sending teams until 1964, when it was part of Malaysia and joined a combined team. In 1965, Singapore gained full independence and continued to join the summer Olympics every year except 1980. That year, Singapore didn't compete because it joined a large Olympic boycott. The country made its winter Olympic debut in 2018, when Cheyenne Goh competed in short track speed skating. Singapore has won five Olympic medals in total. The first was in 1960, the second in 2008, and the third and fourth in 2012. In 2016, they won their first gold medal and their fifth overall.

Donnan Allan Pennebaker, often known as D.A. Pennebaker, was an American documentary filmmaker who lived from July 15, 1925, to August 1, 2019. He made movies about performing arts and politics and was one of the first to use direct cinema techniques. He won a special Oscar award in 2013 for his work. Pennebaker is also known as a key filmmaker who captured the spirit of the 1960s counterculture.

Pullman is the biggest city in Whitman County, Washington. It is in the southeastern part of the state, in the Palouse region of the Pacific Northwest. The city had 29,799 people in 2010 and around 34,506 in 2019. Pullman was first called Three Forks, but it was renamed after the industrialist George Pullman in 1884. It is famous for its fertile land and agriculture, with many hills and fields growing wheat and legumes. Pullman also has Washington State University, a big school where people do research. It's home to Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories too. Pullman is close to Moscow, Idaho, where the University of Idaho is. People can fly out of the Pullman-Moscow Regional Airport.

International Left Handers Day is celebrated on August 13 each year to honor left-handers. It was first observed in 1976 by Dean R. Campbell, founder of Lefthanders International, Inc. This day aims to celebrate being left-handed and raise awareness about the challenges and benefits of it in a right-handed world. It highlights the uniqueness of left-handers, who make up about 7 to 10 percent of the global population. The day also brings attention to issues faced by left-handers, such as special needs for left-handed children, and the higher chance of left-handers developing schizophrenia. There are roughly 708 million left-handed people worldwide. Men are more likely to be left-handed than women. In the past, left-handers were sometimes forced to use their right hand. For example, former U.S. President Harry S. Truman was made to write right-handed as a child. On International Left Handers Day, we can help raise awareness of the difficulties left-handers face.

Bayzo was born on April 3, 1947, in St. Paul's Bay, Malta. He was a singer known for his special voice. One of his famous songs is "Qalu Li Raw." This song was performed at the Malta Song Festival in 1986. Bayzo lived until February 1, 2018.

Jiang Yi-huah, born on November 18, 1960, is a Taiwanese politician. He was once the premier of the Republic of China (ROC). On November 29, 2014, he quit his job and Mao Chi-kuo took over on December 8, 2014. Before becoming premier, Jiang was the vice premier from 2012 to 2013. He also served as minister of the interior from 2009 to 2012 and minister of the Research, Development, and Evaluation Commission of the Executive Yuan from 2008 to 2009.

Iran is divided into thirty-one provinces. Each province has a local center, usually the biggest city in the province, called the capital (in Persian: "markaz"). The provincial authority is led by a governor-general (in Persian: "ostāndār"). This governor-general is appointed by the minister of the interior and needs the cabinet's approval.

Voltage, which is the difference in electric potential between two points, is the work needed to move a charge between those points. In the International System of Units (SI), voltage is measured in volts. Voltage is like electric pressure, and it is represented by "V" or "U." A voltmeter can measure the voltage between two points. Voltage can be caused by electric charge, electric current through a magnetic field, or time-varying magnetic fields. Voltage can also represent energy, like in a battery (electromotive force) or energy used in an electrical circuit.

Wisconsin's 8th congressional district is in the northeastern part of the state. It is now represented by Mike Gallagher, a Republican. Gallagher won the seat in 2016 when Reid Ribble stepped down. The 8th district has had just two Catholic priests as its representatives, one of them, Robert John Cornell. The district was mostly Republican for a long time. Only four Democrats represented it in the 20th century. But it became more competitive in the 1990s. In 2004, Republican George W. Bush got 55% of the vote, while in 2008, Democrat Barack Obama got 53.6%. Steve Kagen, a Democrat, represented the district from 2007 to 2011. After Kagen lost in 2010, Republicans have won the seat by big margins in every election since 2012. The 8th district includes Green Bay, Appleton, and the Door County peninsula. It also includes most of Wisconsin's counties bordering Michigan, before recent changes.

Merced County is in the northern San Joaquin Valley of California. As of 2010, it had 255,793 people. The main city is Merced. The county is named after the Merced River. Merced County includes the Merced area, part of the Modesto-Merced region. It is north of Fresno County and Fresno, and southeast of Santa Clara County and San Jose.

Fish processing is about handling fish and fish products from catching to delivery to customers. It includes both wild-caught fish and those from fish farms. Big fish processing companies often have their own fishing or farming operations. Products are usually sold to grocery stores or intermediaries. Fish are very easy to go bad. The main goal of fish processing is to keep them fresh. This goal is important during other processing steps too. Fish processing can be divided into two main parts. One is fish handling, which prepares raw fish. The other is making fish products like frozen and canned ones. Humans have been processing fish for a long time. Today, fish processing happens on fishing boats, processing vessels, or at plants.

Lars Mortimer was born on March 22, 1946, and he died on August 25, 2014, in Alfta, Halsingland. He was 68 years old. Lars Mortimer was a Swedish comic artist who created comic strips like "Bubo" and "Häge."

Cagliari was a province in Sardinia, an autonomous region in Italy. Its capital was Cagliari. The province had an area and a population of 543,310 in 2001. It included 71 "comuni" (singular: "comune"). In 2016, the province was changed by a regional decree. It became the metropolitan city of Cagliari.
A blast injury is a type of physical harm caused by an explosion. This can happen from a high-order or low-order explosive. The damage is worse when the explosion takes place in a small area.

Rachel Emily Nichols, born on January 8, 1980, is an American actress and model. She started modeling while studying at Columbia University in New York City during the late 1990s. She began acting in the early 2000s and was in the romantic drama "Autumn in New York" in 2000. She also had a one-episode role in the fourth season of "Sex and the City" in 2002. Her first big acting role was in the comedy film in 2003. She became more famous for playing Rachel Gibson in the last season of the TV series "Alias" from 2005 to 2006 and for her part in the horror movie "The Amityville Horror" in 2005. Nichols got her first main role in a film in 2007 in the thriller "P2." She gained more popularity with the science-fiction action movies "Star Trek" in 2009 and another film also in 2009. She appeared in other movies like "The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants 2" in 2008, "Conan the Barbarian" in 2011, "Alex Cross" in 2012, "Raze" in 2013, and "Inside" in 2016. She also starred in the TV show "Continuum" from 2012 to 2015. She had notable roles in "Criminal Minds" from 2010 to 2011, in the fourth season of "Chicago Fire" from 2015 to 2016, and in the fourth season of "The Librarians" from 2017 to 2018. She also played a Gestapo officer named Martha in five episodes of "The Man in the High Castle."

Mullsjö AIS is a floorball club in Mullsjö, Sweden. It was created on November 1, 1989, by people from the Mullsjö Mission Covenant Church. On March 2, 2008, the men's team won a spot in Sweden's highest division.

Atlantis is a made-up island from an old story by Plato. In this story, Atlantis attacks Athens, which represents Plato's ideal state. Athens wins the fight. The tale ends with Atlantis sinking into the Atlantic Ocean because the gods were angry. This story had a big influence on writers, who used it in books about perfect places. People in the 1800s thought Plato was telling a true story. They wrote books about Atlantis based on this. Plato gave few clues about when the story happened—more than 9,000 years ago—and where—past the Pillars of Hercules. These hints led to lots of guessing about Atlantis. Today, most experts agree the story is not real. They think Plato made it up to teach a lesson. Some say he might have gotten ideas from stories about ancient battles or disasters, like the destruction of Helike in 373 BC. Others think he used the tale of Gyges, a character in one of Plato's other stories.

Jose C. Vitug, born on July 15, 1934, is a Filipino lawyer and jurist. He became an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines in 1993, appointed by President Fidel Ramos. Vitug stopped working there in 2004. He started the Angeles University Foundation School of Law. He also works as an independent director at Abbotie Equity Ventures.

Monster Buster Club is a French-Canadian children's science fiction TV show. It was made by marathon media, an French company, and Image Entertainment Corporation, a Canadian animation studio. It also worked with Jetix Europe. The show first aired on June 2, 2008, on Jetix in Europe. It came on June 9, 2008, in the United States and Asia on May 3, 2008. In Canada, it premiered on YTV. A total of 52 episodes were created.

The Caledonian Railway (CR) was a major Scottish railway company. It was formed in the early 1800s with the goal of connecting English railways to Glasgow. Over time, it expanded its network and reached Edinburgh and Aberdeen. It had many branch lines around Glasgow. In 1923, it became part of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway. Many of its main routes are still used today. The original line between Carlisle and Glasgow is now part of the West Coast Main Line.

The British Rail Class 304 electric multiple units were made for use in suburban areas on the first parts of the West Coast Main Line electrification between Crewe and Manchester/Liverpool/Rugby. Initially called AM4 units, they later became Class 304 under the TOPS numbering system. They operated on most of the West Coast Main Line. These units followed the 1959 design for AC electrical multiple units and looked similar to Class 305, Class 308, and 1,200V DC Class 504 units. None of these units survived to be preserved, and all were eventually scrapped.

Sir Herbert Edwardes was born on November 12, 1819, and died on December 23, 1868. He was a British man who worked as an administrator and soldier in the Punjab area of India. He is famous as the "hero of Multan" because he played a key role in helping the British win the second Anglo-Sikh War.

STS-122 was a NASA space shuttle mission to the International Space Station (ISS). This was the 24th shuttle mission to the ISS and the 121st space shuttle flight overall. The mission, also known as ISS-1E, aimed to deliver the European "Columbus" science laboratory to the station. It also brought back to Earth an astronaut named Daniel M. Tani, who was part of Expedition 16. Tani was replaced by French astronaut Léopold Eyharts, representing the European Space Agency. After landing, the shuttle "Atlantis" was prepared for the final servicing mission of the Hubble Space Telescope, STS-125. The original launch date was December 6, 2007, but it was postponed due to sensor problems. After multiple attempts, the shuttle finally launched on February 7, 2008.
The Cathedral of Solsona is in Solsona, Catalonia. The apse, which has a Roman style, likely dates back to the 12th century.

In mathematics, a continuous function doesn't have sudden changes. Small changes in the input lead to small changes in the output. If a function has sudden changes, it is called "discontinuous." Before the 19th century, mathematicians used general ideas about continuity, and later, specific rules like the epsilon–delta definition were developed. In topology, continuity is studied in a more general way. When we talk about functions with real numbers, there's a stronger type called uniform continuity. The article also covers continuity for functions between metric spaces. In order theory, especially in domain theory, there's a type of continuity known as Scott continuity. For example, a function showing a flower's height over time would be continuous. But a function showing a bank account's balance over time would be discontinuous, as it changes suddenly when money is added or taken out.
